Shorter pieces include Heather Ale, a Galloway legend of a secret brew, and Christmas at Sea, a sailor's bleak holiday. Stevenson writes in strong, rolling verse, keen on place and fate. The book shows his gift for tale-telling in meter, from Pacific isles to Scots glens.
41456-guilty-bonds:
Guilty Bonds, a novel by William Le Queux, appeared in this New York edition in 1895. The tale is told in the first person by a young man of means. He has lost his father, gained a large fortune, and lives in part by his pen. His friend Robert Nugent is a journalist. The first chapter is called The Mystery of Bedford Place.

The opening shows the two men at cards in a London club, then walking home in the small hours. They cross quiet streets by the Thames as dawn nears. The calm start sets up a tale of crime and secret guilt. Readers who like late Victorian mystery tales will find a rich London setting and a narrator drawn into dark events.
41466-the-daffodil-fields:
The Daffodil Fields is a long narrative poem by John Masefield, first set up in 1913 and reprinted often, shown here in the Macmillan edition. It begins beside a hill spring on the ground where Ryemeadows Farm once stood, tracing the brook past woods, farms, and poachers' wires to three fields of wild daffodils.

From that bright ground the tale of love, work, and death unfolds in Masefield's rolling verse. The farm some call the Poor Maid's Hall anchors the story. Masefield had won fame with The Everlasting Mercy, and this poem shares its earthy pity for country folk whose lives turn on small fields.
41497-reynolds:
Bensusan wrote this life and study of Sir Joshua Reynolds, the painter of 1723 to 1792, for the Masterpieces in Colour series edited by Leman Hare. Jack published it at London and Stokes at New York. Eight reproductions in colour illustrate the book, beginning with Mrs Hoare and Child from the Wallace Collection as frontispiece.

The plate list continues with Nelly O'Brien, The Three Graces, The Age of Innocence, and Lord Heathfield, all in the National Gallery. Then come a portrait of two gentlemen, a portrait of a lady and child, and the Duchess of Devonshire and Child at Chatsworth House. Bensusan remarks on the frontispiece that its flesh painting is very fine and the handling of the dress remarkably free. His text opens on men born to every generation who approach life with complete assurance of distinction in whatever work they choose.
41527-highland-targets-and-other-shields:
Highland Targets and Other Shields, by James Drummond, was printed in Edinburgh in 1873 for private use in fifty copies. The paper was first read to the Society of Antiquaries of Scotland in April 1871. Drummond says that Scottish arms and armor have had far less study than like gear in England or on the Continent.

His focus is the targaid, or target, the round shield borne by Highland fighters into recent times. He notes that even Highlanders tend to guess that such shields are of vast age, with no proof. Good drawings, he argues, are key, since the carved detail gives a shield its mark. The study treats form, ornament, and use.
42008-telling-fortunes-by-cards:
Telling Fortunes by Cards is a guide to the art of card fate, out in nineteen fourteen. It was drawn from true wells by one hand and shaped by a next. The front page calls it a meet of the old and new ways of Arab seers, of sibyls, and of the Romany folk. Plain cases and plain steps let any man learn the art with ease, it claims.

A tale of a famed queen of France opens the book. Ways of play run from an old oracle through scores of named forms, stars and short stars. Word books give the sense of each card, first in brief and then in long. Deals by threes, fives, and sevens close the craft parts. Games of love with cards end the book.
4205-berlin-and-sans-souci-or-frederick-:
L. Muhlbach's historical romance turns to Frederick the Great and the dancer Barbarina at Sans-Souci. Resting half reclined on a small crimson divan, arms crossed over her breast, Barbarina fixes blazing eyes on the intruders and sits petrified in stubborn silence.

She has the glance of a panther prepared for death or to slay her enemy, while the king stands quiet and waiting. Muhlbach builds court, love, and power around the Prussian king's circle. Readers who enjoy royal romance will find a dramatic tale of a dancer who would not bend.
42365-the-breath-of-the-gods:
Sidney McCall wrote The Breath of the Gods, a novel for Little, Brown at Boston in 1905. A note at the front says no figure in the book is drawn from any real person. All figures are made up, and no event rests on a real one. In the genre studies alone, McCall says, realism is tried. Most talk put in the mouths of peasants and servants was heard by the writer firsthand. The book is given, for faith and reverence, to Yamato Damashii.

The tale opens at the stone house of Senator Cyrus Todd, much like its neighbors. A map of the house and garden of Tetsujo is the book's one plate. McCall had won note with Truth Dexter before this work. The novel turns to Japan, its spirit, and the clash of East and West in that hour.
42415-storm-warriors-or-life-boat-work-o:
John Gilmore, rector of Holy Trinity, Ramsgate, wrote Storm Warriors, or Life-Boat Work on the Goodwin Sands, printed in London in 1875 in its fourth thousand. Gilmore gives the book to the memory of his father and his eldest brother, both brave sailors of the Royal Navy. A tale from his article in Macmillan's Magazine stands behind the book.

His preface opens with a boy at Ramsgate pier-head hoping to be wrecked on the Goodwins, so the life-boat men may save him. An admiral sent a guinea for each of the men after reading of their deeds. A Kentish squire sent the same, proud of the men of his county. Letters came from Australia and America as the stories spread.
42427-the-kingdom-of-slender-swords:
Hallie Erminie Rives wrote this novel, The Kingdom of Slender Swords, printed at Indianapolis with copyright in 1910. Baron Makino adds a foreword, and A B Wenzell drew the pictures. Chapter heads place much of the tale in Japan, with a land of the gods, a street of prayer, and a shrine of the fox-god. Names in the heads include Barbara, Daunt, and Austen Ware.

The tale runs to fifty chapters, from Where the Day Begins to the final alarm. Heads hint at a web, a trespasser, a silent understanding, and a flight. War cries of Banzai Nippon and a golden crucifix sit side by side in the list. The mix points to love, faith, and danger in a Japan seen by Western guests.
42444-the-face-of-the-fields:
The Face of the Fields is a set of notes on wild life by Dallas Lore Sharp, out in March of nineteen eleven. Sharp was known for books on wild life near home. The book is given to a friend named as a true man of lore. All but two of its parts first ran in a famed press sheet.

Parts treat eggs of the turtle, the edge of night, the lack of skunks, and the craft of the wild life hand. One part treats a famed old hand of that craft. The first part opens with a flash of gray wings and a cry of pain in a hen yard. A marsh hawk swings up into the fall sky with its prey, swift as a bolt. The hand runs to the young hen and finds her dead, her neck laid open as by a knife.
4248-the-problem-of-the-ohio-mounds:
Cyrus Thomas wrote this study to answer a much-debated question. Who built the great earthworks of Ohio? Were they the work of a lost race, or of native peoples known to history? He weighs historical evidence, burial customs, and pottery. He also weighs stone tools and the layout of the mounds.

Later chapters test the case for the Cherokees as mound builders. They cover links to the Tallegwi of tradition. They compare mound burials with Indian practices, such as burial in dwellings and the use of fire. Thomas argues from close comparison rather than legend. The book remains a clear statement that the mounds belong to Indian history.
42495-the-channel-islands:
Joseph E Morris wrote The Channel Islands for Adam and Charles Black at London in 1911, in the Beautiful Britain series. Three chapters cover Jersey, Guernsey, and then Alderney, Sark, and the lesser islands. Twelve plates include St Peter Port, Mont Orgueil Castle, and La Corbière lighthouse.

Standing on Mont Orgueil's battlements, Morris can see the Norman coast twenty miles off, with the twin spires of Coutances inland. The islands, he notes, are the last remnants of the ancient Norman dukedom still held by the English Crown. Fields of chrysanthemums, the Coupée at Sark, and the Casquet rocks fill the plates. The tone is that of a fond guide for summer visitors.
42527-trails-through-western-woods:
Trails Through Western Woods is a book of treks and tribes by Helen Sanders. Photos by the author dress the text of her west road tales. A front print shows a calm lake named for a chief of the place. The book came out in the year nineteen ten.

A gift page sends the book to the west that fades and the brave free life. Parts treat a mild tribe, charm lakes, and shrine posts of the north west. The pass of the great herds earns a long sad part in the list. High cloud trails, a small saint stream, and slide scars mark the climbs. Soft grief for a lost wild tunes the keen eye travel tale.
42566-the-spook-ballads:
The Spook Ballads is a volume of comic verse by Theodore Parkes, issued in a popular edition at two shillings. The press notices printed in front reach for high company. Ingoldsby, Thomas Hood, and Gilbert are the names that occur to one reviewer in placing Parkes. The book deals largely with ghosts and legends.

A dash of diablerie runs through it, of the sort Ingoldsby loved. The Publisher's Circular finds the same thorough abandonment to the humour of the thing. Another notice hopes Parkes may give the age a modern Ingoldsby, and praises the rugged force of The Girl of Castle-something in its list. The ballads are rollicking, verbal, and pictorial fun: spooks made to caper in rhyme for the fireside, not to chill it.
42641-friends:
Friends is a book of poems by Wilfrid Wilson Gibson, published by Elkin Mathews in London in 1916. A list of Gibson's earlier books stands before the poems. Battle, Thoroughfares, Borderlands, and Daily Bread are named there. The volume is dedicated to the memory of Rupert Brooke. A short poem under the dedication mourns Brooke's going. It is dated the twenty third of April 1915. His young eyes shone with a sudden glory, Gibson writes. The contents list Rupert Brooke as the first poem.

A second poem honours William Denis Browne, another fallen friend. Tenants, Sea-change, Gold, and The Old Bed follow in the contents. The Orphans and The Pessimist stand among the titles. The first poem pictures Brooke's face lifted to a golden sky. Flame on flame kindled his throat and hair to gold. War losses shadow this book of friendship and memory.
42726-the-philippine-islands:
Philippine Islands is a survey of the islands by Ramon Reyes Lala, a native of Manila. The book was issued at New York in eighteen ninety nine and carries many pictures. It is dedicated to Admiral Dewey and to President McKinley. Dewey's victory over the Spanish fleet, the dedication says, began a new era for the author's country.

The contents move from an early history of discovery and conquest onward. The British occupation takes a chapter, then the Spanish colonial government. Church rule in the colony is treated next, with its clashes between church and state. The various tribes of the islands fill a long section. Their dress, manners, and weddings are described, with notes on mixed descent groups and on tribes of the interior. Manila itself is pictured at length near the end.
42739-the-migration-of-birds:
The Migration of Birds, by T A Coward, was published at the Cambridge University Press in nineteen twelve. It stands in the Cambridge Manuals of Science and Literature. Putnam's issued it in New York. Coward was a careful field ornithologist, and his manual sums up what was then known.

The chapters ask first what migration is and why it began. Temperature, food, light, and the glacial epoch all enter the argument. Routes, coasting lines, and land bridges follow, then the height and speed of flight. Orientation and route finding puzzle him, as they still do. Maps trace the American golden plover's immense journey and its evolution. Perils from lighthouses and storms close the survey. Coward wrote before ringing was common, and his caution shows on every page.
42950-prophetical-educational-and-playin:
Prophetical, Educational and Playing Cards, by Mrs. John King Van Rensselaer, was published in London in 1912. The author had earlier written The Devil's Picture Books, a history of playing cards.

The book traces cards back to signs, rods, tablets of fate, and the gods of writing in Egypt and the East. Chapters treat the tarot pack and its picture cards, the Book of Thoth, and the fortune-telling uses of cards over the ages. Later chapters turn to teaching cards and to card games in many lands, from Persian and Swedish packs to Austrian tarok. Pictures of early tarot cards face the opening pages, and the text quotes many older writers on the subject.
43051-up-the-mazaruni-for-diamonds:
Up the Mazaruni for Diamonds is a trek tale by William LaVarre. The author bills himself a veteran scout on the front page. The book came out in Boston in the year nineteen nineteen. A front note from a great name praises the trek as sound and keen.

The Mazaruni is a wild river in the Guiana lands of South America. Gem hunts up that stream form the whole task of the young scout. His praise note says hard work and ground work made his trek pay. Book lore and past treks were his school for the rough field craft. Falls, bush camps, and gem gravel bars mark the road of the tale.
43287-father-thrift-and-his-animal-frien:
Joseph Sindelar wrote this children's book of 1918, with pictures by Helen Geraldine Hodge. Its hero is a queer little old man named Thrift, no father at all, who has lived in his quaint town so long that grandparents remember sitting on his lap as children.

The contents take him into the forest, where chapters introduce Great Gray Owl, the busy beavers, gray and red foxes, and what made the bear sick. Later come two bad boys, trouble in the forest, and lessons from insects and worms. Father Thrift is the village's all-round helper, loved for his good advice. Young readers get gentle nature tales with a kindly guide.
43543-adventures-in-the-moon-and-other-w:
Adventures in the Moon and Other Worlds was printed at London in 1836. A journey to the moon opens the contents. Mahomet and the spider, a dialogue, follows. A letter from posterity to the present age and the answer from the present age to posterity stand next. The sleeper and the spirit and a dispute between the mind and the body come after.

Alcibiades and truth released close the main list, with the two evil spirits and the judgment of Mahomet in dialogue at the end. Among inquisitive persons there has always been a wish to know something about the moon, its surface, its people, and their manners, the journey begins. Several philosophers have construed its spots into mountains to satisfy this curiosity. Lunar voyages and moral dialogues share one playful volume.
43581-fruits-of-the-hawaiian-islands:
Fruits of the Hawaiian Islands is a book of plant lore by Gerrit Parmile Wilder. It is a new form of a work first made in nineteen hundred and six. One mint and twenty one half tone plates stand in it. Each plate has its own words past it. The rights were held in two years, the last in nineteen eleven. The book was put out at the chief town of those isles that year.

The index is a roll of the fruits in their lore names. A great pear of the south, with its flesh like a rich cream, heads the roll in three plates. The seed fruit of the old book of faith, in two plates, comes next. The fig in three kinds, plain, white, and sour, stands past them.
43640-lost-in-the-wilds:
Eleanor Stredder wrote a Canadian story published by Nelson at London, Edinburgh, Dublin, and New York in 1893. It opens in Acland's hut, and the contents promise buffalo hunting, a first snowstorm, a Cree Indian named Maxica, a birch-bark hut, and a search for supper on the empty prairie.

The first chapter sets an October sun going down over a wild waste of waving grass, scarlet hips gleaming where summer's roses shed their leaves. A Red River cart driver bids the boy beside him look up: the sky darkens with wild geese flying south, telling of snow to come. Prairie fires shoot up against the Touchwood Hills. A dog-sled, the hunters' camp, and a rescue fill out the tale.
43773-shifting-sands:
Shifting Sands is a Cape Cod novel by Sara Ware Bassett of Massachusetts. Penn Publishing of Philadelphia issued it with rights in 1933. A jacket note tells the plot before chapter one opens the tale. Stanley Heath, a stranger, runs his power boat aground on the shoals. Days of fog cover the treacherous Cape Cod coast in that wreck.

Heath stumbles into the Homestead and into Marcia Howe's life in Wilton. Marcia is a young widow half the village men already love. From his clothing falls a leather case crammed full of gems. That puzzling possession pivots the whole story of suspicion and trust. Marcia's blind belief in his innocence brings its own reward here.
438-underwoods:
Robert Louis Stevenson gathers verse in English and Scots in this volume, first shaped in the 1880s. Book one holds songs of the road, the sea, and friends, including the famed Requiem with its wide and starry sky. Later books turn to Scots speech, doctors, and the sickroom, with a dedication praising physicians as a rule.

Stevenson stole his title from Ben Jonson and owned the theft with a jest. His lines mix cheer, grief, and a traveler's restlessness. The book shows a poet of wide range, at home in both tongues, and it keeps his most quoted short poems in one place.
4381-the-aran-islands:
John M. Synge wrote this account of the Aran Islands off the west coast of Ireland, thirty miles from Galway. He begins with simple geography: Aranmor, nine miles long; Inishmaan, round and three and a half miles across; and Inishere, slightly smaller. Kilronan, the chief village, has changed with the fishing industry.

Synge lived among islanders, listening to their stories, songs, and speech, and watching their work in boats, fields, and stone-walled plots. The book records a world of Irish language, belief, and hardship, before modern change swept it away. It is both travel writing and a source for Synge's plays, and it remains a classic of Irish literature.
44127-fresh-fields: John Burroughs takes readers outdoors in Fresh Fields, one of his nature books, priced with the rest of his shelf in the front pages. The list names Birds and Poets, Locusts and Wild Honey, Pepacton and Other Sketches, Wake Robin, and Winter Sunshine, each in a gilt top binding. Fresh Fields stands at the head of that shelf, the new field book of a writ long at home in woods and fields.
44184-on-the-seaboard-a-novel-of-the-bal:
August Strindberg wrote On the Seaboard, a novel of the Baltic islands, translated from the Swedish by Elizabeth Clarke Westergren in an authorized edition published at New York in 1913. Chapter first opens on Goosestone bay. A fishing boat lies one May evening to beam-wind.

The Rokarna, known to all the coast by their three pyramids, were turning blue, and clouds formed as the sun sank. Dashing outside the points and a flapping mainsail promised the land-breeze would soon break. At the tiller sat the Custom House Surveyor of the East Skerries, a giant with a long black beard. Beside the mast crouched a little gentleman, seemingly afraid and frozen, drawing his shawl closer. Readers get Strindberg's sea novel of an intellectual cast away among islanders.
44593-the-oxford-book-of-ballads:
Oxford Book of Ballads gathers old ballads chosen by Arthur Quiller Couch. The Clarendon Press at Oxford issued the anthology in Great Britain. Quiller Couch gives the book to the one survivor of three great men. Francis James Child, Frederick Furnivall, and John Wesley Hales are those three.

Ballad lovers owe those scholars most in these times, the dedication holds. Snatches from Tam Lin, Sir Cawline, and Cospatrick front the volume. Fair Margaret and Sweet William and Robin Hood and the Monk are quoted. Like the clown in Twelfth Night, the ballad sings high and low alike. The note is unmistakable in either key, the editor proudly says.
44818-christ-legends:
Selma Lagerlof wrote these Christ legends, rendered from the Swedish by Velma Swanston Howard, with decorations by Bertha Stuart, printed at New York in 1908. The contents name eleven tales. The Holy Night opens the book, and The Emperor's Vision, The Wise Men's Well, and Bethlehem's Children follow.

The Flight into Egypt, In Nazareth, and In the Temple carry the child Christ through his early years. Saint Veronica's Kerchief, Robin Redbreast, Our Lord and Saint Peter, and The Sacred Flame close the set. The first tale is framed by memory. The writer recalls her grandmother, dead when she was five, who sat on a corner sofa telling stories from morning to night. Her tale of Jesus' birth is the one the writer still remembers whole.
44966-craft-gilds:
Craft Gilds is a paper by the Reverend William Cunningham. He read it at the thirteenth yearly meeting of the Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings. Cunningham also wrote on the history of trade and the church.

The talk opens with the two aims of the society. Old buildings are worth keeping first as records that can never be replaced once lost. They bear the marks of the ages that made them and the men who raised them. They are worth keeping second as fine things in themselves, well designed and deftly made. Cunningham grants that much of what survives is dull or poor. The skill of past builders is plain to all, and craft workers of old were adepts in numberless arts.
45053-the-churches-and-modern-thought-an:
The Churches and Modern Thought is an inquiry by Philip Vivian, published by Watts in London in 1911. Its subtitle promises an inquiry into the grounds of unbelief and an appeal for candour. A line from Macaulay serves as motto: men settle questions rightly when they discuss them freely. Vivian dedicates the book to his wife and children. The first chapter weighs the gravity of the present situation.

Vivian holds that Christianity and science remain unreconciled. Apologetics, he argues, has been found wanting. The second chapter attacks the defence of miracles as extraordinary. The third calls modern Bible criticism destructive in character. The fourth turns to ancient beliefs and their parallels with Christianity. Krishna, Buddha, and the solar myths all come under study. The book speaks for the rationalist side of the Edwardian debate.
45240-frontier-ballads:
Frontier Ballads, by Joseph Mills Hanson, was published in 1910, with pictures in colour and other drawings by Maynard Dixon. Hanson opens with My Creed, a statement of faith in verse. He calls his paints crude and his pictures rude, but hopes some worth shows to those with free thoughts.

He holds that sea, plain, mountain, wood, and down are better haunts for men than roaring town streets. Sons, he says, should love not gods of gold and greed, but men of brain and brawn who served their country need. Three stars light the trail of life in his creed: the strength of God, a noble woman love, and clean courage. Readers get western ballads built on that creed.
45274-ye-book-of-copperheads:
An unsigned war book of verse and plates mocks the Copperheads of the North. Its verse head quotes Shakespeare's Richard the Third on a league. A Copperhead snake once tried to bite Uncle Sam by fault, it starts. The Seven League Boot on his foot crushed that vile snake fast. Gay spite is the whole tone of the small book's rhymes.

A man back from war with proud scars gets their jeer in verse. Served you right if you had died, the snakes cry in that bit. The old Tory brute is dead but left eggs in her place, it holds. Two broke in the yolk, and the third hatched a Copperhead. War fans get Union spite in rhyme.
45311-the-norwegian-fjords:
A Heaton Cooper painted and described this book on the Norwegian fjords, printed by Adam and Charles Black of London in 1907. Cooper was known as the artist of The English Lakes. Twenty-four full-page plates in colour fill the book, in Black's Smaller Series of Beautiful Books. A front plate of the Sogne Fjord at Gudvangen is noted as missing from this copy.

Cooper claims no literary merit for his words. He offers them as a plain statement of bare facts. The pictures, he trusts, will pay the reader back for any thinness in the text. The book serves travellers on the fjords and those who dream of them at home, in a handy, handsome form.
45388-toots-and-his-friends:
Toots is a baby with a genius for mischief, and Kate Tannatt Woods tells his doings in short tales for young children. He plays hand-organ on the guest-room pillows with a hairpin, and marches blindfold down the stairs. Another night he turns a bath-tub into a circus carriage, with his sashes for reins, because Barnum's show has been in town. Each scrape ends with the household half scolding, half laughing.

Cassell published the book in 1883, with pictures. Later pieces take Toots to kindergarten and through the small events of a small boy's day. The humor is gentle and the scenes are domestic, written to be read aloud to children who will know Toots's kind of trouble well.
45389-two-yellow-birds:
Two Yellow-Birds is a short children's story by an anonymous author. Its heroine, Lucy Tracy, is a very little girl with no brother or sister. Her mother keeps a beautiful yellow bird, quite tame. The bird leaves his cage at breakfast and picks crumbs from the cloth. Lucy calls him Black-pate, for the black tuft on his head. She chatters to him and feeds him lumps of sugar.

He loves to splash in a basin of water and spatter Lucy's face. Her mother alone washes his cage and fills his seed and water cups. She would trust no servant with the task, knowing how pet birds suffer from neglect. The bird is no canary but a wild yellow bird of the woods and fields. Yet he seems happy in his wire house. The tale teaches kind care of small creatures.
45397-a-boy-crusoe-or-the-golden-treasur:
A Boy Crusoe, or the Golden Treasure of the Virgin Islands, is by Allan Eric. Donohue of Chicago and New York put the boys' book out. The tale also ran under the title A Yankee Crusoe, a note says. Twenty-three chapters run from early life to rescue at hand. The teller was born in a little town in Maine, he opens.

His birth fell near the close of the Civil War in America. Heavy weather, the Sargasso Sea, and a terrible storm fill the voyage. Cast up on a tropical island, he builds a house and stockade. A cocoanut calendar, a bow-gun, and turtles' eggs fill his Crusoe life. A snake, a mountain cave, and an attack by pigs test him. Fever, a feathered companion, and a fish trap crowd the mid tale. An ancient ruin holds the golden treasure of the book's title.
454-the-breitmann-ballads:
Charles G. Leland writes comic ballads in the voice of Hans Breitmann, a German-American whose broken English and high spirits carry him through beer halls, battles, and love affairs. The dialect is the joke and the charm. Leland created Breitmann in the 1860s, and the ballads ran in magazines before book form.

Leland, a scholar of folklore as well as a humorist, lets Breitmann blunder through American life with cheerful confidence. The ballads were hugely popular in their day, and they still read as a lively piece of nineteenth-century humour. Breitmann's German-English, full of comic errors, made him a favourite of American readers.
45494-airplane-boys-in-the-black-woods:
Airplane Boys in the Black Woods is a boys air adventure by Craine, published in 1932. The World Syndicate Publishing Company issued the book at Cleveland and New York. A note at the front calls it the seventh book of air adventures in its series. The boys bump into a new mystery, solved only after many pages of excitement, it promises.

Contents list the chapters of the mystery in the northern woods for the heroes. A Reception Committee, Kidnapped, and The Horrible Cavern open the tale in order. Ghosts, The Way Out, and An Old Enemy follow in the list of chapters. The End of the Way, When the Butterflies Die, and The Ghosts of Bloody Dam fill the middle. The Airplane Boys were a Syndicate style crew of young fliers, whose plane takes them where trains and roads cannot follow in the logging country of the tale.
45546-dangerous-deeds:
Captain Frank Cobb wrote this third book in the Aviator Series, copyrighted in 1927 by Saalfield. The name 'Dangerous Deeds' carries the added title 'The Flight in the Dirigible' beneath it. Earlier books in the series were 'Battling the Clouds' and 'An Aviator's Luck' in that order. This volume keeps the same young flying hero at its center.

A heavy fog presses down on Washington as the tale opens. A boy watches from a top-floor window while the mist hides streets, parks and houses. Only the tallest roofs stay in sight. A front plate shows Lawrence working through secret moves with no answer, his worry growing as the flight plot begins.
45554-doctor-birch-and-his-young-friends:
Doctor Birch and His Young Friends was written by Mr M A Titmarsh and published by Chapman and Hall at London in 1840. The narrator has become assistant master at Doctor Birch's Academy at Rodwell Regis. He teaches English and French, flower-painting, and the German flute. He will not say why he left genteel London lodgings for the usher's desk. The fare, the five o'clock rising, and the walks with little boys who play him tricks were hard to swallow, he owns.

Miss Birch's vulgar insolence and Jack Birch's glum condescension season the account. Jack, the doctor's son and partner, is a supercilious little prig in a choking white neckcloth. He writes sanctified letters to parents and dreary sermons for boys. The real master of the school is Prince, a shy, learned Oxford man, crammed with Greek.
45944-elsie-yachting-with-the-raymonds:
Elsie Yachting with the Raymonds, by Martha Finley, is one of the long loved Elsie books. The front pages list the series in order, from Elsie Dinsmore through Elsie's Girlhood and Womanhood. Elsie's Motherhood, Children, and Widowhood follow, then Grandmother Elsie and the later volumes. This yachting book stands sixteenth in the line, after Elsie and the Raymonds.

Finley wrote of Elsie Dinsmore, a pious heroine whose life her readers followed from childhood to grandmotherhood. In this volume Elsie takes to the water with the Raymond family. The author thanks her sources for facts on Revolutionary times and on cadet life at West Point. The Elsie books taught faith and duty through story, and sold in the millions. This one mixes a pleasure cruise with history lessons, in the gentle, earnest manner that made the series a fixture of American girlhood.
46023-the-garden-of-swords:
Max Pemberton wrote a war novel of France in the storm of 1870. The book's rights date to 1898, this form to 1902. Stanley Wood drew its plates. Pemberton wrote Kronstadt and The Iron Pirate. A verse at the front calls war a crop of grief and death.

Man and wife make book one, set in Strassburg's streets. Bonot reads the news, and the herald of the storm comes in. The last day of July and the flight mark the war's birth. Book two is battle: the red day of Woerth in full. A death ride and a dragoon camp close that book.
46038-shinto-the-way-of-the-gods:
W G Aston wrote Shinto: The Way of the Gods for Longmans, Green at London in 1905. Aston had written grammars of spoken and written Japanese, translated the Nihongi, and written a history of Japanese literature. Fourteen chapters map the faith from its sources onward.

Early chapters treat personification, the deification of men, and the work of the gods. Myth and the mythical narrative follow, then a pantheon split into nature-deities and man-deities. Priesthood, worship, morals, law, and purity get their own chapters. Ceremonial, magic, and divination come near the end. A last chapter treats decay and modern sects. Plates show the Sun-Goddess leaving her rock cave and sun worship at Ise.
46046-sonia-between-two-worlds:
Stephen McKenna wrote Sonia Between Two Worlds, a tale of an age in change. George H Doran issued the book in New York in nineteen hundred seventeen. He gives it to a very gallant lady in its front leaf. The wise heart in the house of mourning fronts it from Ecclesiastes.

The tale is told for an eight weeks old godson of the teller. Charles Templeton, his old Oxford tutor, fills the first pages. Templeton spent thirty years on a history of the French Third Republic. At his death the notes stopped short of Charlemagne’s forerunners. The Stranger Within Our Gates heads the tale’s twelve long parts. The Making of an Englishman and Sonia Dainton fill the next span. Years of Carnival and The Five Days darken the bright mid book. The Making of an Englishwoman answers the first great part.
46400-revolutionary-reader-reminiscences:
Revolutionary Reader: Reminiscences and Indian Legends is a school reader compiled by Sophie Lee Foster. Foster was state regent of the Daughters of the American Revolution of Georgia. The Byrd Printing Company published it in Atlanta in 1913. She dedicates it to Georgia's Daughters as a labor of love. Two endorsement letters open the book. Lucian Lamar Knight marvels at the gathering of dramatic phases.

Joseph T Derry hopes school boards will adopt it widely. The contents mix national and Georgia history. Washington's name, inauguration, and Valley Forge life appear. The battles of Alamance, Lexington, and Kettle Creek are retold. Signers of the Declaration and important characters receive sketches. Forts of Georgia, Oglethorpe, and LaFayette serve the state. Margaret Katherine Barry gets a historical sketch of her own. Foster aimed at a supplementary reader, rich in local interest and broadly American in spirit.
46425-glimpses-of-indian-birds:
Douglas Dewar wrote bright notes on the birds of India from his own watch. His book came out in London and New York in 1913. He gave it to Theodore Roosevelt as a hunter and beast man. Roosevelt brought plain sense to beast lore, the gift page says. Birds in a Grove leads the list of Dewar's notes.

The magpie-robin, the snake-bird, and minivets fill the first parts. Pied wood birds, a dry marsh pool, and birds in white come next. The pied crested cuckoo and vultures take their due turns. Robins, the shikra, and a rose hued finch fill the mid list. Lawn birds, the grey hornbill, and flamingos close it. Field fans get a keen eye.
46443-rogues-and-vagabonds:
Rogues and Vagabonds is a novel by George Sims of London life. Chatto and Windus published it at Piccadilly in the year 1892. Sims dedicates it to his good friends Agostino and Stefano Gatti. The story here stands first published in novel form, that page says. Contents open with the wreck of the Bon Espoir at sea.

Topsey Turvey sees a ghost, and Marston meets an old friend after. Number fifteen, Little Queer Street, and Miss Duck has a word follow. An offer of marriage and a chat over old times ensue in turn. Grigg and Limpet explain, and a very nice old gentleman appears. A forged cheque and Gertie's promise crowd the later chapter heads.
46548-children-of-the-dear-cotswolds:
Children of the Dear Cotswolds is a book of stories by Allen Harker, published in 1918. John Murray of London issued it. A dedicatory poem to the Countess Bathurst opens the volume. Its verses praise the small upland town and its steep stone roofs. Beech woods, rolling down, and golden fields of buttercups fill the scene. The folk are slow spoken, kind, and wise with mother wit.

They judge men by their doings, not their looks, the poem says. Harker brings the countess stories of old folk and young. A foreword quotes Harvey on homesickness for the hills. The opening scene is a train at Swindon in wartime. A mud stained soldier home on leave tumbles into the carriage. His old father and a young lad had met him at the junction.
46558-the-demi-gods:
James Stephens, author of The Crock of Gold, wrote this tale in four books. Macmillan first published it in 1914 and reissued it at New York in 1921, dedicated to Thomas Bodkin. The books are named for their people: Patsy Mac Cann, Eileen Ni Cooley, Brien O'Brien, and Mary Mac Cann.

Book one opens on the road. Patsy scolds his daughter Mary for kissing the donkey on the snout, calling it neither natural nor proper. Mary answers that one has to be kissing something, and refuses to kiss her father instead, since he is as old as the hills. Patsy wishes Christian people could eat grass like the beasts, so there would be no more trouble in the world. He takes stock of the basket: a loaf from the shop at Knockbeg, a fresher half loaf from a woman's window, and a white turnip found in a field.
46695-a-visit-to-the-philippine-islands:
A Visit to the Philippine Islands is a travel and survey book by Sir John Bowring, published by Smith, Elder and Company of London in 1859. Bowring had lately been Governor of Hong Kong and the Crown's plenipotentiary in China. His visit to the islands was short, he admits, but well connected.

Authorities and natives of every class received him with friendly readiness. The book begins with Manila and its neighbourhood, then a trip to La Laguna and Tayabas. History, geography, and climate follow. Chapters treat government, population, and the manners and superstitions of the people. Justice, the army and navy, public instruction, and church authority are surveyed. Languages, native produce, animals, minerals, and manufactures fill the middle. Commerce, finance, and the new ports of Iloilo, Sual, and Zamboanga close the survey.
46762-bessie-and-her-friends:
Joanna Mathews wrote Bessie and Her Friends, issued at New York by Robert Carter and Brothers in 1868. She had also written Bessie at the Seaside and Bessie in the City, and her Bessie books ran to six volumes. The book is given to her sister Bella, whose consideration had lightened many a weary hour. Two texts stand at its head: speak not evil one of another, and bear ye one another's burdens.

The twelve chapters treat Jennie's home, the police-sergeant's story, Papa's story, light through the clouds, Uncle Ruthven, blind Willie, and Maggie's book. The front pages list Mathews' many series for children: the Flowerets on the commandments, the Little Sunbeams, and the Kitty and Lulu books, with her sister Julia's series beside them. The tale teaches kindness and burden-bearing through the doings of Bessie and her young friends.
46813-the-romance-of-the-woods:
Whishaw wrote The Romance of the Woods, published by Longmans in London and New York in 1895. He had earlier written Out of Doors in Tsarland. The book joins hunting sketches from Russia and Finland with tales of folk belief among the peasants.

Chapters take the reader onto a Russian moor, into ambush at a lake-side, and after ducks on Lake Ladoga. One chapter is told by a bear, and another collects the folk-lore of the moujik, the Russian peasant. Witches, wood-goblins, and an unbaptized spirit follow. The first chapter opens with a strange dream of the afterlife before settling into outdoor life. Whishaw writes for sportsmen and for readers who like wild country seen through local story and superstition.
46863-old-world-japan-legends-of-the-lan:
Frank Rinder retold the old legends of Japan for English readers, in a book printed in London in 1895. Robinson drew its pictures. A line at the front says the spirit of Japan is as the scent of wild cherry blossom at dawn. The tales start before time, when earth, water, light, and dark were mixed in a vapoury sea.

From that chaos the birth of the gods unfolds. Tales follow of the sun goddess, heavenly messengers, a palace on the ocean bed, and star lovers parted in the sky. Rai-Taro, son of the thunder god, the moon maiden, and a snow white fox fill later pages. Each short tale keeps the wonder and grace of the old myths.
47047-brothers-the-true-history-of-a-fig:
Brothers, the true history of a fight against odds, is a tale by Horace Annesley Vachell, printed at London in 1905. The first edition came in May 1904 and was reprinted six times within the year. Vachell gives the book to all who have striven, the strong who reached their goal and the weak who made the running for them.

A note at the front owns that some readers will know the brothers under their thin veil of fiction. The brother who rose highest in his profession wished the truth of his early years told, but held back. The story of the Samphires, as Vachell names them, is his way of telling it at last.
47115-british-sea-birds:
Charles Dixon describes the birds of the British coasts in a handbook issued in London in 1896. Eight pictures by Charles Whymper back the text. Dixon had already written on game birds, nests and eggs, and the migration of British birds.

Chapters group the birds by kind, opening with gulls, skuas, and terns and their changes of plumage. Plovers and sandpipers follow, then guillemots, the razorbill, and the puffin. Divers, grebes, cormorants, ducks, geese, swans, and petrels each get a full treatment. A last chapter treats land birds of the shore, and one more takes up migration on the coast. Readers get a full Victorian guide to knowing sea birds by look, habit, and haunt.
47178-fairy-tales-from-many-lands:
Fairy Tales from Many Lands is a story book by Katharine Pyle, with pictures drawn by the author herself. Dutton published the work at New York in 1911. The book proved lasting, with printings running into the 1930s. Pyle had earlier written The Counterpane Fairy and other tales for children.

The contents gather fifteen tales from the lore of many peoples. The first, from Serbian folk lore, tells of a king whose golden apples vanish each night. A magician of the lake, a wise gazelle, and the feather of a fire bird fill other tales. Stories come from lands as far apart as the elephant and whale tale of Africa suggests. Pyle retells each in her own clear voice. Her pictures show palace treasures, gulls over a lake, and a girl lifting a heavy pitcher.
47310-a-treatise-on-gunshot-wounds:
A Treatise on Gunshot Wounds, by Longmore, deputy inspector-general of hospitals and professor of military surgery at Fort Pitt, Chatham, was printed in Philadelphia in 1862. Front pages list other Lippincott military books, from cavalry tactics to Crimean surgery, with prices. The treatise itself starts with a definition and a history of gunshot surgery.

Contents sort wounds by missile: grape shot, canister, musket balls, conical bullets, shell fragments, stones, and splinters. Longmore weighs speed, lodged balls, and the effects of balls left in the body, with cases as proof. Round and conical balls are compared, as are the Enfield and Whitworth rifles. The book served army surgeons in the Civil War.
47655-six-girls-and-bob-a-story-of-patty:
Marion Taggart wrote Six Girls and Bob, for Wilde in 1906. A story of patty-pans and green fields is its subtitle. Stecher illustrated the Boston and Chicago edition. The Six Girls series fills a page of the front matter. Each volume runs some three hundred thirty pages.

A sunny maiden bends over a gas range in one plate. The Fourth Floor, East opens the contents of the tale. Fire and other escapes follow in the heads. Keren-Happuch and an angel in disguise follow. The six girls and Betty stand later in the series list. Six girls growing older and grown up close the set of ads. Home-taught children ought to know their arithmetic, a voice jokes in it. You would be poor at figures to try it, she adds. Taggart gives six sisters and one Bob a farm holiday.
47695-kaffir-kangaroo-klondike-tales-of-:
Leavitt wrote Kaffir, Kangaroo, Klondike, tales of the gold fields published at Toronto in 1898. He had earlier written The Witch of Plum Hollow. The three names in the title point to the great gold rushes of the age: South Africa, Australia, and the Klondike in Canada's north.

Seven tales make up the book. They include a strange partner, the black cat of Klondike, a skeleton mine, and a Maori legend. The green door and the three great pearls close the set. The first story is told by Henry Detmold, a young English bank clerk who threw up a salary of eighty pounds a year. A newspaper account of gold in Western Australia fired his spirit of adventure, and he sailed for Sydney.
47757-a-manual-of-philippine-birds:
Richard McGregor's A Manual of Philippine Birds was printed at Manila in 1909 by the Bureau of Printing, as publication number two of the Bureau of Science. Part one, from the game birds to the broadbills, came out on April 15, 1909. Part two, the perching birds, followed on January 31, 1910.

The contents lay out the whole order of the work: classes, orders, families, and genera, with each species numbered and named. Megapodius opens the list, then the pheasant family with the jungle fowl, and the button quails, among them species McGregor himself named. Keys at the front teach the reader how to run a bird down to its name. It is a working handbook, built for use in the field and the museum alike.
48129-the-red-cow-and-her-friends:
Peter McArthur collects farm fun in The Red Cow and Her Friends, printed at Toronto and New York in 1919. Dent and Lane share the book. McArthur had writ In Pastures Green and To Be Taken With Salt. He gives the book to city men who feel sure they could farm at a profit.

His preface owns a debt and a joke. The sketches first ran in print, and his file of cuttings was lost. Readers who had clipped the pieces sent them in from all parts of Canada. Some came from the States next door. His thanks to those unknown friends make the book a joint work. Farm beasts and farm folk fill its light pages.
48311-james-russell-lowell-and-his-frien:
Edward Everett Hale wrote on James Russell Lowell and his friends, printed at Boston and New York in 1898 with portraits, facsimiles, and other illustrations. Lowell from the crayon portrait by Rowse, in the possession of Professor Charles Eliot Norton, fronts the book. Boston in the forties stands among the chapters shown. The brothers and sisters and a man of letters follow.

Lowell as a public speaker, Harvard revisited, and Lowell's experience as an editor fill the middle of the contents. Politics and poetry share the later pages. Hale knew Lowell across a long Boston life of letters, pulpits, and magazines. His book is a friend's portrait gallery of the poet, critic, editor of the Atlantic, and minister to Spain and England. Such volumes fix a whole literary circle in warm, first hand memory.
48469-the-indian-fairy-book-from-the-ori:
The Indian Fairy Book is a set of native legends retold by Henry Schoolcraft. Stokes issued it in New York in 1916. Eight colour illustrations by Choate and Curtis adorn it. Schoolcraft gathered tales from the original legends. The first tale is The Boy Who Set a Snare for the Sun. A boy and his sister live alone in the world there. He kills birds, and she makes him a coat of skins.

The boy parades in his new coat with pride. He asks if they are truly alone on the earth. His sister warns of a dangerous people far away. Those people killed all their kin, she says. Such tales carry the myth world of the woodlands. Schoolcraft was a pioneer collector of Indian lore. His books fed Longfellow's Hiawatha as well. This late edition dresses his tales for children.
48655-dave-dashaway-air-champion-or-wiza:
Roy Rockwood wrote this boys tale of Dave Dashaway, a young pilot hero. The book came out in New York with Cupples and Leon. Front pages list past Dave tales of hydroplanes and giant airships. A plate shows the young pilot slow his craft, the Ariel.

Chapters open at the hangars with target practice and a tramp artist. A startling find, a hidden hand, and a secret foe raise stakes. The big event looms as Dave faces traps set by rivals. Rockwood writes brisk air adventure for boys of the early flight age.
49349-catlin-s-historic-origin-of-the-pl:
Catlin published his Historic Origin of the Playing Cards at Quincy, Illinois, in 1893 from Maine Street. The title page boasts the account full, complete, reliable, and authentic. A second part adds his new game of Guest, praised as the superior game of the period. Two complete works share one volume by his own design.

The preface credits human genius, spurred by the law of progress, for every great device. Cards, Catlin argues, rank among the grand enterprises of the sixteenth century. He traces their design to Egypt and to the divine origin of time itself. Players, he laments, have cared little to learn the tale he now tells. Grand claims and home grown lore fill an earnest oddity.
49459-bonnie-prince-fetlar-the-story-of-:
Marshall Saunders, who wrote Beautiful Joe, told this pony's tale for Doran of New York in 1920. Bonnie Prince Fetlar is the story of a pony and his friends. A verse from Lilian Leveridge heads it: come, walk the open road with us, far out beyond the town.

Where all the winds of Arcady go wandering up and down, the verse runs. If problems vex, leave them all behind. The Boy with the Pale Eyes opens the tale, then the man and the boy. Three friends on Deer Trail follow. The wolf and the lamb, a coward stands aside, and the beloved liar fill the middle. Prize pigs and their dog friends bring Saunders's world of kind beasts and the folk who learn from them.
49803-florida-salads:
Frances Barber Harris wrote this little book of salads at Jacksonville, Florida, in 1914. Milton gives its motto: nothing lovelier can be found in woman than to study household good. Harris tests every recipe herself, as her preface owns.

If she can press on her readers the weight of eating salads, she writes, the book is not in vain. A pretty salad refines the table's look and whets the taste. In this climate, she holds, it is near a need for health. Fruits and vegetables carry the salts the system craves. Pure olive oil is a true beautifier, good authority says. Celery and onions soothe the nerves. Young housekeepers are her hoped-for readers, and her salads are Florida through and through.
50017-yosemite-legends:
Yosemite Legends, by Bertha Smith, was published at San Francisco in 1904, with drawings by Florence Lundborg. A front picture shows the valley in the mist. The legends are listed with their meanings. Yosemite itself is glossed as Large Grizzly Bear, and that tale comes first.

When the world was made, the tale says, the Great Spirit tore out the heart of the Sky Mountains. He left the gash unhealed, and sent Coyote to people the valley. The people called their home Ahwahnee, and themselves the Ahwahneechees. Other legends treat Pohono, Spirit of the Evil Wind, and Hummoo, the Lost Arrow. Pyweack, the White Water, Tutockahnulah and Tissaack, and Kompopaises, Leaping Frog Rocks, follow. Pictures show Mirror Lake, Bridal Veil, El Capitan, and the Three Brothers. Readers get Indigenous valley tales retold for visitors.
50091-silas-strong-emperor-of-the-woods:
Irving Bacheller wrote this tale of the north woods, printed in 1906. It is sent forth to his late friend Archer Brown. The leaf of gift calls back days of past years, when the two men roamed far and sat by springs and brooks to rest. That ground was the doomed realm of Strong, and they spoke of how to save it, and of days to come that were more fair. They knew not then that such days could not be.

A note from the author adds a strange word on his folk. When he tried to bend their acts to the known rules of the craft of tales, they said they were free and would not bend. When he pressed them to speak and act as folk in most tales do, they laughed and felt shame.
50106-greece-and-the-gean-islands:
Greece and the Aegean Islands, by Philip Sanford Marden, is a travel book issued in 1907 at London and Boston. A view of the Acropolis at Athens fronts the volume. Marden opens with a plain disclaimer about his aim. What follows, he says, makes no pretence of being a scientific work.

The book is no archaeology treatise, he warns the reader at the start. He wrote it because no book had covered quite the same ground. Travellers needed a guide that mixed sights with sense, in his view. He admits his opening chapters may sound guide bookish at times. That honesty sets the tone of the whole tour. Islands, temples, and modern Greek life fill his route. The book serves the traveller who wants company, not just facts.
50165-the-flying-machine-boys-on-duty-or:
Frank Walton wrote a boys' tale of flying machines on duty above the clouds. A L Burt Company held the rights in New York in 1913. Walton had written three Flying Machine Boys books before this one. A plate shows two boys greeting the young aviator at his hangar.

Two flyers duel in jest and earnest over New York Bay at June dusk. The Statue of Liberty and Governor's Island watch the chase from below. One pestering machine breaks off west as dark gathers over Pelham Bay. Boys of the day got a fast tale of the new art of flight.
50276-more-tales-of-the-birds:
More Tales of the Birds is a set of bird tales by Warde Fowler, with plates by a named hand. Fowler was known past a past book on a year with the birds. It came out in nineteen two. Nine tales fill it, from the larks nest to a tale named too much of a good thing. A plate of the larks nest heads the book.

The first tale is named a tale of a fight. It opens close past the mid of the warm half, but in cold wet days like the fall. Mist rose past damp fields past the whole land, as war hung in the air with it. The sky lark still rose to sing to his wife on the nest past the chill. He bade her come up past the mist to the sun and see the long lines of men and steeds past.
50315-reynolds:
Reynolds, by Randall Davies, presents Sir Joshua Reynolds through sixteen examples of the master's work. Adam and Charles Black published the volume at London in 1913, the plates reproduced in colour. The plates include Miss Nelly O'Brien of 1763 as frontispiece, The Strawberry Girl, Lady Cockburn and Her Children, Mrs Siddons as the Tragic Muse, and Lord Heathfield.

Davies opens with Benjamin West succeeding Reynolds as President of the Royal Academy at his death in 1792. He notes how far the arts had risen in the half century since Reynolds began painting in London.
50391-the-travelling-thirds:
The Travelling Thirds, a novel by Gertrude Atherton, author of The Conqueror and Rulers of Kings, was published in London and New York in October 1905. The tale follows the Moulton family on a European tour, with a California cousin as its live wire. Chapter one opens in the Place Carnot at Lyons, under thick white clusters of acacia in full scent.

The cousin stands apart from the perturbed group, feet boyishly asunder, head thrown back. All Lyons, the narrator says, has yielded to the fragrance of its favorite tree, yet in the square there is not a murmur. The Moultons have hushed their thoughts in the heavy perfume. Atherton sets a tale of travel, family friction, and a western girl's force among old-world scenes.
50466-animal-chums-true-tales-about-four:
Jean McIntosh wrote Animal Chums, true tales about four-footed friends, in the Fireside Library, printed in New York. Contents name eleven tales. John Willie stands first, then hurry up, Jack. Brer Rabbit's adventure, the greedy lamb, and the sparrow hawks follow. Jacko, the horse that went to church, and the weasel and the rabbit come next. The saucy squirrels, the owl in the dovecot, and a true story of a canary close the list.

The first tale is told by Uncle John to Willie and Tommy. The two boys love a story, and their uncle comes to their nursery each evening to tell one. Have you ever heard, he asks, of any one having a real live goose for a pet? The tale is true, he says; he saw the goose not very long ago. It begins in a country village near the sea.
50663-vaiti-of-the-islands:
Beatrice Grimshaw wrote Vaiti of the Islands, a tale of the South Seas printed at London by George Newnes. A prologue goes back to the seventies, to a grey dawn in Caithness, Scotland. A card scandal at a castle house party has shamed a young officer in the presence of a prince. The prince strikes the host from his list of friends at once.

The disgraced man rows out to his white schooner yacht, the Paquita, which is later reported lost at sea with him aboard. Chapter heads then sweep to pearl lagoons, a race for a fortune, and a lost island. A Paris dress, a witch doctor, rival princesses, and a cannibal party fill the island parts. The tale ends with its heroine queen after all.
50777-beautiful-birds:
Beautiful Birds is a nature book for young readers by Edmund Selous, issued at London in 1901, with many illustrations by Hubert Astley. A lyre bird fronts the volume. The first chapter asks a hard question in plain words: why beautiful birds are killed. Birds of paradise then take up the next five chapters in turn.

The great, the red, the lesser, black, blue, and golden birds of paradise each get their pages. Humming birds follow, bright ones and hermit ones, with chapters of explanation mixed in. The cock of the rock and the lyre bird share a chapter, and the resplendent trogon and argus pheasant another. White egrets, ospreys, and ostrich feathers close the book, returning to its first charge: that beauty in feathers cost the birds their lives for fashion.
50818-how-to-make-friends:
Jim Harmon's How to Make Friends appeared in Galaxy Magazine in October 1962, with illustrations by West. A headnote says every lonely man tries to make friends, and that Manet just did not know when to stop. William Manet is the lone overseer of Atmosphere Seeder Station 131-47 on Mars.

The station runs itself, being fully automatic, but the law feathers the job with one human occupant. Passenger fare to Mars is about one billion dollars, so no relief or visitors come. Manet means to study his own loneliness like an experiment, and has tacked up a picture of Annie Oakley. Lately, the story says, she has begun winking back at him.
50863-alien-minds:
E Everett Evans wrote a science fiction novel printed at Reading in Pennsylvania in 1955 as a first edition. Its hero, George Hanlon, serves in a star corps and works in secret on a far world. Local folk call the world by a hard name, while corps men call it Estrella for ease.

Made up to look like a local man, with ragged beard and long hair, Hanlon shops for wild dog like beasts called roches. He wants eight of them, matched in size, hue, and age, a strange order that stuns the trader. Hanlon can read the top layer of a mans mind, yet fears his false face will still give him away.
51101-nice-girl-with-5-husbands:
Nice Girl with Five Husbands is a short star tale by Fritz Leiber from the April nineteen fifty one Galaxy. Tom Dorset, a lens man on a paid rest grant, roams a red stone vale. A camp of lone art folk who can not make fills his irk in the tale. Winds blow through time as through space, the tale voice claims at length. Strong time winds are rare and fling folk far in past or yet days.

Weak time winds sport with a thing and set it back whole in place. Mind call back is a mere time breeze too weak to stir more than thought. One vale wind blows like the monsoon at set hours each day in the tale. At ten it blows a span of years forth, at two it blows back. A poise rock marks the vale where that strange wind turns.
5149-gold-of-the-gods:
Arthur B. Reeve's mystery follows Professor Craig Kennedy into a case of Peruvian treasure, beginning with a Peruvian dagger and a soldier of fortune. Chapters run through treasure hunters, a Wall Street promoter, the curse of Mansiche, arrow poison. A poisoned cigarette appears, as Kennedy uses X-ray readers, paper fibres, and shoe prints to trace the crime.

The novel mixes archaeology with modern detection, moving from museum relics to laboratory tests. Readers of Reeve's scientific detective stories will find the usual brisk plotting. Inventive gadgets drive a treasure hunt that turns deadly.
51531-with-these-hands:
With These Hands, a story by Kornbluth, ran in Galaxy Science Fiction in December 1951. Karl Rogers drew the pictures for the tale. No self respecting artist can object to suffering for his art, the blurb grants. But not in a society where art is outdated by technology, it adds.

Halvorsen the artist waits in a chancery office in the opening scene. Monsignor Reedy disposes of three persons who came before him. The artist is a little dizzy with hunger as he waits his turn. The prelate’s secretary beckons him toward the inner office door at last. Kornbluth writes of a future that has no use for the handmade thing. His artist carries the old craft in his hands, and the world has priced it at nothing.
51639-implement-sheds:
Ekblaw wrote this farm bulletin, Implement Sheds, issued at Chicago in April 1916 as the first number of a farm bulletin series and revised that September. A cover list gives its whole scope: how sheds should be designed, the simple, open, wide enclosed, and two-story types, the space common implements need, and the choice of building material.

A sharp claim opens the argument. Over fifty million dollars, the bulletin says, is lost every year on American farms because implements and machinery are not properly housed. On the average farm a good shed saves each year about as much as the income from a solid sum at interest. A farmer's care of his tools, Ekblaw holds, shows his thrift at a glance.
51823-the-back-of-our-heads:
The Back of Our Heads is a science fiction story by Stephen Barr, taken from Galaxy Science Fiction for July 1958. Its tag line says she travelled from life to death and back again like a commuter on the 5:15, each trip bringing her nearer the beginning of the line. The tale is cast as a report on a visitor.

The report warns that the word they may mean not separate persons but cells of one organism, as men become in a mob. The one being studied always took female form and showed a marked, combative character. At a hearing she admitted she was always in hot water. The scene then drops to four teenagers in a soda shop, where the girl Miss Framis torments a waitress with an order that changes every few seconds. Two odd men in the booth are listening.
51833-meeting-of-the-minds:
Meeting of the Minds is a science fiction story by Robert Sheckley, printed in Galaxy in February nineteen sixty. Its opening asks what mission the Quedak had been given long ago. Even the Quedak can no longer recall it, yet it will not die. Fragments of ruined cities and dying peoples drift in its failing mind.

A spaceship comes down on a dead, dusty planet where the Quedak waits. It drags itself down a hill, a centimetre at a time, in great pain. On Mars, Captain Jensen of the Southern Cross is bored with the search. His men have found only pottery shards and a corroded blade in ten days. The Quedak hopes the ship can carry it to worlds where it may serve again. Its kind owed a duty to give service to the native fauna.
52082-german-atrocities-a-record-of-sham:
German Atrocities is a British wartime book that records alleged German deeds in the Great War. Its subtitle calls the deeds shameless. The hosted text opens with pages of publisher notices. Those notices push a weekly pictorial war journal. They also offer portraits of Kitchener and Jellicoe. A novel of invasion, The Invasion by Le Queux, is pushed as well. Such matter fixes the book in the first war years.

Books of this kind gathered reports of harm to civilians. They named burned towns, shot hostages, and wrecked homes. Their aim was to stir British resolve and win neutral sympathy. The Kaiser's speech about the Huns is quoted against him. Modern readers treat such books with care. They mix true reports with the heat of war feeling. The volume stands as a piece of wartime persuasion.
52686-a-book-of-birds:
Carton Moore Park wrote this book of birds for young nature readers. Blackie and Son printed it in London in 1900. Short pieces treat one bird at a time in plain, warm prose. A drawing stands with each bird account in the book.

The flamingo waits on one leg in shallow water for fish. Park says its pink or scarlet hue shifts by its home land. The vulture cleans dead beasts, a useful if unlovely bird. The magpie steals eggs, builds a thorn fenced nest, and vexes farmers near and far.
52761-salt-water-ballads:
Salt-Water Ballads is a book of sea poems by John Masefield, first published when he was young. This Macmillan printing of 1915 reprints the 1913 reissue. Masefield's note says some of the book was written in his boyhood and all of it in his youth. The contents open with A Consecration and The Yarn of the Loch Achray.

The poems sing of clipper ships, fever ships, and burial parties at sea. Titles like Bill and Fever-Chills promise plain forecastle tales in verse. Masefield had sailed as a young man, and his ballads speak in the voice of the merchant sailor. The book made his name as the poet of the sea for his generation.
52782-aaron-in-the-wildwoods:
Aaron in the Wildwoods, by Joel Chandler Harris, was published in 1897. Houghton and Mifflin issued it at Boston and New York. Oliver Herford drew the pictures. Harris had won his fame with Uncle Remus. A prelude and fourteen chapters make the tale. The prelude opens on a large plantation in Middle Georgia. A boy called Little Crotchet fell ill as a small child. When the worst passed, he had lost the use of his legs. Told he would never run again, he laughed and asked his father for crutches.

Aaron, the swamp-wise hero of the title, carries the adventure. Contents promise the secrets of the swamp, a hunt begun and ended, and patrollers by night. Fox hunters see an apparition. The little master says good night at the close, and a death ends the pictures.
52787-pussy-black-face-or-the-story-of-a:
Marshall Saunders wrote Pussy Black-Face, the story of a kitten and her friends, for boys and girls. Page and Company of Boston published it in 1913, and a second impression followed within two months. Diantha Horne Marlowe drew the pictures. Saunders had won young readers before with Beautiful Joe, the dog story named under her name.

The kitten tells her own tale. The chapters open by the fire and pass through a surprising change, a visit to her family, and her first fight. The cat rides the train, reaches the country, and spends a summer in Maine among pigs, cows, and chickens. A mole hunt, an owl among the chickens, and the close of summer fill the later pages. Saunders dedicated the book to a leader of the Animal Rescue League of Boston. Children get animal life seen from the animal's side.
52885-scenes-in-north-wales-with-histori:
Wright's Scenes in North Wales, printed for Tegg at London in 1833 with thirty-six engravings, joins views of Welsh scenery to historical illustrations, legends, and biographical notices. The cover shows the Menai Bridge, Beaumaris Castle, and Holyhead Church.

The preface ties mountain scenery to a spirit of independence and love of liberty in the mountaineer. Feudal anarchy raised the castles of Gwynedd, and the ancient Britons remain distinct in customs, dress, feelings, and language. Wright compares them to the Isaurians, who kept their own ways in the heart of the Roman empire. The Cambrians, he says, grafted civilization onto the ancient stem.
53064-die-casting-dies-machines-methods:
Chester Lucas wrote a shop treatise on die casting, printed at New York in 1913 as number 109 of a machinery set. The set forms one shelf of machine design and shop practice. Contents name three parts: die casting itself, making dies for the machines, and one firm's shop practice.

The first chapter calls die casting a new way to make finished parts. Molten metal is forced into steel dies, cools there, and comes out finished and true in size. Such parts serve adding machines, typewriters, phones and motor cars. The writer aims to show what the method can and cannot do, and how the machines and die making work.
53130-a-guide-book-of-florida-and-the-so:
A Guide-Book of Florida and the South is a travel guide by Daniel Brinton, out in eighteen sixty-nine. It is made for guests, for the sick who seek warm air, and for those who would move south. A map of the great stream of that state comes with the book. Brinton took the famed guides of Europe as his mold, as far as the land let him.

He marks with a star each sight of note and each inn known to be well kept. Most spots are told from his own notes on a long tour of the point of land. Fare, beds, and costs rest on word from scores of guests. First hints treat the best term for south trips and the gear to pack. Paths by ship and rail open the main text.
53214-the-mystery-of-the-fifteen-sounds:
The Mystery of the Fifteen Sounds, a boys' science mystery by Van Powell, was published at Chicago in 1937. A note up front insists that every device and theory in it rests on real electrical and chemical practice. Its hero Roger works under his brilliant scientific cousin. Early chapters bring extraverted mice, a creeping thing, and a sound clue.

An electrical trap fails to catch what electricity could not, and ghost voices follow. Roger turns detective and scientist by turns, is captured, and reaches a lamasery where an image speaks. Black silence, a puzzling thump, and an unsent letter deepen the puzzle. Powell packs the tale with sound science, beams, and alarms fit for a young inventor hero. It belongs to the era's run of boys' books that mixed adventure with hands on science and radio age wonders.
54003-farm-legends:
Will Carleton's Farm Legends, from Harper and Brothers at New York, stands as companion to his Farm Ballads. The poems are entered in 1875 and copyrighted again in 1887, and the book is dedicated to the memory of his farmer father.

Carleton states his aim plainly in the preface. Every person, however humble, holds some good worth lifting up and saving, and every life mixes the comic with the sad. The verse groups run from the farm tales themselves to Decoration-Day poems, college poems, and poems of sorrow and death. Among them stand The School-master's Guests, Cover Them Over, The Burning of Chicago and The Railroad Holocaust.
54086-human-leopards:
Beatty, a barrister who lived for some years in Sierra Leone, wrote Human Leopards, published in London in 1915. Sir William Brandford Griffith supplied the preface. The book gives an account of the trials of human leopards before the Special Commission Court, and it carries thirty-three illustrations, opening with a view of Sackville Street, Freetown.

Early chapters explain the ground of the cases, covering the Poro, the Tongo play, borfima, witch-doctors, and oaths. Named trials follow, among them the Kale, Imperri, Kabati, and Yandehun cases, plus cases on borfima and membership. A last part steps back into a note on Sierra Leone, past and present. An appendix prints a despatch from the governor on measures taken against unlawful societies in the protectorate.
54173-how-to-make-candy-a-complete-hand-:
A complete hand book for candy makers was printed in New York in 1891 by Frank Tousey. It covers candy of all kinds, plus ice cream, syrups, and essences. Sugar is the base of the candy maker's art, the book says at the start. A full note tells how raw sugar is cleared for use.

Recipes and methods follow for home and shop use alike. One old recipe in the book calls for half a grain of mercury in each lozenge. A note at the front warns that some old ingredients are poison and the book is best used as a record, not a guide. That warning makes the book a sharp look at past food craft and past risk.
5420-rab-and-his-friends:
John Brown, a Scottish doctor and writer, gathered these sketches and stories around the figure of Rab, a faithful dog, and his master. The collection grew from a lecture Brown gave in his native village of Biggar, where he chose to tell his listeners the story of Ailie, a patient whose courage stayed with him. Warmth, humor, and simple human feeling run through the pieces.

The best-known tale follows a poor Scottish family and their dog through illness and loss, told in Brown's plain, affectionate voice. Other sketches recall doctors, villagers, and everyday kindness in nineteenth-century Scotland. Readers looking for gentle, humane storytelling will find this short book moving without ever turning sentimental.
54418-mr-wycherly-s-wards:
Mr Wycherly's Wards is a novel by L Allen Harker, published by Charles Scribner's Sons in 1912 as a sequel to Miss Esperance and Mr Wycherly. A village is scandalised when a quiet resident of twenty-five years prepares to move south to England, taking household goods with him.

The minister answers critics by pointing to Miss Esperance's will, which left house and furniture to Mr Wycherly in trust for her great-nephews. Villagers still shake their heads, asking what he will do once the little things are away to Oxford. Contents promise chapters called The Flittin, The Princess, The Beggar Maid, and Jane-Anne Swears Fealty. Harker writes in a Scots-tinged voice, and the book turns on trust, guardianship, and village opinion.
54546-time-and-clocks-a-description-of-a:
Time and Clocks is a description of ancient and modern methods of measuring time by H H Cunynghame, printed at London in 1906. The frontispiece shows a Nuremberg clock converted from a verge escapement to a pendulum movement. An appendix treats the shape of the teeth of wheels. Four chapters and an introduction make the body of the book.

Cunynghame opens with a reflection: when we read Homer, Virgil, and Plato, or Dante, Shakespeare, and Milton, we are apt to look with some disappointment upon present times. In the field of art, he grants, we must admit our inferiority to our ancestors in statues and architecture. That leads him to question whether our age equals theirs. But in the measuring of time the moderns have their triumph. The book traces sundials, water clocks, and the slow growth of the wheel clock.
54715-nights-with-the-gods:
Nights with the Gods is a set of imagined talks by Emil Reich. Laurie issued the book in London. Reich also wrote Foundations of Modern Europe. The contents list seven nights of conversation. Gods and heroes of old Greece meet above Florence. The Arno rolls below their terrace. A copy of Michelangelo's David stands on the hill.

Zeus opens the first night's meeting. Aristotle speaks on narrow study in England. Diogenes and Plato judge Tolstoy, Ibsen, and Shaw. Alcibiades holds forth on women in England. Caesar gives his view of the House of Commons. Apollo and Dionysus visit England in their turn. Socrates joins a talk on religion for the last night. The form lets Reich grade modern life through ancient mouths. Dialogue was his chosen tool for criticism.
54851-welsh-poems-and-ballads:
Welsh Poems and Ballads gathers English versions of Welsh verse by George Borrow, issued by Jarrold and Sons in 1915 with a preface by Ernest Rhys. The book is dedicated to Thomas J. Wise, at whose urging this Norfolk budget of Welsh verse was brought together. A picture shows Glendower's Mansion, copied from Borrow's own handwriting.

The poems come from Iolo Goch, Dafydd ab Gwilym, Goronwy Owen, Elis Wynn, and others. Some pieces are drawn from Borrow's Wild Wales, some from his Targum, and some from his papers. Subjects run from Glendower and Taliesin to the mist, the cuckoo's song, riches and poverty, and death the great.
54932-italian-backgrounds:
Italian Backgrounds is a set of travel essays by Wharton, with prints by a named hand. It came out at New York in the spring of the year cut in Roman marks on its title page. Its rights were set that same year.

A group from a famed cross scene heads the book as its front print. Its parts roam the high and low of Italy. A coach inn in the Alps and a weeks dream in high summer open the set. The shrines of the Pennine Alps and what the hermits saw come next. A shrine of Tuscany, a piece in Latin named for lilies, and a spring month in the land fill the mid run. A show piece on Milan closes the set.
55173-golden-dicky-the-story-of-a-canary:
Marshall Saunders wrote the story of a canary and his friends for young readers. Frederick A Stokes Company held the rights in New York in 1919. Saunders had written Beautiful Joe in the same kind vein before. A color front plate by George W Hood shows the hero bird.

Dicky-Dick the canary tells his own life from blind babyhood onward. His friend Chummy Hole-in-the-Wall, a sparrow, brings tales of squirrels and barns. Billie Sundae the dog and Sister Susie the dove fill the cast. Children gain a warm tale that pleads for kindness to beasts and birds.
55200-a-book-about-words:
Graham wrote A Book About Words at London in 1869, for Longmans, Green, and Company. Graham had taught English for a long career and wrote on style, synonyms, and grammar. His preface says more folk now study tongue as a school subject, yet much stays unknown to the lay reader. He offers these pages as a small step toward wider knowledge of words. The book came from his Kensington desk in May 1869.

Contents run from Saxon roots and word kin to Latin and French loans. Later parts take up old and new words, decay of words, and puns. Graham also treats plain and high words, spelling, and the growth of word forms. Readers who love English get a clear, teacherly guide to where words come from and how they change.
55246-yorkshire-vales-and-wolds:
Yorkshire Vales and Wolds is a travel book painted and described by Gordon Home. Black of London published it in the year 1908 for travellers. A front plate shows York from the Minster's central tower high above. Bootham Bar and the city wall stand on the right there. Contents open with Concerning the Wolds and a thirty page survey.

From Filey to Spurn Head and Beverley fill the next two chapters. Along the Humber and the Derwent and Howardian Hills follow in route. A brief description of the city of York fills chapter six. The manufacturing district closes the tour before the index ends it. Colour plates of abbeys, minsters, and mere and coast enrich the text.
55643-the-english-peasantry-and-the-encl:
Gilbert Slater wrote this study of the English peasantry and the enclosure of common fields, printed in London in 1907. The Earl of Carrington, president of the Board of Agriculture, adds an introduction. The front picture shows open fields at Epworth, in the Isle of Axholme. The book sits in a series of studies in economics and political science.

In his preface Slater says the work began in 1894, at the call of Graham Wallas and J A Spender. It grew into a thesis passed by the University of London in 1904. County maps mark each parish where common fields were enclosed by Act of Parliament. The maps, part-printed here, rest with the London School of Economics.
55684-firebrands:
Firebrands, by Frank E Martin and George M Davis, was held under a 1911 copyright and printed in Boston by Little, Brown, and Company in 1912 as a school edition. Photos fill the book. Its tales teach children how fires start and how to stop them.

The list opens with Brownie Misfortune, Careless Joe, May Day, and Camping Out. Thelma Birthday, Forest Fires, Pinch and Teddy, and The Busy Bees follow.
