Two parts teach how not to have fires, one on the kitchen fire. The Fire Drill, Fighting the Fire, and The World Great Fires stand late in the list. What to do in case of fire and first aid close the book. One tale tells of Polly and a big brown rat that came daily for food. School readers get safety lessons in story form.
56155-fairy-tales-from-gold-lands:
Fairy Tales from Gold Lands, by May Wentworth, was printed in New York and San Francisco in 1868. Wentworth gave the book to children at large, and most of all to her niece Mamie and nephew Wentworth. A short verse at the front calls the tales legends from the land of gold.

Ten tales fill the book, from Santa Claus and the Christ Child to The Moorish Pearls and The Two Good for Nothings. Other tales name Ching Chong Chinaman, Zaletta, and The Strong Man of Santa Barbara. One tale treats Emperor Norton, and one is set in Death Valley. The mix ties fairy tale charm to California gold land scenes. Young readers of its day got wonder set close to home.
56298-the-four-roads:
The Four Roads, published in 1921, is Sheila Kaye-Smith's novel of a patch of Sussex. Four roads bound the country below Dallington: the North Road from Rye to Lewes, the South Road along the marsh, the short East Road through woods, and the grass-grown West Road. Farms with names like Cowlease and Padgham string along them.

The book falls into seven parts, each named for a person. Tom, Jerry, Thyrza, Ivy, Nell and a baby take their turns. The last part follows Sumption, a Particular Baptist minister with a small Bethel in Sunday Street. Kaye-Smith roots every life in the same few miles of fields, ponds and lanes, and lets the roads carry the tale.
56980-holden-with-the-cords:
Jay's religious novel Holden with the Cords, published by Dutton at New York in 1874, takes its motto from Richard the Third: sin will pluck on sin. The author of Shiloh defends the religious novel in his preface.

Critics, he says, like a pill none the better for being sugar-coated, but younger readers may take religion gladly in story form. He argues that the great poems of the world are religious poems, so the great novel may be one too. His plot outline came from a yellow, time-worn manuscript purporting to be a true family history. A sculptor named Freeborne also aided him.
57197-mark-tidd-in-the-backwoods:
Clarence B Kelland wrote a boys' tale of Mark Tidd in the woods, issued in 1914. Harper and Brothers held the rights that year in New York and London. Mark Tidd had starred in books set in Egypt, Italy, and trade. Pictures show horse scares, pole leaps, and falls at Uncle Hieronymous's feet.

The tale starts just before school lets out for the long break. A first person voice, one of Mark's friends, tells what befell the group. Camp life, pranks, and small risks fill the summer weeks ahead. Young readers of the time got brisk fun with a fat, shrewd hero they knew well.
57224-the-mystery-of-seal-islands:
The Mystery of Seal Islands is a solve tale by Harrison Bardwell, out in nineteen thirty one. A World Syndicate house brought the book out that year. Roberta Langwell, a girl pilot, pours syrup on hot cakes in part one. Her kin quiz her on a state job for a Mr Howe of the air corps. Her dam fears that work, since past solve runs put her at risk.

Air gangs at Lurtiss Field made that past work a grave game for her. A rich fur wife named Pollzoff has hired her to fly the coast of late. That wife sold her dead man fur stake to a big group combine. Cake praise and Lindbergh hoard jest fill the home first scene. Harv, her brother, backs her at the board in that talk.
57380-eastern-stories-and-legends:
Eastern Stories and Legends is a retelling of the Buddha birth stories by Marie L Shedlock, published in New York by E P Dutton and Company in 1920. Shedlock was a noted storyteller, and the tales here come from the Jataka tradition. The editor's preface praises them in large terms.

These stories of the Buddha rebirths, the preface says, are not for one age or country. They belong to all time and the whole world. Their philosophy could enter the faith of a League of Nations, the editor argues, without destroying any national teaching. Orthodox readers, too, will find their ethics identical with much taught in the stories. T W Rhys Davids, the great Pali scholar, stands behind the volume's authority. Shedlock's gift was oral: simple, grave retellings that carried Asian moral tales to English and American schoolrooms.
5762-grammar-and-vocabulary-of-the-lau-l:
Walter Ivens presents a grammar and vocabulary of the Lau language of the Solomon Islands, published by the Carnegie Institution. The transcriber notes that some fine distinctions of neighboring Saa orthography were lost, while Lau spelling stands as given. Ivens sets out sounds, word forms, and sentence patterns, then supplies a vocabulary for learners and field workers.

The book serves linguists, missionaries, and historians of the Pacific, preserving a record of Lau as spoken in its time. Readers will find a scholarly reference rather than a storybook, with paradigms and word lists as its core. Its value lies in documentation: a language community's speech, captured in print for study and for descendants seeking their heritage.
57729-bumper-the-white-rabbit-and-his-fr:
Bumper the White Rabbit and His Friends is a children's animal story by George Ethelbert Walsh. It belongs to the Twilight Animal Series for boys and girls from four to ten years old. Edwin Prittie drew the coloured pictures. The John Winston Company published the series from Chicago, Philadelphia, and Toronto.

Bumper's adventures fill four books: at home, in the woods, against his foes, and with his friends. Bobby Gray Squirrel carries the later volumes of the series. Walsh wrote the tales for reading aloud at twilight, as the series name promises. Gentle animal talk and small dangers fill the pages for the youngest readers.
57757-two-college-friends:
Two College Friends is a novel by Frederick Loring. The author's brother published it at Boston. The copyright entry dates to 1871. Loring had earlier written a book of verses. A preface in letter form dedicates the novel to a college friend.

The letter explains the book's making. A beloved teacher inspired the story. News of that teacher's death came as Loring wrote the opening pages. Midway through, Loring was called to remote parts of the country. The novel thus became a sketch, a bare outline of his plan. He asks only that one heart throb with love of country. A poem of farewell to soldiers follows the letter. The tale then opens in dream.
57758-bess-of-the-woods:
Warwick Deeping's novel of 1906 opens at Sir Peter Hardacre's dining table, where Richard Jeffray sits ill at ease among men who have fed too well. Sir Peter sprawls in his armchair, Parson Jessel snores with his wig tipping over one eye, and Lot Hardacre, half jockey and half card-sharper, winks and pipes his talk.

Dick wants to leave early, pleading the short day and the saddle, while Lot teases him about his sister Jilian at the harpsichord upstairs. The chapter sets a country-house world of punch bowls, snuff, and blunt talk. Deeping, author of The Slanderers and Uther and Igraine, builds his tale from this company.
57908-bumper-the-white-rabbit-in-the-woo:
George Ethelbert Walsh wrote this animal tale for children, in his Twilight Animal Series. Bumper the White Rabbit in the Woods is one of several Bumper books, alongside Bumper and his foes and friends. Walsh also wrote the Bobby Gray Squirrel tales.

A plate shows the great moment whole: Bumper leaps into the air in one huge spring, clean across to the far side. Colour plates fill the book, as the series promised. Bumper, a white rabbit in a wild wood, must learn what a tame pet never knows: hawks, foxes, and the long winter. Walsh tells animal life close and kind, with the woods as school and danger both.
58185-the-crystal-palace-and-other-legen:
The Crystal Palace and Other Legends is a book of tales retold by Marie Frary and Charles Stebbins, published at New York in 1909. Herbert Martini drew the pictures. The title tale opens long ago in the village of Zurdorf, where a queer little old woman lives alone. One night a knock comes at her cottage door as she knits.

Nineteen legends fill the book. They include the Lorelei, the sunken city, the bell of Atri, and the pot of hot porridge. Charlemagne's generosity, the magic ring, the pet raven, and the swan knight also appear. The tales retell old European lore in plain words for young readers.
58578-historical-tales-and-legends-of-th:
Historical Tales and Legends of the Highlands was compiled by Alexander Mackenzie, editor of the Celtic Magazine. It was published at Inverness by A and W Mackenzie in 1878, with Maclachlan and Stewart of Edinburgh. Mackenzie promises tales and legends of the Highlands, and the book's first long piece is headed Locality.

Locality describes a west coast village cut off from the outer world, without steamers, railways, or even roads. Its people grow their own corn and produce their own beef, mutton, butter, cheese, and wool, doing their own carding, spinning, and weaving. Tobacco and tea, which they cannot produce, come once a month on the back of the district's only merchant. Their houses are undressed stone and moss, thatched with turf or straw held down by old herring nets.
58694-highland-legends:
Highland Legends is a gathering of Scottish tales and scenes by Sir Thomas Dick Lauder, given here in the edition of 1880. Two volumes stand in one. Lauder had writ The Moray Floods and The Wolf of Badenoch. The book is dedicated to the Countess Grey, in honour of her love of Scotland. Its first form bore a longer name: Highland Rambles and Long Legends to Shorten the Way. The rambles, the new preface owns, are a small part of the whole.

The contents open with moorland scenery and the burning of Macfarlane's forest of Benlaoidh. The loss of Scotland's woods gets a grave essay of its own. Tales of reavers, lovers' cairns, and Big John Mackay fill the list. The Findhorn river gives the scenery pieces their ground. The book is a verbatim reprint of the author's own text, long tales for the road and the fireside.
58958-horse-training-by-modern-methods:
Allan Melvill Pope, a first lieutenant of cavalry in the United States Army, wrote Horse Training by Modern Methods for the Franklin Hudson Publishing Company at Kansas City in 1912. A plate shows Galley Slave, a two-year-old filly at Sagamore Farm, winner of three California races and one world record.

Pope says his aim is to set the modern system in the clearest, briefest form for the mounted service. He claims no new methods: where the best horsemen agreed, he took their words, with credit. His debts run to Major Cameron, Captain Short, James Fillis, and the Saumur notes on equitation. Commands, terms, and drills are standardised for army use.
59166-common-sense-for-housemaids:
A lady wrote a handbook of common sense for housemaids, in a second edition printed at London in 1853. Its contents are a working list: how to clean brass, grates, marble, mirrors, lamps, and plate, how to light a fire, and how to prepare pipeclay. The housemaid's daily work takes forty pages by itself.

Extracts from a lady's journal open the book, meant to show the need for it. She recalls arriving in Cavendish Square fatigued, sustained only by the vision of a well-made bed, a clear glowing fire, and a little kettle singing on the hob. Clear-starching, washing muslins and lace, and hints on nursing the sick fill the back.
59304-bright-islands:
Bright Islands is a science fiction story by Frank Riley. The Project Gutenberg text was taken from Worlds of If Science Fiction for June 1955. A line from Rilke stands at its head, on the future entering into us long before it happens.

The story opens in a bare room of a Genetics Center. Miryam holds a red capsule under her tongue and does not yet swallow. Two Geno-Doctors have just left her. She carries a child the Center does not want. Pain moves through her like slow fire. She prays to the old God of the Ghetto, from which she once escaped. She had taught small children in a Warsaw suburb before the agents seized her last fall. The tale holds her at the edge of a willed death, in triumph as she sees it.
60164-fancies-versus-fads:
Fancies Versus Fads is a set of essays by Chesterton, first published by Methuen at London in 1923. A list of his earlier books at the front runs from Charles Dickens to The Flying Inn. The contents open with an introduction and The Romance of Rhyme. Hamlet and the psycho analyst gives the second essay its target.

The Meaning of Mock Turkey and Shakespeare and the Legal Lady follow. On Being an Old Bean and The Fear of the Film keep the comic vein. Wings and the housemaid, free verse, and prohibition and the press fill the middle list. Chesterton argues that fads are dull and fancies are free. His essays turn trifles into philosophy with a laugh. Few essayists of his age matched his swiftness of paradox.
60410-the-life-of-gen-robert-e-lee-for-c:
The Life of Robert Lee for Children, in Easy Words, is a school reader by Mary Williamson. She copyrighted it in 1895 at Harrisonburg, Virginia; this copy is a 1989 reprint by Sprinkle Publications. The front picture shows the unveiling of the Lee monument at Richmond in May 1890. Williamson wrote the life for use in public schools as an extra reader.

Her preface gives teachers her reasons. Children who study history early, she holds, grow in mind faster than those kept to story readers. No American hero, she argues, shows such moral grandeur as Lee. The book uses marked sounds and syllables to help young readers, drawing chiefly on Fitzhugh Lee's life of his uncle.
60839-a-pride-of-islands:
MacApp's A Pride of Islands ran in Worlds of If Science Fiction in May 1960. A tagline asks whether a planet has a right to be so strange that it makes fleas of men.

The strangeness is literal: Alyarsmit and his friend Brusmit are tiny people who live on the back of a giant beast, climbing hairs six man-lengths tall to watch for other beasts. Their clan, the smits, ride their beast across its world, signalling with eyestalks, and dreading the fleys that hunt in the hair forest. Their leader Paboss won his wife by stealing her from a rival clan, and wears the scars to prove it. MacApp builds a whole society, its wars, trades, and thefts, at flea scale on a living landscape.
60885-the-fair-rewards:
Thomas Beer published the novel The Fair Rewards in New York in 1922. Its first chapter, Manufacture of a Personage, opens in August 1895 at rehearsals of a play called Nicoline. The producer, John Carlson, is nervous about the production, and his digestion and temper suffer for it. He abandons the small parts to his stage manager and nurses his two stars toward ease.

Carlson faints at another opening, is revived with brandy, and spends the last six days before his own opening in bed. Still, he dresses grandly for the night and dines with the young adapter who turned Nicoline from the French. Chapter titles trace a theatrical life: progress, full bloom, penalties, and figures named Margot, Gurdy, and Cosmo Rand. Readers get a backstage novel about how a personage is made, and what the making costs.
60977-the-girl-scouts-at-singing-sands:
Mildred Wirt wrote a girls' camp tale printed at New York in 1955, with drawings by Marguerite Geyer. The front picture cries, come here quick, tell me what you see. Twenty five chapters carry the book. It opens as a dusty station wagon turns in at dusk to Pine Cone Camp.

Miss Louise Ward, the troop leader, smiles back at six girls of Beaver Patrol. Their green berets sit at six angles. Heads name a locked door, a hole, night sounds, and a flute song. A white witch, a treasure box, and rich cargo follow. A lost key, smoke in the woods, and a dip into the cave lead to a court of honour at the close.
61096-diamonds:
William Crookes wrote Diamonds, a small book in Harper's Library of Living Thought, in 1909. Harper sold it at London and New York, with twenty-four plates. A photo by Crookes of the Cullinan diamond fronts the book. Crookes was a famed man of science, past head of many learned bodies in Britain. He gives the book to his wife, his companion and friend of fifty-four years. To her judgment and advice, he says, he owes more than he can tell.

The book treats the diamond from mine to cut gem in plain terms. Its history, its tests, and its great named stones all take their turns. Photos aid the eye at each step of the craft. Crookes writes with the ease of a man who knew gems at first hand.
61183-weeds:
Pío Baroja wrote a novel of Madrid life translated from the Spanish by Isaac Goldberg and published by Knopf at New York in October 1923. Baroja's other books are listed: The City of the Discreet, Youth and Egolatry, Caesar or Nothing, and The Quest. Part one opens in a studio, with the life led by Roberto Hasting and Alex Monzón. Señorita Esther Volovitch and a wedding follow.

Manuel, a photographer's apprentice, enters in chapter two. The Europea and the Benefactora appear in chapter three. Weeds is the second volume of Baroja's trilogy on Madrid's struggling poor. Goldberg introduced several Spanish modernists to American readers. Knopf's Borzoi list carried the translation.
61219-central-station-electric-lighting-:
Central-Station Electric Lighting is an engineering treatise by Killingworth Hedges, a civil engineer, enlarged from a paper he read to the Institution of Civil Engineers in 1886. The book describes the systems practically used for lighting from a central station, at home and on the Continent, with notes on the distribution of electricity.

Hedges writes at a turning point. Electric lighting was ten years old, half a million pounds had been sunk in it, and the surviving companies were worth a tenth of that. Yet central-station supply, the subject of Siemens's address of 1882, was now both a scientific fact and a commercial success. Water power or coal could light streets and houses by night and drive small machinery by day. Hedges omits generating plant on purpose and adds a glossary, aiming the book at investors and engineers together.
61567-stonehenge-a-temple-restor-d-to-th:
William Stukeley wrote Stonehenge, a Temple Restor'd to the British Druids, printed in London in 1740. Stukeley was Rector of All Saints in Stamford. He gave the book to Peregrine, Duke of Ancaster and Kesteven, the hereditary Lord Great Chamberlain of England. The Latin motto on the title page is drawn from Manilius.

In a long dedication, Stukeley praises the duke's faith, love of country, and steady conduct. He calls Stonehenge one of the noblest antiquities now left upon earth. He stresses that it is both a religious antiquity and a British one. The dedication also thanks the duke for favours over many years of acquaintance. The book argues that the great stone circle was a temple of the Druids.
6164-the-life-of-the-fields:
Richard Jefferies gathers The Life of the Fields from magazine pieces, thanking editors who allowed reprints. The Field-Play appeared in Time, Bits of Oak Bark and The Pageant of Summer in Longman's Magazine, and Meadow Thoughts and Mind under Water in The Graphic.

Clematis Lane, Nature near Brighton, Sea, Sky, and Down, and January in the Sussex Woods came from The Standard, with other essays from art, nature, and London papers. Contents promise the pageant of summer, field play, acorn gathering, and rural dynamite. Jefferies writes country life with close eyes and a poet's patience.
61796-for-the-birds:
The Fish and Wildlife Service of the United States issued this guide in March 2001. Among the fondest moments of childhood are discoveries of songbirds nesting in the backyard, it begins. Mud-lined nests of robins and their blue eggs captivate people of all ages, the guide says in its opening lines.

House wrens, cardinals and chickadees can stir a lifelong interest in nature, it adds. Readers may improve the habitat of a yard so more birds visit the property. Feeders, nest boxes and bird baths, with trees, shrubs and flowers for food and shelter, are the guide's plain recipe for a bird-friendly home ground.
61802-quaker-strongholds:
Quaker Strongholds is a book on the principles of the Society of Friends by Caroline Emelia Stephen. Longstreth published it at Philadelphia in 1891. Stephen also wrote The Service of the Poor. Chapters treat organization, the Inner Light, worship, and free ministry. Special testimonies and a chapter called Our Calling follow.

Her introduction says that few outside the society are accurately informed about its point of view. Yet almost everyone, she notes, has some link with Friends. Any revival of religion, she argues, must rest on a fresh acceptance of the principles on which Quakerism is built. The book explains silent worship and the refusal of a paid ministry from inside the society.
62230-kitchen-tested-recipes-from-canned:
Kitchen Tested Recipes from Canned Foods opens, in the head, with a guide to common can sizes. Small flat cans for meat spreads such as ham, tongue, and liver come first. A half flat can, used principally for salmon, follows at about one cup.

A number one tall can serves salmon and fruit cocktail. A number two can is used primarily for vegetables, fruits, and juices. Larger cans for fruits, spinach, tomatoes, sauerkraut, beets, and pumpkin are described. The number ten can is the institutional or restaurant size, not ordinarily available in retail stores. An introduction follows: preparing attractive, nutritious meals for the family is an aim in every home. To those who know the economy and convenience of canned foods, the book speaks. Readers get a canning industry cookbook that begins by teaching the sizes of the cans themselves.
62345-collectors-items-fifty-superb-reci:
Collectors' Items is a recipe booklet from the Spice Islands company. Its subtitle promises fifty superb recipes from that brand. A note says the recipes run from appetizers to desserts. They are shared from the company recipe file to the reader's own. The recipes were developed and tested with Spice Islands seasonings. An herb chart is included in the booklet as a guide. That chart helps cooks who like to vary their own favourite dishes.

The booklet teaches that an herb should enhance, not dominate, a flavour. Beginners are told to use just one or two herbs at a time. Spice Islands herbs are said to be grown in California. Farms owned by the company raise select strains of them. That control is said to keep the flavour full and fresh. The booklet is both a cookbook and a piece of brand promotion.
62488-castles-of-ireland-some-fortress-h:
Castles of Ireland gives the histories and legends of some eighty Irish strongholds. Adams compiled the book, with drawings by Canon Lucius O'Brien. Stock published the volume at London in 1904. An Adare Castle plate faces the title page.

The entries run in alphabetical order from Adare to Trim. Blarney, Bunratty, and Carrickfergus stand among the famed names. Dublin Castle and the two King John's castles get their chapters. A verse legend of Kilkea opens the book, telling of a ghostly troop on the Curragh. Adams mixes plain fact with the tales told at each ruin. Many seats were still lived in when he wrote. The book is a gazetteer of Irish history told castle by castle.
62768-the-red-pirogue-a-tale-of-adventur:
The Red Pirogue is a tale of adventure in the Canadian wilds by Captain Theodore Goodridge Roberts. L C Page and Company published it in Boston in 1924. Street and Smith held the 1922 copyright. Frank T Merrill drew the illustrations. The frontispiece shows raging waters rising past a jumping, squirming canoe.

Young Ben O'Dell opens the story at dawn. He carries a paddle through orchard and alder thicket to the river beach. Mist crawls on the sliding water and the sky burns pink and gold. The grey sixteen-foot pirogue waits below the bank. Ben uses it between the point and the island, tending the salmon net. It is heavy and crank but tough. The contents promise a drifting fire, a trap for the hungry, and red dogs at work. A sick man and a rescue in the nick of time close the tale.
62992-the-evolution-of-worlds:
The Evolution of Worlds is an astronomy book by Percival Lowell. Macmillan brought the book out from New York and London alike. A photograph of Saturn from the Lowell Observatory fronts the volume. Slipher took that picture of the ringed planet in September 1909. Lowell directed the observatory at Flagstaff, Arizona, in those years.

He had writ Mars and Its Canals and Mars as the Abode of Life. Medals from France and Mexico honoured his researches on Mars there. The book traces how worlds are born, grow, and die in space. Notes stand changed to plain references so footnotes stay clear for readers. Small capitals stand converted and pictures moved for the text's good. A saying of Napoleon on the exact sciences heads the matter. Lowell taught astronomy at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology as well. His title page crowds with society memberships from many lands.
63075-coco-bolo-king-of-the-floating-isl:
Sidford Hamp wrote a tale for young readers held under a 1910 right, of a king of isles that float. Margaret, near eight, and Frances, six and a bit, chase their own shadows on a road in Southern California. They try to step on their own heads in the sun, a feat they have yet to pull off.

Young Edward, with legs too short for the trek, must nap while his sisters slip out on their quest. Parts to come bring an admiral of boxwood, a royal yacht, the kings hounds, and a court crier. Prints of falls, floats, and flights mark the soft whimsy of the small realm.
63095-quartz-from-the-uplands:
A verse set came out from the Anti-Pessimist Society at Piermont, New York, in 1905. Its name is Quartz from the Uplands. The book is sent forth to the American Antiquarian Society. The first poem takes up a cry of the day: who says that all songs have been sung and all tales told? Who says that live tongues are still, worn smooth by the ways of those who came before?

The poem gives the cry a flat no. In the full state of the soul there lives a wealth that no use can drain, bound strong till a great deed sets it loose. No man should stand mute at the bier of the dead past and grant that all has been sung and writ. He must beat loud on the door of the shrine, steeled to bear the jeers of those in it.
63097-warrior-of-two-worlds:
Warrior of Two Worlds, by Manly Wade Wellman, ran in Planet Stories in the summer of 1944. A man wakes face down in dust on a strange world, his name and past wiped clean. A voice, from no clear place, tells him where he lies: Dondromogon. The Masters of the Worlds had him snatched from Earth for a set fate, to lead here as Yandro, the Stranger of the Prophecy. He does not know if he recalls his home at all.

The voice maps his new world: one face locked to its sun, its metals run in seas of fire; the far face froze in dark. Two twilight lunes shift from night to day and can hold life. Space fans get a lost man, a split world, and a war he must fight on both sides.
6329-catalogue-of-british-columbia-birds:
The Provincial Museum at Victoria publishes this catalogue of birds proven to occur in British Columbia, with a preface that admits its incompleteness frankly. The north and northeast interior remain a valuable field for work, and distribution notes for some species stay thin. Since John Fannin's 1898 list of 339 species and subspecies, the compiler adds twenty-four more, with thanks to constant observers like A. C. Brooks of Chilliwack and the Okanagan.

Entries run in systematic order, with places and seasons noted. A red backed sandpiper is common in spring and autumn migration along island and mainland coasts, taken at Chilliwack. A semipalmated sandpiper is not uncommon on the coast and common at Metlakatla. The catalogue is a working list for naturalists, plain in form and rich in local record, valuable precisely because it names its gaps and its helpers.
63523-coming-of-the-gods:
Chester Whitehorn wrote this Mars tale for Planet Stories, where it ran in the Summer 1945 issue. Its head note says Mars had never seen men like these. They came from black space with strange guns, to fight for a race they had never heard of.

Ro, a Martian, picks his way through the jungles of his home world. He knows the swamp snake Gin and its swift poison well. He has seen the Droo, plants that eat men, cast out the bones of the luckless. Quicksand pools and beasts of prey thin his friends' ranks. Ro is bound home, light of heart, yet he takes no step in that jungle without care.
63786-engines-of-the-gods:
Engines of the Gods is a science fiction story by Gardner Fox, taken from Planet Stories for the spring of 1946. The engine was the wealth of Mars. With it Kortha could save his people, or the evil Guantra could rule the universe. But neither could use the machine until its secret was solved. So they fought and schemed for the knowledge, and their planet lay on the brink of destruction.

Kortha the smith broods over the great red waste of desert. Men said Kortha was a genius, the biggest man on Mars, strong as an ape. But Kortha brooded because Kortha was a coward. He was not afraid for himself; he was afraid of himself. With those sun-bronzed, hamlike hands he had killed men, and had crippled his best friend for life.
63795-the-shadow-gods:
Vaseleos Garson wrote a science fiction tale that ran in Planet Stories in summer 1946. Curt Wing watches from a ship as fireflies of light slip past the dark side of the Moon. Hundreds of small craft blink on by ones, twos, and threes as they clear the moon's rim. Curt whistles low at the sight.

Lieutenant George Packer pulls on his helmet and reaches for a red button. The crew has waited two weeks, and for seven hours has gone half mad with strain. Mercurians are out there in the dark, the men know. A blurb tells of tortured humans fleeing shadow things and a blue flower that crushes and sears. Space dread drives the tale.
63843-the-madcap-metalloids:
W V Athanas wrote this science fiction story, printed in Planet Stories in the summer of 1949. Two intrepid Terrans are plucked from the space-lanes by ravening magnetism and defy the death of a radioactive worldlet by playing games with its roly-poly natives, the blurb promises.

Jonathan Drake swims back to consciousness slowly, as a bubble rises through molasses. His arms lie heavy on the shock-chair rests and his lids droop against his brain's shouted commands. He works a hand along the rest like a spider until a finger finds the release button. The pads fall free and the seat tips him gently onto the floor. Readers get a crash-survivor opening in pulp style.
64078-nibble-rabbit-makes-more-friends:
John Breck tells woodland tales in Nibble Rabbit Makes More Friends, printed at Garden City, New York, in 1923. Doubleday Page made the book, first edition, with plates by William Andrews. It stands in the Told at Twilight Stories, mostly about Nibble the bunny. A plate shows Watch making friends with Nibble.

Thirteen chapters follow the bunny. Why Nibble bunny was puzzled, and how Nibble the bunny was caught, open the run. How Nibble tricked a foe and made a friend follows. Why dogs love babies and Nibble's doubts about dogs bring the dog in. The cleverness of Chirp Sparrow and how a bunny could help a boy vary the tales. What Doctor Muskrat thought about traps, and his singular mishap, close in on wise words from a wise beast.
64079-the-happy-hunting-grounds:
Kermit Roosevelt's Happy Hunting-Grounds was published in London by Hodder and Stoughton in 1920, from copyrights of 1912 and 1920. Roosevelt illustrates the book from his own photographs and dedicates it to the Mistress of Sagamore. The opening essay argues that men show themselves truly when they are off in the wilds.

He recalls his father's test of a hunting companion: whether the man fished in the pot for the best piece of meat. Chapters hunt sable antelope and the sheep of the desert, and go after moose in New Brunswick. Two book-hunters in South America and a sketch of Seth Bullock, sheriff of the Black Hills country, round out the contents.
6408-letters-of-anton-chekhov-to-his-fam:
Constance Garnett chooses from eighteen hundred and ninety letters published by Chekhov's family those that best show his life, character, and opinions, with a memoir abridged from his brother Mihail's sketch. Letters to his wife after marriage were not yet published when she worked. The sketch opens in 1841, when a serf of a Russian nobleman bought freedom for himself and his family. The price was three thousand five hundred roubles, seven hundred a soul, with a daughter Alexandra thrown in for nothing.

That serf's grandson was Anton Chekhov, and the nobleman's son was Tchertkov, the Tolstoyan. Chekhov writes to family and friends with a doctor's eye and a storyteller's brevity, reading Bourget's Disciple in Russian and judging him gifted, intelligent, cultured, and steeped in natural science method. Garnett's volume is a life in letters, where a grandson of a serf becomes Russia's clearest witness.
6418-five-little-peppers-and-their-frien:
Margaret Sidney dedicates this book to her daughter Margaret, who embodies Polly Pepper in girlhood for her friends. A preface explains that so many interesting friends of the Five Little Peppers deserved their own stories, and this volume gives them. A five o'clock tea opens, with Phronsie sitting in the middle of the stairs, Clem Forsythe, and Miss Taylor's working bee.

Grandma Bascom, a disappointment, a garden party, and a ten dollar bill follow, with trouble for Joel, Rachel, and doings at the parsonage. Rachel laughs at a fine lady's dignity, doubles up her thin figure, and goes off in a gust of mirth. Sidney writes warm family comedy, where friends widen the Peppers' world and kindness, not wealth, settles each trouble.
64407-dick-merriwell-s-ae-ro-dash-or-win:
Dick Merriwell Aero Dash is a boys tale by Burt Standish, out in nineteen ten. A Street and Smith house of New York holds that right claim in full. Its next name calls it a win above the clouds in the scheme. Brose Stovebridge, a wild wheel man, heads the first part in a crash. He guns a new high force car down a flat two mile road at dawn.

Wheat fields wave on both sides of that road in the scene set. Fear strikes him when law, jail, and a hurt child crowd his mind. Part names mix ball play and sky race in one wild scheme. A scrap of note, a dark fight, and Dick wins fill first ranks. Three men of wealth, a hid house, and cliff shade stand mid parts.
6480-on-the-study-of-words:
Richard Chenevix Trench, archbishop, delivers On the Study of Words as lectures, in a twentieth edition revised by A. L. Mayhew. Coleridge's motto opens it: language is the armoury of the human mind, holding trophies of past conquests and weapons of future ones. Trench urges something beyond books: not in books only, nor connected oral discourse, but in words contemplated singly lie boundless stores of moral and historic truth, passion, and imagination.

Lectures cover poetry in words, morality in words, history in words, rise of new words, distinction of words, and the schoolmaster's use of words. A mid passage notes how idiot came to be called innocent, one who does no hurt, assuming hurt and harm are men's chief employment. Trench writes philology as moral history, where each word carries a lesson worth learning.
6489-a-book-of-golden-deeds:
Charlotte M. Yonge asks what a golden deed is, then answers with stories from Alcestis and Antigone to the Vendeans. The cup of water, how one man saved a host, the pass of Thermopylae, and the rock of the Capitol open the book. The two friends of Syracuse, the devotion of the Decii, and Regulus follow. The brethren of Judah, the chief of the Arverni, and the last fight in the Coliseum follow. Guzman el Bueno, faithful till death, the keys of Calais, and Sempach follow.

The constant prince, the carnival of Perth, the crown of St. Stephen, George the Triller, and Sir Thomas More's daughter sit beside heroes of plague, gunpowder perils, and soldiers in snow. A mid passage shows a penitent emperor, crown, purple robe, and buskins laid aside, prostrate before Ambrose, who pronounces forgiveness in his Master's name. Yonge writes heroism for young readers, deed by deed.
65065-base-ball-ballads:
Base-Ball Ballads is a book of poems about baseball by Grantland Rice, sporting editor of the Nashville Tennessean. It was printed at Nashville by the Tennessean Company in 1910. The pictures are by Wellington. All are bound alike, it says, by the bondage of the full box score.

The contents list some sixty ballads. Play Ball opens the book. There are songs of the road to Rooters' Row, a day in the bleachers, and Mudville's Fate, Rice's answer to the famous Casey poem. The poems are written in the slang and swing of the sporting page. They show the game as its fans lived it in 1910: a summer religion with its own heroes, heartbreaks and holy days.
65139-history-of-birds:
History of Birds is a small plate book for the young on the birds of the world. It came out at London from a press of church books. Each bird gets a drawn plate and a short note in plain words. Each note ties the bird to a line of the old book and to a rule for the young.

The great flight less bird leaves its eggs in the waste and can lose them, the first note says. In the old book the cruel and lax are set past that bird. The great bird of prey is strong and fierce, yet it heeds the word of God and is used to chastise the proud. The proud bird of fine plumes shows that all gifts come from God. The goose, thought a fool, proves more wise than its fame, a hint for how the young judge their mates.
65195-quicksands:
Quicksands is a novel by Croker, author of The Cat's Paw, issued by Cassell and Company of London and New York. The tale is told by a woman who looks back on her life with her brother Ronald. It opens on a sultry day in flat, marshy country in England, by a small bridge over a slow stream.

Chapter heads trace a path from the marshes to India, with a hill station, a residency ball, and days at Bangalore. Names like the notorious Mrs. De Lacy and places like Hyder Ali's garden hint at Anglo-Indian society. The tale mixes home scenes, club life, and hard turns of fate across two worlds.
6524-stray-birds:
Tagore lines up more than three hundred tiny poems, each no more than a few lines, like birds that land, sing, and fly on. Summer birds at a window, autumn leaves with no song, desert sand begging for a tune, and tears that keep smiles in bloom all pass in quick succession. The book takes its shape from that brief, bright movement.

No poem stays long enough to grow heavy, yet many leave a clear image or a sharp turn of thought behind. Love, loss, the earth, and the small wonders of a day are the chief subjects, handled with a light hand. Stray Birds suits slow reading, a page or two at a time, with room to pause between each flash.
65524-modern-street-ballads:
John Ashton made this set of the street songs of his day, printed at London in 1888. Fifty-six cuts go with the text. His first word is a wail for the kind. Ichabod, he cries: their fame has fled. The street songs held their own for long years, brave and well. But they have sunk in front of a new order of things.

A new breed of men will not stop in the street to hear a song sung, he says. They like their tune served hot, with warmth, light, ale, and leaf to smoke, at the halls of song. And they pay for it, he notes. In their prime the street songs were made in a few hours of any deed of note.
65555-green-timber-thoroughbreds:
Theodore Goodridge Roberts wrote a tale of north woods men and fine bred stock. Green Timber Thoroughbreds is its full proud name in print. The book came out in 1924 at Garden City, New York. Rights date to 1923 and 1924 in two claims in front. In the Nick of Time leads its list of twelve parts.

Joe, throw backs, and the dire danglers fill the front parts. A walled road, a warn, and a knock out mark the mid turns. The raid and the way out build the late hunt in the woods. Deep trails, a buy, and no risks close the list of parts. Old Dave Hinch wakes to smoke in his nose on page one. His beard's risk wakes him fast.
65626-simple-poems-for-infant-minds:
Short poems for young children fill a small book issued in New York by Kiggins and Kellogg. The Sail Boat opens the set. A little boat glides like a bird, pressed forward by the tides. The child speaker would like to live upon the sea, free of trouble.

Yet a storm would send him back to his mother's arms for safety. A Little Story praises a boy who minds his errands and holds his fork as he should. The poem asks the youngest reader if that boy is you. My Little Doll Rose and My Bird Is Gone follow in the same vein. Each verse is brief, rhymed, and easy to learn by heart.
65813-citadel-of-the-star-lords:
Citadel of the Star Lords is a science fiction story by Edmond Hamilton, printed in Imagination magazine in October 1956. The blurb promises a conquering horde out of the dark void, incredible and unbeatable, with Earth's only weapon a man from the past. The tale opens at night over the deserts of California and Nevada. Price guns his plane northward without lights.

He thinks of a fairground roller-coaster, and of the big plunge he is now on, ending in prison, escape, or a crash. He keeps high and clear of the airways, watching for Border Patrol planes on his tail. News in the tale tells of a fiery exile smuggled over the border, and a wide air hunt for the unknown pilot who flew him.
65825-marching-sands:
Harold Lamb wrote Marching Sands, issued in New York and London by D Appleton and Company in nineteen twenty. Copyright also rests with the Frank A Munsey Company from nineteen nineteen. Twenty six chapters fill the novel. Chapter one is The Lost People. You want me to fail, a man says in a level voice to open it. He sat staring in front of him, hands crossed over his knees.

Legends and Delabar Discourses follow the opening. Warning, Intruders, and Mirai Khan come next. The Door Is Guarded and Delabar Leaves lead to The Liu Sha, the moving sands. The Mem Sahib Speaks and Sir Lionel enter the tale. A Message from the Centuries and The Desert fill the middle. The Yellow Robe, Bassalor Danek, and Concerning a City raise the mystery. Rifle against Arrow and The Bronze Circlet close it. Adventure readers get a Central Asia lost race tale.
66069-choice-recipes-and-menus-using-can:
Choice Recipes and Menus Using Canned Foods is a cook book built on tinned goods. It opens with a guide to common can sizes. The half flat can holds about one cup and is used chiefly for salmon, at seven and three-quarter to eight and a half ounces. The 8Z tall can holds about one cup too, at eight ounces, for some vegetables and fruits.

The guide runs on through the sizes of the trade. The 300 can holds about one and three-quarter cups, for meats and specialties. The 1 tall holds about two cups and serves for salmon, fruits, and more. The 303 holds about two cups for vegetables, fruits, juices, and soups. The 2 can holds about two and a half cups, and the 2 and a half about three and a half, chiefly for fruits. The book is a home guide to meals from the store shelf.
66160-the-origin-of-metallic-currency-an:
William Ridgeway, who taught Greek at Queen's College in Cork, wrote a study of how coined money and weight units first arose, issued at Cambridge in 1892. Coin men before him had stuck to the first coins of Lydia, Greece, and Italy. Weight men had stuck to the systems of Babylon, Egypt, Greece, and Rome.

Ridgeway brings in the matched study of many peoples to find first rules for both crafts. He traces the first Greek coin types, the first silver coins, the obol, the Sicilian litra, and the Roman as. He also weighs where the mina and the talent came from, and how gold spread through the old world. The book is dense but bold in scope.
66314-beware-the-star-gods:
Beware the Star Gods, a science fiction story by Byrne, was printed in Imagination in June 1954. Kuru stood his ground bravely as the ship flamed down from the sky. Truly this was a great and terrible moment, the headnote says: he must warn his people. Kuru pauses over a kill, stone knife poised, sniffing the wind.

He stands and looks through the trees at the small valley beyond the ridge. Birds cry raucously and the tree people flee in panic, gathering in the branches over his head. Kuru longs to run to his people, but what would he tell them? That he ran from the cry of birds, unseen? Then the ship floats down on pillars of fire, bright under the triple suns. Byrne tells a first contact from the stone man's side.
66355-the-canary-islands:
The Canary Islands is a travel book of the isle group off the shore of Africa, by Du Cane. Sixteen full page prints in colour, by a kin of her house, fill its form. It was first set in print in the years just past, printed in Britain.

Its parts dwell long on the first great isle. Eight parts in a row take that isle point by point: its ports, its peak, its vales, and its towns. The next great isle then gets its share of parts, and the small isles close the trip. Notes at its front tell how its print form was set, with spell and breaks made one through the text.
66357-hawaiian-historical-legends: W. D. Westervelt wrote this set of the old lore of Hawaii. The title page names him as the author of a past book on Maui, the great hero of the isles. The tales in the set are tales of the past of the isles, told as lore that has come down by word of mouth. No more of the start of the book is shown here. The work stands as a set of the myths and tales of old Hawaii, set in print for readers of English.
66460-the-book-of-gallant-vagabonds:
The Book of Gallant Vagabonds is a set of lives of great rovers by Beston, with prints through the text. Its rights were set in law in the mid nineteen twenties at New York. A front print shows a Salem ship as it leaves an old port of Italy. That port is shown as it stood in a bards day.

Its gift word makes it out to a past chief of the republic and his wife. It thanks them for long years of kind warmth and cheer. Its rovers then march in rank. First comes a young Yank who walked to the far east. A strong man who raised the great stones of Egypt comes next. A sea bard of the Greek isles, a wild chief of a feast hill, and a Scot of the great springs fill the run. A boy bard of France closes the set.
66538-revolt-of-the-outworlds:
Milton Lesser wrote Revolt of the Outworlds, a tale first printed in Imagination in December 1954. Alan Tremaine knows that Mars gets its water by a warp in space from Venus. If that life line were cut, the blurb warns, war and the end of man would come. The tale opens in the great square of Syrtis Major City.

Two hundred thousand folk, all the town, crowd the square in cold wind. The blue and gold flag of the Outworld Federation rises by the flag of Earth. The crowd cheers Alan, but he knows the cheers are for his late sire. That man made the dream of free rule real, then fell to a shot from an unknown hand two weeks back. Alan has been rushed from his school on Earth for the rite. A scroll of free rule is then read to the worlds by screen.
66597-early-carriages-and-roads:
Sir Walter Gilbey wrote this illustrated history, published in London in 1903. Gilbey notes that most books on coaches were written by builders of carriages. His aim is different: to trace wheeled travel in England from early times to his own day, and to show how coaches shaped social life.

The chapters move from Saxon carts and horse litters to the first coaches used by Queen Elizabeth. Hackney coaches, stage wagons, springs, glass windows and mail coaches follow in order. Pepys, Swift and the crowds and rules of London streets all appear, along with fares, winter roads, coachmen and the fast coaches of the golden age.
66976-upside-down-or-backwards:
Upside Down or Backwards is a Western tale by Tuttle, told in the voice of Ike Harper. Ike and his partner Magpie Simpkins own the Silver Threads mine. Magpie has just come back from a trip east in search of money men. His partner greets him at their cabin with dry suspicion.

Magpie cuddles his long legs under his chin and praises the East. He sports a hard derby hat, a loud shirt from Chicago, and a ten dollar pin that mimics a diamond. Ike teases him for hanging himself with ornaments. The pair struck nine hundred dollars in gold from their placer claim. That strike gave Magpie the itch to find eastern backers with deep pockets. Tuttle tells the yarn in broad dialect comedy.
67165-in-the-garden-of-the-gods:
In the Garden of the Gods, a western tale by William McLeod Raine, opens among red rocks. The narrator lies among kinni-kinic in the shade of a silver spruce at noon. His mood, for private reasons of his own, is thunderous in that bright place. He uses the climbing sun as a text on the futility of life.

What is the use of arranging things when they disarrange themselves, he muses. The name Katherine breaks off his thought at the edge of the scene. A revolver crack splits his sombre discontent in the next breath of the tale. Running feet and the swish of petticoats follow hard on that shot. A rough command to stop brings him to his feet at once. Colorado scenery and a lady in flight launch the Raine plot.
67184-elsie-and-the-raymonds:
Elsie and the Raymonds is a tale for the young by Martha Finley. It came out at New York in eighteen eighty-nine. A front list shows the long row of Elsie books past it, past twenty in all, with a next set of a girl of a next house. Finley was known past the whole of both sets. The tale opens in a city street past a shy voice.

A girl of the name house and her kin have just stepped down past their coach for a spot of shop work. A meek voice asks her if she knows of a lady in want of a sew wife. The girl halts past the walk to watch the coach roll off past the street. Her sire has trade work in the city that day and has set a time and place to meet.
67254-out-of-the-woods:
Elisabeth Sanxay Holding wrote Out of the Woods, billed on its title page as the story of an artless girl, a hungry wolf, and a wonderful grandmother. Holding warns the reader at the start that the tale is Little Red Riding Hood in new dress. The heroine Ethel sets off through the woods to visit her sick grandmother. She carries a box of candied fruit, not butter and cake, and no red hood is in fashion for her.

Nor will this grandmother be eaten up, Holding promises. Ethel wears a sulky look, and with cause: she is a bone of dispute in a split family, fought over and seldom asked her own mind. The old tale turns into a study of a child used as a pawn.
67271-chit-chat-or-short-tales-in-short-:
Short tales in short words make a small book for the very young. A second, larger form came out in London in 1831. Sixteen cut plates aid the tales. Its author had wrote a book named Always Happy. A hymn at the front likens life to a summer day.

Youth is the bright morn in that hymn's scheme. Age spent in wise ways meets death with calm, it says. Each tale keeps its words short and its point plain. Good acts, care, and kind hearts rule the small plots. The book sat in a line of small books of use for the young.
6742-the-school-for-husbands:
Molière's School for Husbands, first played in Paris in June 1661, was the first play to use School in its title as a promise of a lesson. The notice explains that Molière wished hearers to know he meant to teach married men, not just to amuse them, and to answer those who called theatre harmful or trivial. Sheridan and others later copied the title trick.

Two brothers, one strict and one easy, raise two wards in opposite ways, and the strict man's ward teaches him a lesson in love. The verse moves briskly, with wit as its weapon. The School for Husbands is a clever, enduring comedy on how not to rule a wife.
67906-a-hermit-s-wild-friends-or-eightee:
A Hermit's Wild Friends tells of a man who lived with wild things. Mason Walton, the Hermit of Gloucester, wrote the book in 1903. He spent years in the woods and claims fresh finds from that life. The book is given to the friends of wild life in all lands.

Walton holds that a cow bird guards its young in a strange way. The bird then takes full charge of the young one in the end. A white foot mouse is dumb, he says, and talks with its toes. A thrush holds a song school for its young in his woods. A small cheek bird can count, by his long watch of its ways. He owns his claims will be hit hard by men of the craft. He bids them look with care in the field ere they scorn his finds.
68102-the-squaw-spy-or-the-rangers-of-th:
Captain Chas Howard wrote The Squaw Spy, or the Rangers of the Lava-Beds, a pocket novel. Beadle and Adams sold the tale in New York, with rights held from eighteen hundred seventy three. Howard wrote a long line of such tales, from The Elk King to The Girl Avenger.

General Gillem counts a black day in the Modoc war at dusk. Good men fell that dawn to three score Modoc rifles. His scout Kit South waits with him for the spy Artena. She rides with the foe and was due at sunset. Captain Jack, the Modoc chief, is the prize Gillem wants most. Hoofs sound in the dark as the tale takes off. Artena rides in with news from the lava beds.
68198-forest-friends:
Forest Friends is a children's nature book by Royal Dixon, author of The Human Side of Plants, printed at New York in 1916. Robert Shepard McCourt painted eight illustrations in colour. The contents open with Mrs Elephant's Moonlight Dance. Under the moonlight there is a great gathering of friends in the forest.

Elephant, the kangaroos, the foxes, and the handsome leopards sit in a great circle around the pleasant pool. Sprightly little Miss Lynx and the aristocratic jungle deer join them. Other chapters tell of Old Lady Wildcat's feast, Mrs Frog changing her dress, and Mr Mocking-Bird and his prize song. Mr Raccoon's oyster supper, Mrs Goose and her swamp cousins, and why Mrs Crow is black follow. Baby Fox and Mrs Bear, Mother Rabbit's advice to her babies, and a Christmas Eve piece fill the later pages. Dixon teaches woodland life through talking animal tales.
68292-tales-from-silver-lands:
Tales from Silver Lands gathers nineteen folk tales of South America, retold by Charles Finger. Doubleday first published the book in 1924, with woodcuts by Paul Honore. Finger dedicates the work to Carl Sandburg and to his own children. The tales come from the lands of silver in the book's title.

A tale of three tails and a magic dog open the run. The hero twins and the four hundred draw on old Maya story. The killing of the giant Cabrakan shakes the earth in another tale. A magic knot, bad wishers, and a hungry old witch fill the middle. Rairu and the star maiden close the book with the cat and the dream man. Finger tells the tales in a warm voice for young readers. The book won wide praise as a doorway to southern story.
68490-the-charm-of-reynolds:
The Charm of Reynolds is a study of the painter Sir Joshua Reynolds by James Mason. Jack published the book at London and Edinburgh. A portrait of two gentlemen from the National Gallery serves as frontispiece. The sitters are a clergyman who once studied art with Reynolds and a friend with a violin.

Mason opens by calling Reynolds portraits a national asset. He grants that their worth varies widely across a huge output. The painter may have made four or five thousand portraits in his life. At busy times he finished three or four in a single week. Mason laments that the beauty of the canvases began to fade within the artist's own days. Many great works now show only a pale shade of their first selves. Plates gather famed sitters, from Nelly O'Brien to the Duchess of Devonshire.
6851-ruth-fielding-at-snow-camp-or-lost-:
Alice Emerson sends Ruth Fielding to Snow Camp, lost in the backwoods, opening with a lively time and a surprising appearance. A newspaper clipping, the strange behavior of Fred Hatfield, and a trip off for the backwoods follow, with a train ride, a runaway in earnest, and first days at Snow Camp. Long Jerry Todd, bears, frost games, and peril with a taffy pull fill the winter.

A telephone chase, a battle in snow, a besieging storm king, a snow shroud, and a double captivity test Ruth's pluck. Emerson writes with bright, clean humor for girls. Ruth Fielding at Snow Camp is a cheerful, snowy adventure of friendship and courage.
68584-lost-in-the-backwoods:
Lost in the Backwoods, a boys adventure novel by Edith C Kenyon, was issued in London by S W Partridge and Company and reached a fourteenth thousand. Its hero, Cyril Morton, is twelve years old. He sails to North America with his father after the death of his mother. Their goal is to find the father's long lost brother, Gerald Morton, last heard of in Michigan.

The tale opens with a train robbery, a masked man levelling a revolver at Cyril's father. Later chapters bring bears, a saw mill, snow, and a ghost. Cyril speaks up for the Indians he meets along the way. A confession and a joyful meeting close the story.
68698-dick-and-dr-dan-or-the-boy-monster:
Two boys of about eighteen, Dick Darrell and Charley Nicholson, work in the paleontological department of the National Museum in Washington, sorting the bones of prehistoric animals. Little's story ran in the Happy Days story paper from March 17 to May 3, 1900, and was printed by Frank Tousey of New York. When Professor Poynter summons Dick, the errand is not another bone hunt in the fossil beds but a stranger mission into the Bad Lands.

The tale is a dime-novel adventure in the story-paper line, built on secrets, telegrams, and a professor with a hidden letter. Dick's luck and pluck have won him the post, and the hunt for monsters soon follows. It never appeared in book form, and it survives as a lively piece of the boys' paper trade of 1900.
6895-the-camp-fire-girls-go-motoring-or-:
Hildegard Frey sends the Winnebago Camp Fire Girls on an automobile trip in September, told by the group's own reporter at Nyoda's urging. The girls have just come home from Onoway House when a runaway girl, met in some distress, sets their journey in motion. Sahwah jokes that only a ride in a patrol wagon was missing, and the tale keeps that high spirited tone throughout.

Much of the fun springs from small things, including the craze for tan khaki outing suits that summer. From evening stars over a window to roads, mishaps, and new friends, Frey follows a band of girls learning to fend for themselves on the open road. Campfire loyalty is their guide.
69016-the-construction-and-maintenance-o:
Construction and Maintenance of Earth Roads is a bulletin by Richard Lyman of the University of Utah. It is bulletin number three of the Utah Engineering Experiment Station, dated January 1910. The station was a department of the State School of Mines at Salt Lake City. Lyman was professor of civil engineering in that school of the university.

 It was established by an act of the state legislature in March 1909 for its work. It is authorised to carry on experiments and investigation on questions that admit of laboratory methods of study. Earth roads, the dirt roads of a rural state, were its fitting early subject for inquiry. In 1910 most American roads were earth, and their grading, drainage, and dragging decided whether a county moved or stuck in the mud. Lyman bulletin is applied science aimed at county road men and farmers.
69061-precision-locating-and-dividing-me:
Precision Locating and Dividing Methods is Number 135 in the Machinery set of shop books. The Industrial Press put it out in New York in 1914. Each book in the set is one unit in a full shelf on machine design and shop work. The text was drawn from the journal Machinery, in new form.

The first part deals with how to set work in the right spot with great care. It shows the button method, with holes laid out and marked in a jig plate. Screws clamp small round buttons where the holes must go. A second part deals with how to split a circle or a line into true parts. A last part deals with work set for a bore on a mill. Shop men who cut tools and gauges are the chief readers.
69097-christmas-in-austria-or-fritzl-s-f:
Christmas in Austria, or Fritzl's Friends, is a children's story by Frances Bartlett, published at Boston in 1910. Bertha Hoxie drew the illustrations. The tale opens on Christmas Eve in Vienna. On the snow-covered stones of the Stephansplatz, Fritzl dances with his terrier Tzandi.

The boy dances because it is Christmas Eve, and because movement makes his thin body forget its poor clothing. A violin is tucked under his chin, and he plays snatches of Hungarian folk songs and Viennese waltzes as he dances. The passers-by hurry faster, but not one coin has yet come to his hand. The story follows the small fiddler and his dog through a Viennese Christmas.
69257-time-out-for-redheads:
Time Out for Redheads, by Miriam Allen deFord, is a science fiction story. It ran in Startling Stories in the summer of 1955, the note says. Mikel Skot, thirty four, sells tickets for Time Travel Tours, Unlimited, daily. For twelve years, since 2827, he has worked one window without a raise earned.

Shy and dusty, he has never known a girl by her first name. Two weeks in Rome in 45 BC costs a customer eight hundred fifty creds. England in 1600 runs five hundred creds a month for travelers there. Teleports, costumes, and language transformers serve the crowds he only watches pass. A lonely clerk in a time of tours is the tale seed.
69707-princess-sukey-the-story-of-a-pige:
Princess Sukey, the story of a pigeon and her human friends, by Marshall Saunders, was copyrighted in 1905 and published at New York by Eaton and Mains. Saunders dedicates the story to her brother-in-law, Clarence King Moore of the University of Rochester, who showed a kind interest in every living creature on her farm. Twenty-eight chapters follow the pigeon.

The chapters open with The Pigeon Princess and Mrs Blodgett's opinion, then happy times in the pigeon loft. A judge runs through the book: the judge's vow, a surprise for the judge, and calls on the judge follow. The English boy, the yellow spotted dog, and Higby and the owls add to the farm cast. Saunders, known for animal stories, teaches kindness to creatures through Sukey's adventures among her human friends.
69963-isaac-watts-his-life-and-writings-:
Isaac Watts: His Life and Writings, His Homes and Friends is a biography of the hymn writer. The Religious Tract Society published it in London from Paternoster Row. A portrait of Watts, presented by Miss Abney to Dr Williams' Library, fronts the book. Two judgements head the title page. Dr Johnson praised Watts for instructing every age, from children lisping lessons to readers of Locke. Lord Selborne called the Independents, in Watts, the real founders of modern English hymnody.

The preface admits that Watts has more monuments in stone than readable biographies. His life was quiet, equable, and passed in much seclusion. Ill health and taste kept him from the world's presence. Recorded incidents are few. The biographer aims instead at his mental character. Watts disclaimed the rank of poet, the preface notes. Yet his powers as preacher, theologian, and metaphysician shine equally, and his charity crowns the portrait.
7001-history-of-the-philippine-islands:
Antonio de Morga's history of the Philippine Islands, translated by Blair and Robertson, runs from Magellan's discovery in 1521 to the start of the seventeenth century. Morga, alcalde of criminal causes in the Royal Audiencia of New Spain and counsel for the Holy Office, wrote his Sucesos in Mexico in 1609. This volume one, issued separately from the fifty five volume Philippine Islands series, adds descriptions of Japan, China, and adjacent countries.

Appendices treat the expedition of Thomas Candish, and facsimiles accompany the text. Blair and Robertson edited and annotated the translation for the Arthur H Clark Company in 1907. The book remains a first hand Spanish account of the islands, their trade, wars, and peoples, at the dawn of colonial rule.
70196-evil-eye-in-the-western-highlands:
Evil Eye in the Western Highlands is a folk-lore study by Doctor Maclagan. David Nutt of London brought the book out in the year 1902. The volume forms number 47 of the Folk-Lore Society publications. Maclagan had writ The Games and Diversions of Argyllshire before this. Contents run from an introduction to the belief's locality and holders.

Chapters describe possessors of the evil eye and how folk shun meeting one. Avoiding suspicion of the eye gets a chapter of careful Highland lore. The eye acts apart from its possessor's will, one chapter argues. It takes effect even on things not seen by the possessor. Things that specially attract the eye stand listed for the wary. Strangers stand specially liable to be accused of holding the power. Symptoms in animals ascribed to the eye fill a later chapter. After long Christianity, our own superstitions stand forgotten, he opens.
70301-my-leper-friends:
My Leper Friends, by Mrs M H Hayes, was printed by Thacker at London in 1891, with a chapter on the disease by Surgeon-Major G G Maclaren. Alice Hayes tells in her preface why she wrote: to stir the public for the white lepers left with no home in India. Gains from the book go to the Leper Fund she raised, run at Calcutta by Archdeacon Michell, with aid given to all creeds alike.

Her heads walk through the work: a first home in Calcutta, a leper refuge, and the tales of those she nursed. Bridget, Daisy, and Bella live again in her pages, as does her mate in the wards, Brother John. A stage show raised cash for the fund. Kind readers get true scenes of the most shunned sick of the age, told by a friend.
70344-odds-and-ends:
Croker gathered sixteen tales in this volume and gave it a frank name: Odds and Ends. Hutchinson printed it in London. Croker had written Her Own People, In Old Madras, and The Company's Servant by then, tales of India and Ireland both.

The Spare Bed opens the set on a dull September night in the west of Ireland. Two ladies sit stuck in a great Daimler on a dark country road. Aunt Lizzie, brisk as ever, bids her niece open the window and find out what is wrong. The North Verandah, Imitation Pearls, and The Ship's Cat fill the list. A red bungalow, a scarecrow, and a dark horse close the mixed bag.
70641-three-little-maids:
Ethel Turner wrote this story, Three Little Maids, printed at London, Melbourne, and Toronto. Turner also wrote Seven Little Australians and The Camp at Wandinong. A dedication in verse gives the book to her tiny daughter, as a chain of pansies and white marguerites. It warns her that the pansies, unlike the marguerites, did not all grow true in life.

Contents divide the tale into play days and scribbling days. The first part runs from a midnight opening through pretending, family matters, and a winter Sunday, to travels in foreign countries, a last Christmas in England, a sea voyage, and Australia. The second part turns to rhyme and rhythm, letters, and the trials of Weenie, ending with one glorious hour and then no more.
70794-in-the-bad-lands:
Bertrand Sinclair wrote this western tale of the Wineglass range country. Bad Land Bill, the new rider, was a likable kid, the story begins in its opening lines. He was a mystery to the bunch, and another strange man stumbling into the campfire light deepened it, the opening goes on.

Charlie Shaw flattens his nose against a west-facing window as the tale settles in. April rain has turned to wet snowflakes the size of thumbnails over Plentywater, he sees. Six inches of snow lie while sheepmen lamb in the storm, and cattlemen like Shaw grin at weather sheep cannot stand, in Sinclair's range war ground.
70832-the-valley-of-lost-herds:
Valley of Lost Herds is a Western story by Tuttle, of cattle rustlers and a new kind of ranch foreman. It opens in the town of Tomahawk on the big night of the month in the text. The Tomahawk saloon, gambling palace, and honkatonk blazes with lights in the first lines. Cowboys jostle at the long bar, and the roulette whirrs above the roar of the crowd.

It is pay night on the Reber ranches, and the small ranches to the north pay off and let their men come to town as well. Reber owned the Tomahawk Saloon, and nearly everything else in the town, as far as that went. Tuttle, who had been a Montana sheriff, wrote Westerns with a law man knowledge of rustlers, brands, and the valley politics of cattle in his tales.
70966-the-tracy-diamonds:
Mary Holmes wrote this novel, published by Dillingham in New York in 1899. Holmes had written 'Tempest and Sunshine,' 'Lena Rivers' and 'The English Orphans' before it. Part one opens at the Prospect House, with a chapter on the cause of the battle there.

Uncle Zach and Craig Mason enter early in the contents list of the tale. A tragedy, expected guests and the Tracys follow in the chapters. Alice's story runs through meetings with Jeff and Craig, a coquette and a haunted house, until the diamonds of the title force the denouement and close a season of love and trouble.
71192-five-thousand-pounds:
Agnes Giberne tells of a cottage family raised by sudden wealth in a tale issued at London by James Nisbet and Company. The narrator speaks in the first person from the age of fourteen.

Her cottage home opens the book, a happy house by a pond outside a large town. Tree shadows lie on the water at evening. News comes in chapter two, and the money in chapter three. First purchases and congratulations follow. Then an alarm sounds. The family must choose to go or to stay. A new house brings a strange trouble: nothing to do. Later chapters promise a damp dwelling, scenes, and trouble before the end. Giberne turns a windfall of five thousand pounds into a quiet test of character.
71332-history-in-english-words:
Owen Barfield reads the past in words in History in English Words, first published in London in 1926. Methuen made the book. Two parts carry the argument: the English nation, and the western outlook.

Chapters in the first part treat philology and the Aryans, the settlement of Europe, and England before the Reformation. The second part turns to myth, philosophy and religion, and devotion. Experiment, personality and reason, mechanism, and imagination close the survey. Chapter one opens with five specimen words: electric, quality, garden, mead, timber. It argues from a forgery test: a letter of Johnson that used the word telephone would betray itself, since no such thing existed until long after his death. Words date thoughts, the book holds.
71450-my-heart-s-in-the-highlands:
My Heart's in the Highlands is a novel by Amy Le Feuvre, published in London and Melbourne by Ward, Lock and Company. A frontispiece shows a child with sunny brown curls dashing in. The tale is built in three books, and its scene is the Scottish Highlands of glens and lairds.

The contents open with a doctor's verdict. Rowena Arbuthnot, leaning on a windowsill, begs her sister to be serious, and quotes Shelley on man's power to do and suffer. Chapters on being alone, on Mysie Macdonald, and on a birthday gift follow. Miss Falconer, friendly talks, and the laird's awakening fill the first book. The second moves to the Green Cottage, with a new friend, an accident, and the laird speaking. The third gathers guests, a Hector Ross, winter in the glen, Rowena's power, and a bride.
71590-the-hermit-hunter-of-the-wilds:
Gordon Stables's The Hermit Hunter of the Wilds was published by Blackie and Son Limited of London, Glasgow, and Bombay, with four page illustrations. A publisher's list of Stables's other boys' books, with press notices, fronts the title page. The Methodist Recorder sums this one up as pirates and pumas, mutiny and merriment, a castaway and a cat.

The contents open by the firelight and among the woods of Craigielea. Then they promise a brother's scalp hung up, a shower of poisoned darts pattering on the stockade, and a dying ayah telling of Bernard. Later chapters bring a chest filled with gold doubloons, a ship struck and staved, and strange life on a beautiful island. Stables signs himself with his naval and medical letters, and had already written The Naval Cadet and Westward with Columbus.
71740-three-pretty-maids:
Three Pretty Maids is a tale for girls by Amy Blanchard. Alice Stephens drew the prints that dress the text of the book. Ads praise her pure tone and true feel for girl life in her work. The book came out in Philadelphia in the year eighteen ninety seven.

A gift page sends the book to the authors two sisters with deep love. One plate shows a maid bent in thought on work at a small loft desk. School, home, and first cares of heart form the stuff of the tale. Keen sight of girl ways marks the hand that penned the set. The book stands in a line of clean tales for young maids.
71760-aunt-milly-s-diamonds:
Aunt Milly's Diamonds is a Christmas story by Ruth Lamb, published by the Religious Tract Society of London. Its seven chapters open with Grandmamma's Story and close with A Pleasant Ending. A frontispiece shows the family group at Denesfield Manor. On Christmas Eve the grandchildren, tired of merry games, cluster round their grandmother in the dim twilight. They beg her, before the gas is lighted, to tell them all about those diamonds.

Yes, children, she says, I will tell you the story of Aunt Milly's diamonds. In telling about them, she warns, you must hear the tale of her own life almost, for the two can scarcely be separated. A passage preserved in the copy gives the family history. There was a great difference in their ages, and still more in their worldly positions.
71770-the-gallery-gods:
Murray Leinster wrote The Gallery Gods, a story that opens in the tropics with a white fruit steamer leaving port and a big man on a veranda. Beckwith sits in spotless white duck, cigar in hand, his left thumb bandaged in splints. The thumb is a souvenir he smiles at: Conway broke it in their last struggle, two weeks before, in New York. Conway is dead.

A house-boy brings the New York papers Beckwith had sent down on purpose. They hold the tale of how William Beckwith killed Hugh Conway, millionaire and patron of the arts, in the open. He left a letter pinned to the dead man's breast telling his reasons and how he meant to escape punishment. Beckwith settles in to savor the outrage and the loophole he used. Readers get a cool, amused portrait of a killer watching his own headlines from beyond the law's reach.
71780-direct-methods:
Thomson Burtis, author of There and Back and Feud's End, wrote Direct Methods, an aviation tale opening over Langham Field. A De Haviland airplane spirals down as its young pilot throttles the big Liberty motor that carried the ship from Washington. His passenger peers down with interest.

Twenty-two massive twin-motored bombers line the eastern edge of the field, nose to nose in two lines, like waiting monsters. Sunlight flashes from metal and instrument glass until the ships seem alive. The passenger climbs out in civilian clothes, takes a soft hat, and lights a cigar. Readers get a postwar flying story where the airfield itself is the first character.
71848-rogues-and-vagabonds:
Rogues and Vagabonds, by Compton Mackenzie, copyright 1927 from the George Doran Company of New York, is a novel that opens with a piece of print. The page is a fireworks bill for the Neptune's Grotto tavern and tea gardens at Pimlico, dated Thursday, July 20, 1829. Madame Oriano, pyrotechnic to His Majesty, promises water fireworks on the Grosvenor Basin.

Twenty five chapters follow from that vanished pleasure garden through factories, proposals, pantomimes, and roads south to Sorrento. Mackenzie, author of Sinister Street and Sylvia Scarlett, loved the theatre's fringe world. The novel is a pageant of show folk, drifters, and lovers across a long life.
71876-the-fairchilds:
The Fairchilds: or, Do What You Can, by Lucy Ellen Guernsey, was published by the American Sunday-School Union at Philadelphia, entered according to Act of Congress in 1871. Guernsey's earlier titles include Irish Amy, Comfort Allison, and Nelly; or, The Best Inheritance.

Eben Fairchild opens the story by making up his mind: he must go to work and earn his living the best way he can. His late father had set his heart on a college education for the boy, and his mother and sister Flora feel the change keenly. The chapters follow Eben finding something to do, taking a drive with Flora, and displaying his accomplishments. He tries to serve two masters, catches a ride and something else, and gets an advance before a new place.
71992-two-sailor-lads:
Gordon Stables, a surgeon in the Royal Navy, wrote Two Sailor Lads, a story of stirring adventures on sea and land, here in a new edition from a London house. Stables fills thirty-five chapters with the wanderings of two boys, Frank and his young charge Toddie, from a Scottish fishing village to the far southern seas.

The first chapter opens at evening on the bay of Methlin, a village of whitewashed cottages under high hills. Contents promise early wonders: tea taken inside a stranded whale, playing at pirates, a storm, and a wreck that strands the boys on a desert island. Further chapters bring the good ship San Salvador, a mystery brig, a swim pursued by sharks, and islands where the whole beach lines with yelling savages. Readers get a hearty boys' sea yarn of the old school, generous with peril and pluck.
72033-the-woods:
Douglas Malloch wrote a book of verse dated 1913 on life in the woods, given to the memory of his young son. The lead poem holds that all men own the woods and the sun, though deeds and maps say else. A boss in town may count his wealth in land, while the man on the stoop breathes it in for free.

Geese on the wing, spring fever, pigeons now gone, and the chickadee mark the turn of the year. Dialect tales of camp men, the flag of a pine, and the call of the woods fill the set. Malloch had writ a prior book of forest verse, and fans of that work will know his warm, plain tune.
72204-tom-slade-in-the-north-woods:
Tom Slade in the North Woods is a scout tale by Percy Fitzhugh. Tom heads a long line of scout tales by the same keen hand. The scout corps of America gave the book its seal of praise. Rights date the work to the year nineteen twenty five.

A front print shows the troop in line, packs on backs, in deep woods. Parts treat a strange man, a sad event, and a new camp task in turn. Signs on a peak, a shade from the past, and a ghost on the wire follow. Doubt, loss of hope, and a bright pal named Peters mark the late turns. Wood craft and faith in pals drive the famed scout line fare.
72216-cicero-and-his-friends:
Cicero and His Friends is a study of the life of Rome in the time of Caesar, by Gaston Boissier of the French school of high lore. Jones made the English form of the book, with an index and a full list of parts. The host print is the third form of that work. The first words treat the notes of Cicero him self, and the weight of such close writ in the old world.

Then the book takes Cicero in his state life and in his home life in turn. His birth, his thought, and his cast of mind set his path in the state. He stood first past the great lords, then sought a mid camp, then joined the lords at last.
