72582-the-little-book-of-british-quadrup:
The Little Book of British Quadrupeds, by May and printed for Tilt of Fleet Street at London, gives some forty-five animals four pages apiece. Horse, race horse, cart horse, mule and ass follow the oxen, and the sheep, goat, stag and boar give way to cats, weasels, the badger, the fox and the wolf. Dogs of many breeds, the hare, the squirrel, the mole, the hedgehog, the bat and the otter fill the rest.

The Kyloe Ox leads off: a black, thick-hided, long-horned native of Scotland, said to take its name from crossing the kyles, or ferries, of the Highlands. Young readers learn that its flesh is the finest beef, its hide makes leather, its gristles glue, its horns knife-handles and cups, and its bones serve in place of ivory. Most entries carry a picture of the beast.
72776-flowers-and-their-friends:
Flowers and Their Friends, by Margaret Warner Morley, was copyright 1897 and published in Boston, New York, Chicago, and London. Morley had also written Seed Babies and A Few Familiar Flowers. A letter to the readers of the book opens the volume, addressed dear children.

It would be very stupid, she writes, to try to read a book in Arabic or Hebrew; we should soon tire and put it down. English words whose meaning we do not understand are just as uninteresting. If you do not know what a word means, find out. A list of hard words stands at the back to help. Some day, she promises, you will find the dictionary an exciting and interesting volume. Meantime, enjoy the flowers and their insect friends all you can. Readers get a childrens nature book on how insects and flowers work together.
72909-tumbleweeds:
Hal Evarts wrote Tumbleweeds, a western novel published by Little, Brown in Boston in 1923. Evarts had written The Settling of the Sage and The Passing of the Old West. His new book opens with a challenge. An official report had claimed that the whole country west of Fort Riley held barely four hundred thousand acres of farmable land. Settlers answered by fencing thirty million acres within thirty years.

Against that background Evarts sets his people. Old Joe Hinman, counted a wise man among his fellows, sits his horse on a rise and laments his own lack of foresight. A frontispiece shows two brothers and the woman whose thoughts centre on the younger. The novel belongs to the range fiction of the nineteen twenties: land hunger, cattle country, and families divided by the rush to settle a country that the experts had called worthless.
73021-myths-of-northern-lands:
H A Guerber retells the myths of the northern lands in a handbook issued in America in 1895. Guerber had already written Myths of Greece and Rome, and this book follows it in the same series. She aims to acquaint English students with the faith of their own heathen forebears.

Guerber marks two traits in the northern tales, a grim humor found in no other faith and a dark thread of tragedy through the whole. Chapters treat the beginning of all things, then Odin, Frigga, Thor, Tyr, and the rest of the gods in order. The Norns, the Valkyrs, Balder, Loki, giants, and dwarfs follow. A glossary and full index fit the book for schools and libraries. Readers get the classics of the North in clear order, with their sway over custom and letters kept in view.
73126-mystery-at-lynden-sands:
Mystery at Lynden Sands is a detective novel by Connington, set at a seaside place of the title. Contents list seventeen chapters for the investigation of the tale. The Death at Foxhills and A Bus Driver Holiday open the book in order. The Police at the Caretaker and What Happened in the Night follow in the list.

The Diary, The Beach Tragedy, and The Letter carry the inquiry to the sands of the title. The Colt Automatic and The Second Cartridge Case mark the turn to ballistics in the case. An attack on an Australian and the evidence of a French witness fill the middle chapters. The Fordingbridge mystery, a telegram, a method of coercion, and a man hunt on the beach close the shown list. Connington, a Belfast civil servant, wrote puzzles of timetables and cartridge cases, in which the detective reasons like a chemist from traces.
73245-the-secret-of-oaklands:
M Harding Kelly wrote The Secret of Oaklands, issued in London by the Religious Tract Society and Lutterworth Press. Kelly had earlier written Philip Campion Will, Roy, and Tom Kenyan. Twelve chapters fill the tale. A front plate shows Margaret crying, What a jolly little place, of Oaklands. Margaret Woodford is the young heroine.

Chapter one, Parting of the Ways, opens in a breakfast room in shock. Margaret finds her father Cyril Woodford stunned, with ashen face and shaking hands. He points to a newspaper head that cries a great financial crash and the failure of Sampson Bank. Later chapters promise trials, a great fight, Bob in trouble, and a discovery. Fire, an old crime, and happiness close the tale. Young readers get faith and pluck under sudden ruin.
73636-new-nick-carter-weekly-no-11-march:
An issue of the New Nick Carter Weekly, dated March 13, 1897. Street and Smith published the five-cent paper at New York. Number eleven carries the tale Trim in the Wilds. Its subtitle promises hunting a criminal on the Dark Continent. Trim is a young detective in the Nick Carter stable. An old sailor serves as his companion.

The opening scene sits in Kimberley police headquarters. Trim proposes capturing Jemmy Miller, a steeple climber turned criminal. Miller once tried to murder him and escaped by climbing. Cape Town and Kimberley police both want the man. Diamond thieves in Kimberley have lately used his warnings. Poker talk opens the bargaining with the chief. The tale belongs to the dime novel's golden age of weekly detective fiction.
7381-the-eustace-diamonds:
Anthony Trollope's novel turns on a necklace and a widow who will not give it up. Lizzie Greystock, married briefly to Sir Florian Eustace, claims the Eustace diamonds as her own property. The family lawyers insist they are an heirloom that must pass to the heir. Lizzie, charming and unscrupulous, fights her case in drawing rooms, in the press, and finally in court.

Around the diamonds gather suitors, a scheming clergyman, a loyal friend in Lucy Morris, and a London world eager for scandal. Trollope uses the dispute to satirize society's greed and its love of a good story, while keeping sympathy for the people caught in the machine. The novel is one of his Palliser-era masterpieces of social comedy, sharp, funny, and unsparing.
73842-rose-buds:
Gerson made this picture book for children for White, Stokes, and Allen in 1885. Buds are its measure: each poem is a page or two, with a picture. Josephine Maud opens the book, lying on the floor in a heap, not asleep but in a temper. She has thrown down her doll, crushed its pink nose, torn off its wig, and whipped it with a crabapple sprig.

Temper does not last, and Josephine is sorry by the last verse. Naughty Tommy Warner, papa gone to sea, and the little tar follow. Three bells ring through the book: the church bell, the school bell, and the tea bell. There are six little chickens, soap bubbles, a Japanese doll, and a lump of sugar. The index is a nursery's calendar, bed-time and croquet, made for the children of 1885 to be read to, one bud at a time.
73987-rivals-of-the-clouds:
Raoul Whitfield wrote this air war tale of Lieutenant Adams and his squadron. A plate shows a German plane, afire, crash into Adams rudder. Thick fog rolls down on the small pursuit field at dawn. Two ships are out on patrol and due back soon.

Lieutenant Ben Chapin waits and worries in the cold white fog. Adams flies with Langdon, a new and wild young officer. Chapin trusts Adams skill but fears what Langdon may try. The tale builds toward a fierce fight in blind cloud and fog. Whitfield was known for crisp, fast tales of war in the air.
73990-nigeria-and-its-tin-fields:
Albert F Calvert wrote Nigeria and Its Tin Fields, issued at London in 1910 by Edward Stanford. Calvert had writ Western Australia and Its Goldfields and The Exploration of Australia. A list of illustrations runs to dozens of plates. Part of the Marina at Lagos leads the plates. Customs houses, markets, and the railway at Iddo fill the early list.

Forcados and its dry dock, botanical gardens at Ebute Metta, and Burutu market sit in the middle plates. Fulani sheep and a bullock cart show country life in the views. The book pairs a survey of Nigeria with a close account of its new tin fields in the north. Photos serve as evidence for investors and officials who would never see the colony. Trade, ports, and mines are the core themes throughout.
74046-the-lakewood-boys-in-the-south-sea:
The Lakewood Boys in the South Sea Islands is a boys' adventure novel by Wyman, dean of the Pennsylvania Military College, published by Burt in 1925. It belongs to a series of stories for boys of twelve to sixteen. Companion volumes take the boys to the frozen north, a ranch, a lost mine, and the polo field. The frontispiece shows a dozen men rising from nowhere all about the heroes.

The chapters open with a surprising proposition, then go to sea. A rescue and the catching of a shark come early. Suspicions follow, and then the boys are captured by savages. They are saved by magic, attacked in the fog, and face a close call. One boy, Josh, goes missing, and the party finds a cave. A tall, well-built man stops Bob in the barracks wash room with the news that starts the voyage.
74235-british-birds:
Hudson describes the home birds in British Birds, printed in London and New York in 1921, a new impression. Longmans Green made the book. A chapter on structure and classification by Frank Beddard stands in front. Eight coloured plates from drawings by Thorburn dress the volume, with plates and figures in black and white besides. A golden eagle fronts it.

The anatomy of a bird leads, then classification. Species entries run in order, with Latin names given. The missel thrush, song thrush, redwing, and fieldfare open the passerine run. The blackbird and ring ouzel, wheatear, whinchat, and stonechat follow. Redstart, redbreast, nightingale, and whitethroat stand in the long list. Field readers get a standard survey of the birds of Britain, plate by plate and species by species.
74284-danish-ballads:
Danish Ballads, translated by E M Smith-Dampier, was printed at the Cambridge University Press in 1920. An introduction precedes four groups: historical ballads, legendary ballads, ballads of magic, and miscellaneous ballads.

The historical set gives two versions of Valdemar and Tove, Queen Dagmar's bridal and death, the king-slaying in Finderup, and Niels Ebbeson. The notes explain that Valdemar the Great had a mistress Tove who bore him a son, Christopher. Legendary pieces include Havbor and Signelil and Holger Danske, while magic brings the elfin shaft and Agnes and the merman.
74337-horsesense-hank-in-the-parallel-wo:
Horsesense Hank in the Parallel Worlds, by Nelson Bond, is a science fiction tale from Amazing Stories of August 1942. A headnote asks what would have happened if Washington had not crossed the Delaware, and says Hank found the strange answer when he traveled into the past.

Hank Cleaver never finished high school, yet his gift for solving any science problem by plain common sense lifted him from a turnip patch to a university chair. Now the government has brought him to Washington, where the head of its physics research, Jamieson, riles him past bearing. Hank's friend Jim tells the story, with Hank's sweetheart Helen working at the service headquarters nearby.
74340-in-love-s-hands:
Bertha Clay wrote a tale sold at New York as number 370 of her own library set. The set came out twice a month and claimed to be the only full line of her tales. A full page ad for a famed smoking leaf stands oddly at the front of the tale. News dealers sold the books, or readers could send to the house with four cents more for postage.

The list at the front names scores of her tales, all kept in print. A Bitter Atonement stands first, and Dora Thorne second. A Golden Heart, Lord Lisle's Daughter, and A Dark Marriage Morn follow. Titles promise sins, secrets, divorces, and hearts in thorns. Clay's tales of love and wrong had a vast public among cheap book buyers.
74589-saddle-room-songs-and-hunting-ball:
Frederick C Palmer wrote Saddle Room Songs and Hunting Ballads, verse of the chase and stable. Mawson, Swan and Morgan issued the book at Newcastle-upon-Tyne in nineteen hundred seven. Palmer gave the small book to his mother. A hunting song of hounds in full cry leads the set.

Reynard slips his lair as the pack strikes up its loud song. Tally Ho rings as whip and field dash for the wall in turn. The Squire’s Daughter then rides into the next long ballad. Diana Harding, famed for hands and seat, leads that bright field. Three suitors, a captain, Jim Ashton, and a parson, chase her. An empty loose box and a sold old saddle turn the mood sad. A London cab horse tells his own life in one droll piece. A five furlong race and a toast round out the horse book.
74612-diverging-roads:
Diverging Roads, a novel by Rose Wilder Lane, was published by the Century Company at New York in 1919. Its prologue sings California's early days as an epic: an immortal song of daring, hope, and youth on unknown trails. Across the great plains the adventurers came, writing their passing in lines of blood. Others beat around the Horn in windjammers into the strange Pacific.

They woke California's hills from centuries of sleep and pitched tents and cabins by the thousand in Cherokee Valley. Tales came down to Masonville, where the stage changed horses and drivers and prospectors gathered in Mason's bar. A Chinese laundryman found a nugget worth sixteen hundred dollars beside his cabin. The stage to Honey Creek was held up north of Cherokee Hill. Lane sets her novel in that gold country as it settles into farms.
74706-in-the-clouds:
Charles Egbert Craddock's In the Clouds was published by Houghton, Mifflin in 1887, under a copyright of 1886. Craddock was Mary Murfree, as the copyright line owns, and the publisher's list at the front prices her Tennessee books at a dollar twenty-five each. In the Tennessee Mountains and The Prophet of the Great Smoky Mountains stand in the list with this novel.

Chapter one opens on Thunderhead, the massive peak of the Great Smoky Mountains, shaped like the cumulus cloud it is named for and charged with the portent of the storm. Kindred thunderheads of the air lean on its shoulder and rise away; the earthbound peak cannot soar. Ben Doaks herds cattle on Piomingo Bald, a few miles off, and turns his eyes to it as he comes and goes. He sits for hours on a summit rock, smoking his pipe and watching its changing aspects.
7473-lost-on-the-moon-or-in-quest-of-the:
Roy Rockwood, the house name behind many boys' adventure series, sends his heroes to the moon in this novel. The chapters tell the plan in order. First comes a wonderful story, then something about the heroes. Then come preparing for a voyage, an accident, and the work of an enemy. At last they are ready for the moon, and off at last. A field of diamonds near the Sea of Tranquility is the prize they seek.

On the moon come torches of life, the edge of a crater, a breakdown, and the dread of being lost on the moon itself. Mark is captured, Jack is puzzled, and Washington sees a ghost, in the breathless sequence boys' fiction loved. The book is a period piece of early space adventure, written when the moon still seemed a place a clever boy might actually reach.
74913-told-in-gallant-deeds:
Belloc Lowndes wrote Told in Gallant Deeds, a child's history of the war, published in London by James Nisbet and Company. The book is dedicated to the Happy Warrior, and Wordsworth's whole poem on that character stands at the front as its standard. The war is the Great War then in progress.

The contents open where the war opened for Britain: Belgium. Then come the White Ensign for the navy, Britain to Arms, and the Battle of Mons. The Great Retreat follows, with Cambrai, Landrécies, and Saint Quentin. Battles of Meaux and the Marne take the story to the turn of the tide in France. Each chapter tells the fighting through deeds a child can grasp and honor. Parents and teachers got a way to tell the young what their fathers were doing, in the war's own first seasons.
75478-the-crystal-planetoids:
The Crystal Planetoids is a science fiction story by Stanton Coblentz. The tale appeared in Amazing Stories in May 1942. A blurb above the story speaks of a vast web in the sky. Invisible beings perch on that web, and the reader is asked what it all means.

The scene is the laboratory of a research institute late in the day. Ronald Gates bends over lenses, batteries, and wires, sure he has beaten his problem at last. His rival Philip Dunbar watches with a dark, doubting air. Eleanor Firth, a young worker at the institute, hurries in with praise for Gates. The narrator notes that both men look at her with softened eyes. All three have taken to working overtime, and not only for the invention's sake.
7552-quotes-and-images-from-motley-s-his:
John Lothrop Motley's History of the Netherlands is the classic American account of the Dutch revolt against Spain, and this volume gathers its quotations and images. Illustrations show the siege of Antwerp, William of Orange, called the Silent, the Earl of Leicester, Alexander Farnese, Prince of Parma, and John of Barneveld. The Hague in 1566, the last year of peace, opens the story.

The quotations catch Motley's republican spirit: a pleasantry called voluntary contributions or benevolences, a good lawyer is a bad Christian, and a common hatred united the provinces for a time at least. In that republic, the notes add, it was a penal offence to talk of peace or truce. The collection is a doorway into Motley's great narrative of a small country disinherited by nature, winning its freedom.
76059-the-thing-in-the-woods:
Harper Williams's mystery novel The Thing in the Woods was published in New York by McBride and Company in 1924. The narrator, Haverill, has just finished his term as a hospital interne when his chief Murchison shows him a letter. A country doctor named George Lennox, in Pennsylvania, wants a substitute for three months while he takes a holiday abroad for his health.

Haverill takes the small practice as a working vacation among mountains, fishing and quiet roads. The contents promise stranger fare: a light in the woods, a mysterious call, a dead cyclist and a boycotted household. A cry in the night, a midnight chase and what the men find in the saw-mill lead to the thing itself, and to a silver bullet.
76463-bog-trotting-for-orchids:
Bog-Trotting for Orchids is a botanical ramble by Grace Greylock Niles, published by G P Putnam's Sons of New York and London in 1904. Its motto is Thoreau's saying that he enters a swamp as a sacred place. Illustrations from nature accompany the text. The book is dedicated to Genevieve Farnell.

The first season opens off to the hills of Berkshire and Bennington. Ball Brook and the bogs of Etchowog follow, names of the author's own mapping. The haunts of the ram's head moccasin flowers and the stolen moccasins fill the early chapters. The pink moccasin flower, Cypripedium acaule, serves as frontispiece. Niles hunts wild orchids through swamps and hail storms, plant by plant. Her book joins field botany to the nature essay, in the years when wild orchids were still being picked toward scarcity.
76713-blue-eyes-and-diamonds:
Lemuel De Bra wrote a crime tale of a wife, a past love, and a wild plan. The tale ran in Argosy All-Story Weekly on March 9, 1929. Betty Danford has lost at cards and fears the cost. She turns to Harry Milholland, a sleuth she once turned down. They meet in a lone room of a fine inn.

Harry calls Betty a madcap, spoiled and sweet at once. He vows he will not join her wild scheme this time. Betty begs with tears and a wag of her hand. A key to a south door plays a part in the plot. Pulp fans get fast talk and a tense close.
76817-disease-in-captive-wild-mammals-an:
Disease in Captive Wild Mammals and Birds was written by Herbert Fox, a doctor who worked as pathologist for the Zoological Society of Philadelphia. The book came out in 1923, with a foreword by Charles B Penrose. Fox based his work on a large list of post mortem exams done at the zoo.

Chapters move through the body in order, from the heart and blood vessels to the lungs, gut, liver, and kidneys. Later parts cover bone, nerves, diet, tumors, and germ diseases. Fox sets out how often each ill shows up and how it looks in wild stock kept in pens. The work gives zoo staff and vets a rare record of health in captive wild life.
76941-naval-songs-and-ballads:
Firth, regius professor of modern history at Oxford, selected and edited these naval songs and ballads for the Navy Records Society. The volume, number thirty-three of the Society's publications, was printed in 1908 on the 1907 subscription. Its object is to bring together ballads that trace the British navy from the sixteenth century to the middle of the nineteenth. At every period since printing began, Firth notes, the exploits of English sailors found someone to sing them.

The pieces reprinted belong to the rough class of ballad meant to carry the news of the day, or to say what the people felt at the moment. Their details cannot be fully trusted, Firth warns, yet they hold an element of truth. The elaborate poet and the rough-hewn ballad-writer both appear in his account, with the humbler sort given the place of honor here.
77026-vanilla-culture-as-practiced-in-th:
Galbraith of Mahé, in the Seychelles Islands, wrote this farming bulletin on how vanilla is grown there. The Department of Agriculture in Washington printed it in 1898 as Bulletin Number 21 of the Division of Botany. Fairchild, whose name the catalog record carries, wrote the introduction that presents Galbraith's paper.

The contents walk a grower through the whole crop. First come the general conditions of the islands, then the starting of a vanillery and the training of the vines. A full section treats the hand pollination of the flowers, with a drawing of the act. Curing the pods for market gets its own plan of a curing house. Planters in warm colonies got a working manual from a man on the ground.
77259-excursion-to-the-orkney-islands:
Excursion to the Orkney Islands is a Florence story by Jacob Abbott, published by Sheldon in 1861. The Florence stories follow young Florence and her family on improving travels abroad. Engravings show a landing at Ben Nevis, choosing the state rooms, and the Orkneys visit. Contents open with a letter from Singapore and the taking of passage north.

Preparations, a letter of credit, and the embarkation fill the early chapters in order. Life on board ship and the steamer Iona carry the family toward Scotland northern isles. Crossing the Mickle ferry and the black craigs stand among the pictured scenes. Abbott teaches geography and conduct through one girl journey, chapter by chapter.
77373-fire-brands:
Tuttle wrote this western novel, Fire Brands, having written Masked Law and Straight Shooting before it. A note at the head says there was something queer about the sale of the Bar S Ranch. Cowmen Sad Sontag and Swede Harrigan sense it at once. They take a hand only when Speck, the youngster whose inheritance the ranch should have been, stirs their interest.

The tale opens in a saloon, where Sad Sontag climbs on the bar to swat a horsefly with his hat. He knocks the bartender's glasses down and misses the fly, the first that ever bit him from behind and got away. The bartender's wrath and Sad's solemn squint set the comic tone of the partnership.
7776-the-call-of-the-cumberlands:
Charles Neville Buck's The Call of the Cumberlands opens near the backbone of the Cumberland ridge, where sun hesitates above a sugar-loaf cone over Misery Creek. Light still crowns the hillsides while gloom thickens below, where water tosses in small cascades between mossy boulders.

A native would know the rough creek bed as a country road, though no traveler passes now, save a partridge calling Bob White and a cardinal flashing among pines. Through mountain speech and feud country, the novel follows families bound to these hills, and a call home that proves hard to refuse.
7801-five-little-friends:
Sherred Willcox Adams's Five Little Friends, pictured by Maud and Miska Petersham, follows Bob, Betty, Paul, Peggy, and little Dot at school and on vacation. Bob wears a brown suit, Betty a checked dress, Paul a white blouse, Peggy curls, and Dot bobbed hair, all under teacher Miss West.

One morning Miss West hides a large round parcel on her desk, and the children guess balloon or football, both wrong. Through classroom surprises, games, and holidays, the book offers small readers a warm, orderly world where five friends learn, play, and look out for one another.
78103-the-trouble-at-pinelands:
The Trouble at Pinelands is a detective story by Ernest Poate. Chelsea House published it in New York in 1922. The contents list twenty three chapters of southern mystery. The Poltergeist opens the tale with a haunting. Bobwhite, A Bad Spell, and A Feud follow in order. A Tragedy stands fifth in the chapter list. Uncertainty, Investigation, and The Inquest move the case forward. A Conflagration and a frustrated lynching raise the danger. The Poltergeist Again returns midway through the book.

A fishing trip and some clews come before an unusual wedding. Somers Disgraces Himself gives a chapter its blunt title. An Explanation and A Flirtation precede the illicit enterprise chapter. The Showdown stands near the end of the contents. A caption shows a man swearing to tote another to death with him. The tale mixes ghost talk with feud country crime.
78186-the-princess-welcome-to-the-highla:
The hosted text is the Gaelic song itself, stanza after stanza with a returning chorus. The chorus calls on the royal daughter to rise and come, and to take up her dwelling among the Gaels. The princess is named in the verses as Louise, the fair and noble maid.

It praises her mother, the dear Queen of Britain, land of freedom. When word comes that she is bound in marriage, fires of joy will blaze on every hill. Thousands of welcomes wait her in the Land of the Gael, in the Gaels' own tongue. Not the Campbells alone will show their love: every clan among the Gaels will be bound in friendship. It is a clan welcome song for a royal bride coming north.
78216-the-dashwoods:
The Dashwoods, by Steele Rudd, came out at Sydney in 1920, with fifteen full page plates by Claude Marquet. Rudd, whose true name was A H Davis, wrote On Our Selection and a string of kin books. This tale is a sequel to On an Australian Farm, first held in rights in 1911.

The Dashwood clan spends a full week in the great city, and each day shows fresh wonders. All love it but the mother and Maria. The mother tires in a day and longs for Fairfield, its fowls, cows, and wheat fields. Maria finds a baby a sore bar to peace in town. Chapters take the clan to the theatre, to church, and to the surf. A sheriff, a top lawyer, and a man named McClure cross their path. Farm fans get broad fun with a bush clan in town.
7846-departmental-ditties-and-ballads-an:
Rudyard Kipling's Departmental Ditties and Ballads and Barrack-Room Ballads joins two early volumes of verse on empire, office, and army life. The first runs from army headquarters and a legend of the Foreign Office through Uriah, public waste, and a code of morals to the last department.

The second brings the Ballad of East and West, the King's Mercy and Jest, Boh Da Thone, Danny Deever, Tommy, Fuzzy-Wuzzy, Gunga Din, Mandalay, and the Widow at Windsor. The opening lines eat bread and salt beside the dead, a pledge of shared life that runs through both books.
78726-blood-lands:
Blood Lands is a science fiction story by Alfred Coppel. It opens with a native chant against the men from the stars. You will never take us away from our land, the chant says, and no one who has touched this sacred land shall ever leave it.

Kenyon, a starman, waits at the edge of a plume-grove where the land runs down to a tideless red sea. The rendezvous is well away from the stinking ground burned by the starship's landing. He feels sick, and the flat island offers no hiding place, for the ship's spire commands a view of everything. He is waiting for Elyra, a native girl, to come out of the grove. Liaison with native women, he tells himself, is common enough among starmen, if not in the best taste. But this mission is one of repatriation, and the land itself seems to rage against it.
78879-animals-of-ancient-lands:
Carroll Lane Fenton describes the first beasts to live on land in a small book issued at Girard, Kansas, in 1922. The booklet was number 274 in the Ten Cent Pocket Series edited by E Haldeman-Julius. Fenton says the text grew from a talk he gave often to general audiences.

Inside, the first chapter follows the move from sea to land, as fins became feet and legs before the end of the Devonian age. Fenton leans on the work of Professor Case, the leading expert on Permian backboned beasts of the time. Plates show the strange forms that followed. Readers get a plain, picture-led tour of early land life, with charts and hard terms left to companion volumes in the series.
79088-a-prisoner-of-the-reds:
A Prisoner of the Reds is a memoir by Francis McCullagh, printed at London in 1921. McCullagh was a captain in the Royal Irish Fusiliers. John Murray issued the book, which he dedicates to the British officers and soldiers captured with him at Krasnoyarsk, Siberia, on January 6, 1920. A front picture shows the Tsarina and Tsarevich.

The contents begin with the flight from Omsk, by train and then by sleigh. Capture follows, then the horrors of the retreat, with typhus hospitals and scattered families. Face to face with Bolshevism, the prisoners are kept as hostages. McCullagh tells what a British officer saw inside the Russian civil war.
79277-moods:
Mercedes de Acosta wrote Moods, a book of prose poems published by Moffat, Yard and Company in New York in 1919. The pieces are short and named for states of feeling: Memory, Faith, Love, Disgust, Joy, Despair, Tenderness, Hurt Feelings, and Weariness among them. Later pieces treat time, revelation, finding God, and peace.

Memory opens the book. The speaker, who always preaches looking forward, sits looking backward into a cloud of memory. A touch of a hand, a strain of music across far waters, or the smell of dead violets in a box can open whole vistas of the past. By day, tasks crowd memory out; by night it returns with tragic eyes. The poems are early work by a writer later known in theatre and film circles.
79563-buzzards:
Tuttle wrote a western in his Hashknife and Sleepy line, billed as a new mystery of the range trails. Beginning an orphan's odyssey opens it. Rex Morgan came back from his mother's funeral and sat on the front porch of the little place he had always known as home. He was a slender young man of twenty, with somber brown eyes and an unruly mop of black hair.

His black suit was slightly threadbare, and his shirt cuffs were rough edged from many washings. The doctor had said it was heart failure. Just now he stared at the skyline of Northport, California, and wondered who would pay for everything. He had no money, as far as he knew, and was all alone in the world. Hashknife Hartfield and Sleepy ride to a young orphan's rescue.
79572-man-s-descent-from-the-gods:
Anthony M Ludovici wrote a case against Prohibition wrapped in a study of old myths. William Heinemann issued Man's Descent from the Gods in London in 1921. Ludovici had written A Defence of Aristocracy, as the title page notes. He gave the book to Mr and Mrs Edmond Hunt with warm regard.

Chapters treat Prometheus and Dionysus as men first, then as gods in tale. Fire, food, drink, Pandora, and Eve all get long, bold study. Ludovici follows Herbert Spencer against sun-myth readings of Max Muller and others. The drink laws of his day stand as the true target of the whole argument.
79739-a-conquest-of-two-worlds:
Edmond Hamilton wrote A Conquest of Two Worlds, a science fiction story printed in Wonder Stories in February 1932. The editor's foreword frames the tale as a warning. Just as white men have little to be proud of in the conquest of the Americas, he writes, mankind may not be proud of conquering the planets.

The story asks whether a reader would aid the greedy exploitation of other worlds, if it meant wiping out their harmless peoples. Its hero is Mart Halkett, once a student in New York in the spring of 1962. That year Ross Gillen, a shy Arizona scientist, solved atomic power after sixteen years of work and changed the world. Hamilton, a pioneer of space opera, here turns the space adventure against itself.
8393-life-in-the-backwoods:
Susanna Moodie wrote Life in the Backwoods as a sequel to Roughing It in the Bush, her famous account of settling in Upper Canada. Where the earlier book told of arrival and hardship, this volume sketches from nature. Its epigraph says the later life of a settler family is painful experience in a distant land, made her own, whether grave or gay.

Moodie, author of Life in the Clearings and Flora Lyndsay, writes with a settler's eye for neighbors, seasons, and the slow work of making a home. Readers of Canadian pioneer literature get a direct, often sharp voice, unsparing about both the bush and the people who came to it. The book stands as a classic of immigration writing.
8441-between-friends:
Robert W Chambers published Between Friends in 1914. It opens with Drene, a man who has entered into the obscurity of himself, like a man reentering a darkened house and lying down, aware of sunlight, bird-calls, and breeze outside. Through twilit corridors of his mind, Chambers follows a bruised soul, in the psychological manner of his later novels.

Chambers, once famous for weird tales, turned in his later years to society and psychological fiction, and this novel shows that turn. Readers get a story of friendship and inner life, told in the lush, slightly overwrought style Chambers favored. It suits readers tracing how popular novelists handled the new psychology of the 1910s.
8534-daily-strength-for-daily-needs:
Mary Wilder Tileston selected Daily Strength for Daily Needs, following her Joy and Strength for the Pilgrim's Day and Quiet Hours. Each day gives verses for strength, opening on January 1 with they go from strength to strength, and first the blade, then the ear. That the full corn in the ear, under the motto, as thy days, so shall thy strength be.

Tileston's devotional belongs to the Victorian habit of a verse for each morning, chosen to carry readers through the day. The selections draw on Scripture and hymns, arranged by calendar. Readers who keep a daily devotional will find a classic of the genre, plain, brief, and meant to be read slowly, one day at a time.
8777-authors-and-friends:
Annie Fields recalls the writers she knew in Authors and Friends. Opening with Chaucer's company of the leaf, whose laurel chaplets keep beauty fresh and green against every storm. Her contents read like a literary guest list: Longfellow from 1807 to 1882, glimpses of Emerson. Oliver Wendell Holmes with personal recollections and unpublished letters, days with Mrs Stowe, Celia Thaxter, Whittier's life and friendships, and Tennyson with Lady Tennyson.

Fields writes as a hostess and friend, not a critic, preserving talk, letters, and small kindnesses from Boston's golden age of letters. Longfellow's chapter begins with lilac buds bursting their sheaths each year, a fitting image for memory's return. Readers of American literature will find warm, firsthand portraits, best read as companions to the authors' own works rather than as formal biography.
9088-thoroughbreds:
W. A. Fraser wrote this novel of horse racing in upstate New York, dedicated to his wife, a thoroughbred herself. The scene is Brookfield, a village pinched into quiet isolation by a century of growth around it. Into its calm bursts horse racing, unearthed by Reverend Dolman and led by John Porter, called Honest John.

Porter's father raced in old Kentucky for sport, and the son kept the love. Fraser follows bets, breeds, and village talk with warmth. The novel charms as a tale of sport, character, and a small town stirred by speed and pride.
922-sunday-under-three-heads:
Charles Dickens wrote this short work on Sunday, dedicated to the Bishop of London. He takes Sunday under three heads, asking how the day should be kept, and for whom. His target is the strict Sabbatarian view that would shut the poor out of innocent recreation, while the rich enjoy their own Sundays in private.

Dickens argues with humour and humanity for a Sunday that allows rest, fresh air, and simple pleasures to working folk. The pamphlet shows his early social conscience and his gift for pleading a cause in plain prose. It remains a lively piece of Victorian debate, on a question that still divides opinion.
931-the-bab-ballads:
W. S. Gilbert wrote these comic ballads under the pen name Bab, for the magazine Fun and later collections. Sailors, policemen, ghosts, and lovers tumble through topsy-turvy plots, told in brisk rhyme with a logic that turns sense on its head. The 1920 Macmillan edition gathers the set for a new generation.

Gilbert's humour is dry, precise, and absurd, and the ballads were the seed of his Savoy operas with Sullivan. Many types and jokes from the stage first appear here, in verse. The book is a treat for lovers of nonsense with a sharp edge, where rhyme and reason play a merry game.
933-more-bab-ballads:
W. S. Gilbert gathered more of his Bab Ballads in this companion volume, with tales such as The Bumboat Woman's Story, The Two Ogres, Little Oliver, Mister William, and Pasha Bailey Ben. Lieutenant-Colonel Flare and other comic heroes follow, each caught in a plot where logic leads straight to folly.

Gilbert's verse is brisk and witty, with rhymes that snap and morals that wink. The ballads show the same topsy-turvy world as the first set, where rank, love, and law are turned upside down. The volume is a further feast for Gilbert fans, and a fine sample of Victorian comic verse at its most ingenious.
9405-the-book-of-old-english-ballads:
George Wharton Edwards gathered this book of old English ballads, with decorative drawings and an introduction by Hamilton Mabie, in 1896. Contents include Chevy Chace, King Cophetua and the Beggar-Maid, King Leir and his three daughters, and Fair Rosamond. Robin Hood tales, Barbara Allen, Sir Patrick Spens, and The Nut-brown Maid follow.

Mabie's introduction opens with Chevy Chace itself, a woeful hunting in the border hills. The ballads sing of love, war, and fate in old, plain speech. The book remains a handsome gateway to the ballad tradition, for readers and singers alike.
9482-what-sami-sings-with-the-birds:
Johanna Spyri, best known for Heidi, wrote What Sami Sings with the Birds, here in Helen B. Dole's 1917 translation. Sami is a poor Swiss boy whose hard life leaves him few joys, save the songs of birds by Lake Geneva. The tale follows him from Old Mary Ann's care to his grandmother's house, through want and loss. Birds, heard each spring, mark his hope.

As Sami grows, he learns to sing with the birds, and song steadies him through hard times. Spyri keeps the prose simple and the feeling warm, with Swiss fields, brooks, and ash trees close at hand. A reader gets a gentle story of a child who finds courage in nature and music, and a fine short companion to Spyri's better-known Alpine tales.
9500-farm-ballads:
Will Carleton wrote Farm Ballads, a book of poems drawn from farm life and country folk. Carleton says he wrote them in the open air, on trains, and in editors' rooms, then printed them in papers where readers met them with favor. Friends across the country asked him to gather them in lasting form. The book answers that call with plain, heartfelt verse.

Poems sing of teams afield, harvests, home, and the toil and humor of rural days. Carleton's voice is simple and direct, with a farmer's eye for work and weather. A reader gets a beloved set of American country poems, warm and easy to read aloud, from a poet who knew the fields first hand.
9649-with-trapper-jim-in-the-north-woods:
Lawrence J. Leslie wrote With Trapper Jim in the North Woods in 1913, a boys' camp tale of the Campfire and Trail series. Three chums reach Trapper Jim's hunting lodge in the far North Woods, led by luck and pluck. Toby Jucklin, the stuttering lad of broad shoulders, steals early scenes. Chapters promise woodcraft, trapping secrets, and a silver fox.

Later chapters track a thief, a clog trail, and a bruin surprise, with smoking out intruders and steady shooting beside. The boys learn the woods by doing, not by books. A reader gets a rousing outdoor adventure, full of camp lore, animal craft, and the fun of chums on the trail.
9778-vane-of-the-timberlands:
Harold Bindloss wrote Vane of the Timberlands, a novel of Canada's woods, coasts, and lumber camps. Vane, a young man of the timber country, faces a friend in need, a breeze down a fir-scented inlet, and an afternoon ashore. Chapters follow Vancouver, a sail north, a first mishap, and the bush, with floods, trails, and an intercepted letter. Lucy Vane, Jessy, and Evelyn cross his path.

Later chapters bring a search, a flood, and convincing testimony, till Vane is reinstated at the last. Bindloss writes with brisk, outdoor verve. A reader gets a rousing Canadian adventure, full of canoes, camps, and a hero's fight for his name.
9852-the-man-from-the-clouds:
J. Storer Clouston's 1919 novel opens with a man found on a shore after coming down from the clouds. A small community takes him in, but a suspicious stranger, a doctor, and questions about who he is soon unsettle the place.

As the story moves into its second part, an idea, a little dinner, and a test bring the stranger's secret closer to exposure, with a pursuer named Bolton on the track. Clouston keeps the mystery light and brisk. Readers get a puzzle about identity, told with humor and a seaside setting.
9854-frank-roscoe-s-secret-or-the-darewe:
Allen Chapman's 1908 boys' book follows Frank Roscoe and his Darewell chums on a woodland holiday that turns into a mystery. The boys plan a dinner, stumble on a conspiracy, and watch as Ned is captured and hears strange talk in the woods.

Suspicions grow around a stranger in town and a neighbor's queer behavior, while the chums camp, race, and use a telephone wire to untangle the plot. Chapman writes in the brisk school-story manner of his day. Young readers get friendship, camping fun, and a secret worth guarding.
a-book-for-kids: Clarence James Dennis writes this book of verse for children in a playful Australian voice. Its poems visit a baker, a postman, a swagman, a pieman, and other figures of a local street. A kindly gentleman urges a boy to treasure his books and to keep them as companions rather than toys. The verses mix humor, rhyme, and everyday scenes that young readers can enjoy aloud.
a-book-of-golden-deeds:
A Book of Golden Deeds, published in 1864 by Charlotte M Yonge, gathers true tales of brave and selfless acts. Yonge was a popular Victorian novelist and writer for young readers. Rather than inventing a story, she collected real deeds of heroism from history and retold them in short, clear accounts meant to be remembered.

Each tale shows someone choosing courage, loyalty, or sacrifice at a hard moment, often at risk to their own life. Together the stories form a kind of moral gallery, offered to readers as examples worth copying. The book was a Victorian favorite for family and school reading, and it shows how the age taught character through story.
a-bundle-of-ballads:
Henry Morley edited this gathering of old English ballads, with an introduction on the minstrels who once carried such songs from house to house. The contents open with Chevy Chase in two versions, then The Nut-Brown Maid and the outlaw tale of Adam Bell, Clym of the Clough, and William of Cloudeslie. A glossary closes the book.

Robin Hood rides here, with Sir Patrick Spens, Edward Edward, Barbara Allen's Cruelty, The Children in the Wood, and Casabianca. Morley, a tireless editor of cheap classics for working readers, chose ballads for story and singability alike. The volume is a pocket library of the people's poetry, from border raids to ghostly lovers.
a-collection-of-ballads:
Andrew Lang edited this gathering of old English and Scottish ballads, first published in 1897 and reprinted in 1910, with an introduction and notes. The contents open with Sir Patrick Spens, the Battle of Otterbourne, Tam Lin, and Thomas the Rhymer. Many of the songs are centuries old and were carried by singing rather than by print.

The ballads tell of sea wrecks, border raids, fairies, ghosts, true love, murder, and betrayal, in short stanzas made to be sung. Names like Kinmont Willie, Johnnie Armstrong, and the Twa Sisters fill the list. Lang chose well-loved versions, so the book works as a first shelf of the folk ballad tradition.
a-countess-from-canada-a-story-of-life-i: Bessie Marchant tells a backwoods story of a countess from Canada. Its chapters move beyond the second portage through accidents, floods, business bothers, and a stranger who proves a friend. A woman of business, a first fishing, and new friendships fill the Canadian tale. Marchant writes an adventure of courage and resource in the northern woods.
a-string-of-amber-beads: Martha Everts Holden strings short essays like amber beads in this volume, copyrighted in 1893 and dedicated to Andrew Shuman, her literary adviser and truest friend. The contents run from I Didn't Think and Stay Where You Are through a cowardly mate, being shut in, and the circling year as a clock. Later beads include sermons from flies, the man who knows it all, bald heads and unequal chances, and human straws. Each bead is a small observation polished by wit.
about-orchids: Frederick Boyle chats about orchids in this 1893 volume with coloured illustrations, inscribed to his guide, comforter, and friend Joseph Godseff. The contents run from his gardening and an orchid sale through orchids themselves to cool, warm, and hot orchids, a lost orchid, an orchid farm, and orchids and hybridizing. Vanda Sanderiana fronts the book, with Odontoglossum, Oncidium, Dendrobium, Coelogene, Cattleya, and Cypripedium among the plates.
allan-and-the-ice-gods:
Allan and the Ice Gods, published in 1927 by H Rider Haggard, is the final volume of the Allan Quatermain saga. It forms the fourth part of a loosely linked series that began with Allan and the Holy Flower. Quatermain, Haggard's famous hunter hero, once more takes the hallucinogenic taduki drug, as he did in earlier novels of the series.

Under the drug, he finds himself reliving a past life as Wi, a civilized man living in the barbaric ice age as part of a clan of cavemen. The device lets Haggard set a modern mind inside a prehistoric struggle for survival. The book closes the Quatermain sequence with its strangest journey, into deep time rather than across Africa.
an-alphabet-of-old-friends: Walter Crane makes an alphabet of old friends for the nursery, with a zodiac to match, in pictures and short verses. Each letter brings a familiar figure or creature, drawn in Crane's bright, decorative style. The book is a charming example of Victorian picture-book art, meant to teach letters through delight.
an-unprotected-female-at-the-pyramids:
Anthony Trollope tells a tale of Egypt from the 1864 Chapman and Hall collection Tales of All Countries. He begins by remembering how Grand Cairo filled his young imagination from the Arabian Nights: fantastic houses, beautiful or cunning women, and good-natured, capricious monarchs. The grown traveler finds a different Egypt, full of tourists.

Among them is an English lady traveling without protector or chaperone, determined to see the Pyramids on her own terms. Guides, dragomans, fellow tourists, and a persistent admirer test her independence at every step. Trollope, who knew the tourist world well, mixes satire of travelers' pretensions with real sympathy for his heroine's nerve.
austin-and-his-friends:
Frederic H. Balfour published this book with Greening and Company of London in 1906. Its advertisement explains the experiment: old ghost stories were ghastly affairs of white sheets and clanking chains, enjoyed until bedtime. Balfour instead attempts a cheerful ghost story, fronted by a picture of Daphnis at the fountain.

Austin and his friends talk with, rather than flee from, the departed. One voice argues that the dead are not shadows of living men; rather the living move in a vain show until the spirit, the true substance, is set free. Darkness itself gains a revealing power in these conversations. Balfour, a writer on Taoism as well as fiction, turns the haunted-house tale into genial philosophy about death, light, and the soul's real life.
authors-and-friends:
Annie Fields, the Boston hostess whose Charles Street salon drew writers for decades, gathered these portraits of her circle. Longfellow opens the volume, in a chapter dated by his life, 1807 to 1882. Glimpses of Emerson follow, then personal recollections of Oliver Wendell Holmes with unpublished letters, days with Mrs. Stowe, and pieces on Celia Thaxter, Whittier, and the Tennysons.

Fields writes from inside the friendships, with letters and talk quoted freely. Harriet Beecher Stowe appears in 1862, deep in drains, sewers, and manure heaps for her Hartford house of eight gables, gazing with joy on the growing establishment. Lilac time recalls Longfellow's presence each spring. The book preserves literary Boston and its visitors as one insider knew them: kindly, exact, and close to the fireside.
ballads:
Robert Louis Stevenson's Ballads, in its second edition of 1895, gathers his long narrative poems drawn from Pacific and Scottish legend. The Song of Rahero tells a Tahitian tale of slaying and vengeance, with Stevenson's own notes attached. The Feast of Famine does the same for Marquesan manners.

Ticonderoga retells a West Highland legend about a name that brings doom, and Heather Ale recalls the last makers of the Picts' secret drink. Stevenson wrote these poems during his South Seas years, testing whether ballad meter could carry foreign folklore without flattening it. The notes show how carefully he learned the stories from island tellers and Highland tradition.
barrack-room-ballads:
Rudyard Kipling's barrack-room verse fills two series here, the first of 1892 and the second of 1896, forty songs and ballads in all. The dedication is to Thomas Atkins, the ordinary British soldier, in the person of T. A. The contents list the famous names: Danny Deever, Tommy, Fuzzy-Wuzzy, Gunga Din, and Mandalay.

Kipling writes in the soldier's own barrack slang, cockney dropped aitches and all. The subjects are the private's whole world: hangings and route marches, cholera camps and loot, the Widow at Windsor, and the long sail home in Troopin'. Gentlemen-Rankers gives the ruined officer serving in the ranks his own bitter song. No book of verse did more to put the common soldier's voice into English poetry.
beasts-men-and-gods:
Ferdinand Ossendowski's Beasts, Men and Gods carries an explanatory note vouching for its author, a Polish scientist, whom Dr Albert Shaw called the Robinson Crusoe of the twentieth century. The editor admits the adventures seem too highly colored to be real. Part one, Drawing Lots with Death, follows Ossendowski's flight from Bolshevik Siberia in 1920, through forests, frozen rivers, and Red partisans.

Part two enters Mongolia, where he meets the Baron Ungern, the mad White general who took Urga, and hears prophecies in mysterious Tibet. A young woman's corruption shows him, he writes, what depravity Bolshevism brought into the world. The book was a 1922 sensation; historians still argue over how much Ossendowski embroidered.
berlin-and-sans-souci-or-frederick-the-g:
L. Mühlbach's Berlin and Sans-Souci continues her Frederick the Great romances, following the king from the throne room to his beloved palace of carefree ease. Sans-Souci, the little vineyard palace at Potsdam, gives the book its second capital: there Frederick plays the flute, writes French verse, and gathers philosophers instead of courtiers. Voltaire's residence at court stands at the story's center, friendship curdling into rivalry. Berlin supplies the counterweight of guards, parade, and the king's Spartan discipline.

Mühlbach, whose header here reads Louise Muhlbach, writes the enlightened court as domestic drama. Ministers, generals, mistresses of ceremony, and the king's family circle through receptions, concerts, and campaigns' returns. Readers who finished Frederick the Great and His Court get the reign's second act here, the philosopher-king whose friendships were waged like his wars.
between-friends:
Robert W. Chambers published this novel in 1914, opening on Drene, a sculptor who has entered into the obscurity of himself like a man re-entering a closed, darkened house. Life, Chambers insists, goes on even when the sky crashes earthward. Drene comes out of his catastrophe lean, grey at the temples, his youth finished, persuaded it has been winter for many years.

Friendship is the treatment. Dinners at the seashore, every summer entertainment in town, and cooler, starlit evenings in the studio slowly change him. A woman friend reads aloud, chats, and discusses his work in hand across a wider range than he had ever opened to anyone. The dark preoccupation lifts in her company. Chambers, famous for The King in Yellow, writes here a quiet Künstlerroman of grief cured by talk, work, and one faithful witness.
big-people-and-little-people-of-other-la:
Edward R. Shaw, dean of the School of Pedagogy at New York University, wrote this children's geography for the American Book Company in 1900. Big people and little people of other lands are shown at home, in school, and at work, in short chapters with pictures. China opens the tour: schools there are only for boys, and the boys make a great deal of noise.

A Chinese teacher, Shaw explains, thinks boys idle unless they study aloud, so each shouts as loud as he can. Having learned his lesson, a boy gives his book to the teacher, turns his back, and shouts the whole lesson out to prove it known. Eskimo chapters follow the same plan. A winter house has one room, entered by a long passage that keeps out the cold. Sealskin beds line a bench, and lamps give heat, light, and cooking at once.
bleek-mantis-friends:
Dorothea Bleek edited The Mantis and His Friends for print in 1924. The tales come from her father Wilhelm Bleek's old notebooks. /Xam storytellers had dictated them in the 1870s at Cape Town.

The trickster Mantis leads a cast of beasts, stars, and spirits. His pranks, lusts, and sorrows shape a whole mythic world here. The tales rank as the richest first record of San oral art. Bleek's team caught the voice of tellers whose world was vanishing. Readers meet Bushman folklore at its source, strange and deeply human throughout. The Mantis himself shifts from fool to maker within a single tale.
boy-blue-and-his-friends:
Etta Austin Blaisdell and Mary Frances Blaisdell wrote Boy Blue and His Friends, copyrighted by Little, Brown in 1906. The Blaisdell sisters built the reader around Mother Goose rhymes, so young children meet old friends on every page. Short, direct sentences grow harder step by step.

Stories explain why Mary's lamb went to school and what the mouse sought up the clock. Five little pigs, Jack and Jill, Jack Horner's pie, and the old woman in the shoe follow in turn. Boy Blue and his dog Shep play through the fields between tales. A party scene with cakes and maple candy shows the home side. First graders got a graded reader that felt like play, at school or at home.
britannica-1911-abbasids:
Abbasids names a dynasty in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, the caliphs of Bagdad, second great house of the Muslim empire. The entry grounds their claim in descent from Abbas, the Prophet's eldest uncle. That claim set them against the Omayyads as rightful heirs.

Revolt ripened under Merwan the Second: Ibrahim the Imam rose, fell, and his brother Abu'l-Abbas as-Saffah crushed the Omayyads at the Greater Zab in 750. Mansur moved the seat to Bagdad. Harun al-Rashid and Mamun brought splendour, then decay set in. Turkish guards swallowed the caliphs' power, provinces fell away, and Hulagu burned Bagdad in 1258. A shadow line lasted in Egypt till Selim took the last caliph to Constantinople.
britannica-1911-aids:
Aids, a term of medieval finance, is explained at length in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. An aid was part of the service a man owed his lord. It rested on the idea that followers should help their lord in special emergency or need. Just when an aid could be demanded, and how much, were matters of constant dispute.

Custom in twelfth-century Normandy and England recognised two clear occasions: knighting the lord's eldest son and marrying his eldest daughter. England's Great Charter of 1215 fixed a third, the lord's ransom from captivity, and required any aid to be reasonable. That clause later gained huge importance as an early root of taxation by consent. The entry follows aids alongside tallage, a lower and more arbitrary tax, down to Edward I's forced surrender of 1296 and 1297.
britannica-1911-aland-islands:
Åland Islands, a group at the entrance to the Gulf of Bothnia, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. The islands lie about 25 miles from the coast of Sweden and 15 from Finland. They form part of a Finnish province and number nearly three hundred. About eighty are inhabited, and the rest are desolate rocks. They continue a dangerous granite reef along the south coast of Finland.

The islands once belonged to Sweden and were ceded to Russia in 1809. Their people number about 19,000, most of Swedish descent, and are hardy seamen and fishermen. The soil is thin and sandy, and the climate keen. Yet fir, spruce, and birch grow there, and rye, barley, and flax meet the people's needs. Cheese, butter, hides, and salted meat and fish are exported.
britannica-1911-aran-islands:
Aran Islands are three islands across Galway Bay. They lie off Ireland's west coast. Sailors see them as a natural breakwater. County Galway claims them politically. Their population in 1901 was 2,863. Inishmore is the northernmost and largest. Inishmaan is the middle island. Inisheer is the eastern island. Carboniferous limestone forms all three.

Ancient remains make the islands remarkable. Dun-Aengus stands on Inishmore's cliff. That circular stone fort rises 220 feet high. Tradition links it to the Fir-bolg settlers. Seven similar structures survive in the group. Saints also gave Inishmore fame. Recluses settled there in early centuries. Holy wells and shrines still attract visitors. The Congested Districts Board aided the islanders. It improved fishing methods especially. A fish curing station operates at Killeany.
britannica-1911-azo-compounds:
Azo Compounds are organic substances built on two nitrogen atoms double-linked, joining an aryl group on one side to an alkyl or aryl group on the other. Chemists make them by reducing nitro compounds in alkaline liquid, by oxidizing hydrazo compounds, or by coupling a diazotized amine with a phenol or amine.

Strong colour marks the whole family, yet they serve as dyes only when they also carry acid or basic salt-forming groups. Oxidizers turn them into azoxy compounds; reducers give hydrazo compounds or amines. The entry then works through members: azo-benzene, orange-red plates found by Mitscherlich in 1834, and amino-azo compounds, yellow-brown to red crystals that heat with aniline salts to yield induline colors.
britannica-1911-bagshot-beds:
Bagshot Beds, in geology, are a series of sands and clays laid down in shallow water. Some are fresh-water beds, some marine. They belong to the upper Eocene rocks of England's London and Hampshire basins. They take their name from Bagshot Heath in Surrey and show well in Hampshire and the Isle of Wight too.

Three divisions are accepted: upper Barton sand and clay, middle Bracklesham beds, and lower beds seen at Bournemouth and Alum Bay. The lower sands and clays carry plant-bearing layers famous for fossil leaves, eucalyptus, sequoia, and palms among them. Pipeclays of the formation are greatly valued for pottery. They are dug near Wareham and Corfe and shipped from Poole. In the London basin the beds cap hills of London clay. Hampstead and Harrow show such caps.
britannica-1911-bahrein-islands:
Bahrein Islands are a group in the Persian Gulf, some twenty miles east of the El Hasa coast south of the port of El Katif, once a great mart of Indian trade. The largest island, Bahrein itself, runs twenty-seven miles long: a low, sandy flat broken by palm groves and the rocky Jebel Dukhan, hill of mist.

Coral islands complete the group, Moharek next in size. The soil is mostly fertile, water plentiful, citrons prized, and fish cheap and abundant. Shallow, reef-shut seas admit only native craft. Bahrein has always centred the Gulf's pearl fishing, with about 400 boats paying tax to the sheik. The capital, Manameh, holds about 8,000 people, chiefly of the Wahabi sect.
britannica-1911-balearic-islands:
The Balearic Islands form a Spanish province in the Mediterranean, off the east coast of Spain. Four large islands and eleven small ones make up the group, with 311,649 people in 1900 and an area of 1,935 square miles. The 1911 Britannica entry divides the group into eastern and western parts.

Majorca and Minorca lead the eastern group, once the ancient Insulae Baleares, with islets such as Cabrera and Dragonera. Iviza and Formentera lead the western group, the old Pityusae or Pine Islands. Cabrera gets a grim note: French prisoners landed there by Spanish captors in 1808 were left almost to starve. Majorca, Minorca, and Iviza have entries of their own.
britannica-1911-banda-islands:
The Banda Islands are a group of the Dutch East Indies in the Banda Sea, south of Ceram, under the residency of Amboyna. Three chief islands and several smaller ones make up the group, with a total land area of about sixteen square miles. Great Banda, or Lontor, is the largest; Banda Neira lies to its north.

Lontor, Neira, and Gunong Api form part of the rim of a drowned crater, much like Santorin in the Aegean. Gunong Api, Fire Mountain, rises 2,200 feet and still erupts; quakes and a huge sea wave wrecked the islands in 1852. The 1911 Britannica entry notes the chief town, Banda, on Neira, guarded by two Dutch forts of the early 1600s, Nassau and Belgica.
britannica-1911-barton-beds:
Barton Beds is a geological name explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It labels a series of soft grey and brown clays with layers of sand, of Upper Eocene age, found in the Hampshire Tertiary basin. The beds show especially well in the cliffs of Barton and Hordwell and in the Isle of Wight. A table in the entry lines the series up with matching rocks in the Paris Basin across the Channel.

Two parts make up the series. The lower Barton Clay is rich in fossils, holding shells such as Fusus and Ostrea, fishes, and even a crocodile named Diplocynodon. Above it lie the Barton Sands, with few fossils, which are very pure and were used in glass making. The entry notes that the beds are missing from the London basin and gives the continental name Bartonien, introduced by Mayer-Eymar in 1857.
britannica-1911-bay-islands:
Bay Islands, in Spanish Islas de la Bahía, is a small group of islands in the Caribbean Sea, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The group lies off the coast of Honduras and forms a district of that country. Its people numbered about 3000 in 1905, some 500 of them Indians. The chief islands are Roatan, Guanaja, and Utilla, with Barbareta, Helena, Morat, the Hog Islands, and many small cays, or low islets, besides. 

Roatan takes the lead in the account. It is about thirty miles long by nine broad, with hills rising to 900 feet, covered in valuable woods and full of deer and wild hogs. Its trade, mostly with New Orleans, is in plantains, coconuts, and other fruit. Columbus found Guanaja in 1502, but settlement waited for British logwood cutters in the 1600s. Britain annexed the islands in 1852, then gave them to Honduras in 1859.
britannica-1911-bembridge-beds:
Bembridge Beds are strata, layers of rock, of Oligocene age in the Isle of Wight and Hampshire, England. They belong to a fluvio-marine series, laid down by rivers and sea together. In order they sit between the Hamstead beds above and the Osborne beds below.

Two parts make up the group. The Bembridge limestone, a freshwater pool deposit fifteen to twenty-five feet thick, holds large land snails and the fruit of the plant Chara. Above it rest the Bembridge marls, clays seventy to a hundred and twenty feet thick, mixing freshwater shells with sea forms like Ostrea. One thin sandy layer in the marls has yielded many fossil insects and leaves.
britannica-1911-big-rapids:
Big Rapids is a Michigan city and the county seat of Mecosta County. It stands on both sides of the Muskegon River, 56 miles north by east of Grand Rapids. The 1911 Britannica entry gives 4,686 people in 1900 and 4,519 in the 1910 census. The Père Marquette and Grand Rapids and Indiana railways serve it. The town took its name from the falls of the Muskegon at this spot. The river drops 16 feet inside the city limits.

A dam south of the city yields 16,000 horse-power. Part of that power passes to the city itself. Lumber and furniture lead its manufactures, with saw-filing machinery behind them. The Ferris Institute, opened in 1884, is a large private co-educational school in the town. Settlement began in 1854, and city charter came in 1869. Numbers were already falling when the entry was written.
britannica-1911-bonin-islands:
The Bonin Islands, called Ogasawara-Jima by the Japanese, are a chain of twenty small islands in the Pacific belonging to Japan. They run near north and south about 500 miles from the Japanese mainland, with a coastline of 174.65 miles and a total area of 28.82 square miles. Only ten islands are of any real size.

Family names charm the map: Bridegroom, Go-between, Bride, Elder and Younger Brother, Father, Mother, Niece, and the sisters. European geographers grouped them as the Parry, Beechey, and Coffin or Bailey islands. Chichi-jima, the second largest, was named Peel Island by Captain Beechey in 1827. The entry goes on through the islands' rocks, plants, animals, settlers, and their passing from whalers' use into Japanese rule.
britannica-1911-brionian-islands:
Brionian Islands are a group of small islands in the Adriatic Sea off the west coast of Istria, split from the mainland by the narrow Canale di Fasana. They belong to Austria and number twelve in all. For centuries their stone, not their soil, drew the world to them.

Quarries worked for ages supplied building stone for the palaces and bridges of Venice and the whole Adriatic coast, and in later years for Vienna and Berlin as well. Position adds a military role: the islands command the entrance to the naval harbour of Pola, so Fort Tegetthoff rises on the largest island, Brioni, with smaller works on others. About 100 Italian quarrymen live there, a tiny population for islands whose stone built so widely.
britannica-1911-burns-and-scalds:
A burn is the mark of dry heat laid on a part of the body, while a scald is the work of wet heat. In sick care there is no gap between the two, the 1911 Britannica entry says. Their sorting and their cure are one and the same.

The entry takes up a scale of six grades of burn, ranked by the worst part of the hurt. Burns of the first grade show sharp pain, a red skin, a brief swell, and a peel of skin in time. Burns of the next grade raise small blisters of clear fluid on the lit skin. Below the blister lie the raw nerves of the skin. Such burns leave no scar, though they may stain the skin for good. Third grade burns kill part of the true skin.
britannica-1911-bury-st-edmunds:
Bury St Edmunds is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a town in Suffolk. It stands on the Lark, eighty-seven miles north-east of London by rail. The count for 1901 is 16,255 folk in the town. It sits on a low rise in a rich farmed district.

The church gate tower is a fine bit of early Norman work. The west gate shows rich work of a later church age. Those gates and ruined walls are all that is left of the great abbey. St Mary's church holds the tomb of Mary Tudor, queen of France. Its carved roof dates from the early fifteenth century. Ruins in gardens behind show the abbey's plan in part.
britannica-1911-cape-verde-islands:
Cape Verde Islands form a group of isles off the west coast of Africa. The 1911 Britannica entry lists them as a holding of Portugal. Ten isles make up the group, plus four small islets with no folk. The whole spans some 1,475 square miles of land in the sea. Its count in 1905 was about 138,620 souls in all.

The isles form a loose crescent open toward the west. Six of them make the windward group, and four the leeward group. The isle of Boa Vista lies some 300 miles from the African shore. All the isles rose from fire in the deep past. Fogo still holds a live volcano that smokes at times.
britannica-1911-caribbee-islands:
The Caribbee Islands are a chain of islands in the West Indies. The name is now chiefly of historical importance. This short 1911 Britannica entry fixes its proper use. It is sometimes applied to the whole West Indies. Strictly, it covers only one long chain of islands. That chain stretches from Porto Rico to South America. The islands are also known as the Lesser Antilles.

Most of them fall into two named groups. One group is the Leeward Islands. The other is the Windward Islands. The entry is only a few lines in the original. It gives the name's strict sense and its looser one. It adds the Lesser Antilles name and the two groups. A reader gets the geography of the term and nothing further. That is the whole content of the notice.
britannica-1911-caroline-islands:
Caroline Islands is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a widely scattered Pacific archipelago east of the Philippines and north of New Guinea, then held by Germany. The islands fall into Western, Central, and Eastern groups between 5 and 10 degrees north. Their total land area is about 380 square miles, most of it in four main islands: Ponape, Kusaie, Truk, and Yap. The highest ground, on Ponape, nears 3000 feet, while most other islands are low coral islets.

The entry counts about 36,000 people, describes the islanders as skilled farmers, boatbuilders, and navigators, and names copra as the chief export. Germany ran the group from two seats, at Ponape and Yap. A historical sketch runs from the Portuguese sighting in 1527 through the Spanish naming of 1686, early missionary killings, and Spain's late attempt to assert its claim in 1875. The entry gives a compact survey of a remote German colony.
britannica-1911-chatham-islands:
Chatham Islands is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a small group in the Pacific Ocean, part of New Zealand. The group lies 536 miles due east of Lyttelton, near 44 degrees south. It holds three islands: Chatham Island, Pitt Island, and South east Island, with several rocky islets. Chatham Island is about 38 miles long and 25 miles across at its widest. Its area is 321 square miles.

The main island is known for its many lakes and for the bogs over its uplands. At its centre lies Tewanga, a large brackish lake parted from the sea by a sandbank 150 yards wide. The geology is mainly volcanic, with schists and limestone. It points to an old land link with New Zealand. Lieutenant Broughton discovered the islands in 1791 and named them for his brig, the Chatham. The soil is very fertile, and fern and flax grow richly where the ground drains.
britannica-1911-chiltern-hundreds:
Chiltern Hundreds names the device by which a member of the House of Commons could in effect resign a seat he could not formally give up. Old law held that a member, once duly chosen, could not resign. Escape came by accepting an office of profit from the crown. A statute of 1707 made such acceptance vacate the seat, with re-election possible in most cases. Crown stewardships, above all that of the Chiltern Hundreds, became the nominal office used.

The Chiltern Hundreds formed a bailiwick on the Chiltern Hills, where bandits in the woods once led to a special steward for protection. First used for Parliament in 1750, the post was granted by the chancellor of the exchequer. Each new warrant revoked the last holder's grant. Other stewardships, Northstead, East Hendred and Hempholme, served the same end at times. Only the Chilterns and Northstead survived in practice.
britannica-1911-comoro-islands:
Comoro Islands are a group of volcanic islands held by France, set out in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. They lie in the Indian Ocean, at the north entrance of the Mozambique Channel. They sit midway between Madagascar and the African mainland. Many small coral islets stand with the four large islands.

A table gives area and population for each of the four. Great Comoro is the largest and most westerly. Near its south tip rises a fine dome shaped volcanic mountain. That peak is over eight thousand five hundred feet high. It can be seen from more than one hundred miles away. Its slopes are clothed in dense growth up to about six thousand feet. Blasts are recorded for several years in the last century.
britannica-1911-cook-islands:
The Cook or Hervey Islands form an archipelago in the Pacific Ocean, a dependency of the British colony of New Zealand. Nine islands make up the group, part volcanic and part coral in build. Rarotonga heads the list, hilly, fertile and well watered. Its volcano rises 2,920 feet, the high point of the whole group. Mangaia, Aitutaki and other named isles follow.

Total land area comes to 111 square miles. A healthy, even climate fits the isles for European settlement. Fringing coral reefs make approach hard, though, and good harbours are lacking. The natives are of Polynesian stock and speech. Their legends tell of a crossing from Samoa. They say their forebears found black people on the isles when they came. A strong Melanesian type still shows among the people. The governor of New Zealand annexed the group by proclamation in June 1901.
britannica-1911-copperheads:
Copperheads was an American political nickname of the Civil War years. Union men pinned it on Northern men who held the Confederacy beyond conquest. Such men pressed hard for peace on that ground. They fought the war policy of the president and of Congress. They were not, the entry is clear, of need friends of the Southern cause.

The term arose in the autumn of 1862 and spread fast through the North. By early 1863, in the Western states, Copperhead and Democrat meant much the same thing. The name drew on the venomous copperhead snake and its fancied match to the peace party. Men threw it as a term of scorn at first. Those it named took it up with a will of their own. That swap of insult into badge of pride closes the entry.
britannica-1911-creeds:
Creeds, or confessions of faith, are reasoned statements of religious belief, and this long entry surveys them across history. It opens by linking the idea to Christianity, then widens the view through the study of comparative religion. Early hymns, it argues, already act as creeds in embryo. It cites a hymn in the Book of the Dead and praise of Amen-Ra in Egypt, then turns to the Indian Vedas. From there the survey moves toward the formed Christian symbols.

The body of the entry works through the great Christian statements in order. It treats the Apostles' Creed, the Nicene Creed in its liturgical forms, and the Athanasian Creed, comparing their clauses line by line. A second part covers modern confessions, including the Augsburg Confession drawn up by Melanchthon. Lutheran, Zwinglian, and Calvinist formularies each receive their own treatment. A full bibliography of works on the symbols closes the entry.
britannica-1911-crozet-islands:
The Crozet Islands are a group with no people, set in the Indian Ocean. They are steep, with tops from 4,000 to 5,000 feet high. The group falls in two parts: Penguin or Inaccessible, Hog, Possession, and East Islands, and the Twelve Apostles. Like Kerguelen and other groups in those south seas, they seem to be of fire-born rock. Their harsh weather and hard reach mean that few men land there.

The islands have not been searched since Marion-Dufresne found them in 1772. They are named for one of his officers. Possession, the highest, has a snowy peak said to top 5,000 feet. Hog Island takes its name from hogs set loose there by an English captain long ago. Those hogs have since died out. Rabbits dig in the heaps of cinder on the slopes of the hills, the article adds.
britannica-1911-elkington-george-richard:
Elkington, George Richards (1801–1865), founder of the electroplating industry in England, was born in Birmingham on 17 October 1801. He was the son of a spectacle maker. Apprenticed to his uncles, who were silver platers in Birmingham, he became sole owner of their business on their death. He later took his cousin Henry Elkington into partnership.

The science of applying electricity to metals was then in its infancy, but the Elkingtons saw its promise early. They had taken out patents when, in 1840, John Wright, a Birmingham surgeon, found the value of a solution of cyanide of silver in cyanide of potassium for plating. The Elkingtons bought and patented Wright's process and gained the rights to other methods as well. Large new works for electroplating and electrogilding opened in Birmingham in 1841. George Richards Elkington died on 22 September 1865.
britannica-1911-ellice-lagoon-islands:
Ellice (Lagoon) Islands form an archipelago of the Pacific Ocean, lying between 5 and 11 degrees south and about 178 degrees east, nearly midway between Fiji and the Gilbert group. The islands came under British protection, being annexed in 1892. They comprise many low coralline islands and atolls in nine clusters. The clusters stretch about 400 miles, with a total area of 14 square miles and about 2400 people.

The chief groups, all yielding coco-nuts, pandanus fruit, and yams, include Funafuti, Nukulailai, Nukufetau, Nui, and Niutao. Nearly all the natives are Christians, and Protestant missions have long been settled in several islands. The people of Nui speak the Gilbert islanders' language. The others speak Samoan, and their tradition of coming from Samoa thirty generations back is backed by research. Borings at Funafuti in 1897 point to recent sinking of the whole region.
britannica-1911-gabriel-hounds: Gabriel hounds are a spectral pack believed in the north of England to foretell death by yelping in the night. The legend holds that they are the souls of unbaptized children wandering through the air until the day of judgment. They are also called Gabble Ratchet. A plainer account, given in Atkinson's Cleveland Glossary of 1868, takes the night yelping to be large flocks of wild geese flying in the dark.
britannica-1911-galapagos-islands:
