Galapagos Islands are an archipelago of fifteen islands in the Pacific, on the equator, 580 miles west of Ecuador, to which they belong. The name comes from galápago, a tortoise, after the giant tortoises of their fauna. Spaniards found the group early in the 16th century, uninhabited, and buccaneers later gave English names to the islands. The islands are volcanic, with about twenty-five craters, over 2870 square miles of land.

Ecuador annexed the group in 1832, and a governor followed in 1885. The low grounds are parched and rocky, while above 800 feet a rich zone flourishes under cloud from July to November. Since Darwin's visit in the Beagle, science has prized the group. All seven tortoise species are native, each kept to its own islet. Most birds belong to peculiar genera, and more than half the flora grows nowhere else.
britannica-1911-gilds:
Gilds, or guilds, are the own subject of the main part of a shared page in the 1911 Britannica. The page first ends a note on gilding, then turns to the guilds. In the middle ages such groups were free clubs formed for aid and guard. Men joined for the help of their peers in work and want. A strong sense of kin bond and church hope ran through the clubs.

Old roots of the word gild reach to more than one sense. Atonement, fine, rite meal, and dues all crowd at its base. The text says it is hard to fix which sense came first in time. That doubt opens a longer past of how craft and trade clubs grew. More of that past lies past the part of text shown here.
britannica-1911-golds:
Golds are a Mongolo-Tatar people who live on the Lower Amur. The 1911 Britannica entry sets them in south eastern Siberia. Their chief villages stand on the right bank of the Amur. Others line the Sungari and the Usuri rivers of that region. In build they are of a classic Mongolic type and cast.

Like the Chinese they wear a pigtail, the entry notes in passing. From the Chinese too they learned the art of silk embroidery. The Golds live all but wholly on fish from those rivers. They are first rate boatmen and keep herds of swine and dogs. Eagles hold a high place in their awe and in their cult.
britannica-1911-goodwin-sands:
The Goodwin Sands are a line of shoals at the mouth of the Strait of Dover. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places them six miles off the Kent coast. The Downs anchorage lies in their shelter. Parts of the sands show at low water. They shift without pause, and ships wreck on them often. Lights and bell buoys have not made them safe. Tries to build a fixed light have failed.

Lore links the sands to a drowned island called Lomea. It was said to have belonged to Earl Godwine in the 1000s. Funds meant to guard it were spent, the tale goes, on a church spire at Tenterden. Four lightships mark the edges of the sands today. They fire rockets to call the lifeboats when a ship is in trouble. The worst loss named came in a storm of November 1703. Thirteen warships went down in that one night.
britannica-1911-goto-islands: The Goto Islands are a Japanese island group west of Kyushu, covered in a short entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The two main islands are Fukae-shima in the south and Nakaori-shima in the north. The group lies on the steamer route between Nagasaki and Shanghai, about fifty miles from Nagasaki. The entry notes dome-shaped hills above the old castle town of Fukae, well-farmed land, deer and other game, trout in the mountain streams, and a people of whom most were Christians.
britannica-1911-graphical-methods:
Graphical methods, ways of showing numbers as geometric figures, are the subject of this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. The methods turn data from measured events into pictures. Their simplest use is with tables, such as those found in statistics. Most such tables pair one value of one quantity with one value of another. The article explains how such a table becomes a graph.

Two axes are drawn at right angles, crossing at a point called the origin. Distances along one axis stand for values of the first quantity. Upright lines are raised at those points, and distances along them stand for the paired values. A curve through the points is the graph. At a glance, the curve shows the main features of the table. A poor corn yield shows as a dip, a rich one as a peak. Graphs also let readers compare sets of figures with ease.
britannica-1911-haemorrhoids:
Haemorrhoids, commonly called piles, are swollen veins of the bowel. They form at the lowest part of the bowel. Some sit just outside its opening. Internal piles are covered by mucous membrane. External piles lie beneath the skin. Dilated veins bulge within the bowel lining. Growing larger, they escape through the anus. Eventually they may stay protruded all the time. Inflammation, ulceration and bleeding commonly follow.

Pressure on the great abdominal veins can cause piles. Liver disease, tumours and pregnancy all raise that pressure. Weak vessels and habitual constipation predispose to them. Straining or sitting on damp ground may trigger them. Piles are often only a symptom of deeper trouble. Removing the cause may make them vanish. A protruded pile can be strangled by muscular spasm. Treatment sections cover fomentations, incision and surgery in detail.
britannica-1911-hampton-roads:
Hampton Roads is a channel in Virginia. The James, Nansemond and Elizabeth rivers pass through it. They empty into Chesapeake Bay between Old Point Comfort and Sewell's Point. Norfolk, Portsmouth and Newport News trade through it. It is the chief rendezvous of the United States navy. Federal dredging deepened it to 30 feet by 1905. Fortress Monroe guards its entrance from Old Point Comfort.

History made the Roads famous in March 1862. The first fight between iron-clad vessels happened there. Confederates had raised the burned frigate Merrimac from Gosport yard. They rebuilt her as the iron-clad Virginia. Her casemate carried iron four inches thick over heavy timber. She made only five knots and turned very slowly. Ten guns and an eighteen-inch ram armed her. Her duel with the Monitor fills the long narrative. Sources from Battles and Leaders close the account.
britannica-1911-ionian-islands:
Ionian Islands is the shared name for seven Greek islands, taken up in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. They are Corfu, Cephalonia, Zante, Santa Maura, Ithaca, Cythera, and Paxo. Folk also call them the Heptanesus, or Seven Islands. Yet the entry warns that the seven have no true oneness of land or place.

Their shared name may come from old Ionian settlers on those coasts. As one state they stood free for just seven years, from 1800 to 1807. The same waves of rule and conquest washed all of them, but hit each one in its own way. The article goes on to the rocks of the group, beds of chalk age and later. It then turns to a joint history that starts in the ninth century.
britannica-1911-juan-fernandez-islands:
The Juan Fernandez Islands are a small group in the South Pacific, between 33° and 34° south and near 80° west, belonging to Chile and placed in the province of Valparaiso. The main island, Mas a Tierra, lies nearest the mainland. The smaller Mas a Fuera stands 100 miles farther west, and the islet of Santa Clara lies off the southwest of the main island.

Mas a Tierra is 13 miles long by 4 wide, steep volcanic rocks rising to El Yunque, 3225 feet high, clothed in rich plant life. Cumberland Bay on the north side is the only fair anchorage, and only some twenty people lived on the islands. The plants and animals are mostly Chilean, but about a third of the plants are found nowhere else, and ferns stand out. There are no native land mammals, though stock brought in by men now runs wild. A Spanish pilot named Juan Fernandez found the islands in 1563.
britannica-1911-keeling-islands:
The Keeling Islands, often called the Cocos and Cocos Keeling Islands, are a group of coral islands in the Indian Ocean, between 12 and 13 degrees south. The group gave Charles Darwin his typical example of an atoll, or lagoon island. It counts twenty three small islands in all, and the whole atoll is about nine and a half miles across at its widest.

The lagoon is very shallow, and the gaps between many islands can be crossed on foot. An opening on the north side of the reef lets vessels into the upper lagoon, which forms a good harbour named Port Refuge, or Port Albion. The coconut, as the name Cocos tells, is the mark of the islands and is grown on all of them. The plant life is scanty in kinds. One common creature is a huge crab that lives on the coconuts.
britannica-1911-kei-islands:
The Kei Islands, native name Ewab, are a group in the Dutch East Indies, in the residency of Amboina, between 5 and 6 degrees south. The group has four parts: Great Kei, Little Kei, the Tayanda group, and the Kur group. Great Kei differs in build from all the rest.

Great Kei is of Tertiary formation and holds a chain of volcanic heights along its axis, rising to 2600 feet. Its area is 290 square miles, of a total land area for the group of 572. All the other islands are of later formation and level in surface. Shallow sea joins the group under water to the islands toward Ceram, while deep water splits it from the Aru Islands in the east. Its products count coconuts, sago, fish, trepang, timber, copra, maize, yams, and tobacco. The entry is a compact survey of position, rock, and trade goods.
britannica-1911-laccadive-islands:
The Laccadive Islands are a group of coral islands in the Indian Ocean between 10° and 12° 20′ N. Their name, from Malabar usage, means "the hundred thousand isles" and probably once covered the Maldives too; the natives call them simply Divi. There are seventeen separate reefs but thirteen islands, of which eight are inhabited. The northern group belongs to South Kanara and includes Amini, Kardamat, Kiltan and Chetlat; the southern, under Malabar, includes Agatti, Kavaratti, Androth and Kalpeni; Minikoi lies apart toward the Maldives.

The islands sit on the eastern, sheltered side of each reef; the west lies open to the south-west monsoon. None is over a mile broad; the whole area is about 80 sq. m., lying very low. The people are Moplas, of mixed Hindu and Arab descent, and Mahommedan, they speak Malayalam written in Arabic letters. The chief industry is making coir, work done by the women.
britannica-1911-leeward-islands:
The Leeward Islands are a group in the West Indies, named for their place away from the trade wind. The 1911 Britannica entry calls them the most northerly of the Lesser Antilles. They form a bent chain that runs south west from Puerto Rico to meet the Windward group.

The entry lists the isles and sorts them by the powers that held them. Britain, Denmark, Holland, and France each held shares, from small isles used just for a light tower to rich sugar isles. Most British isles formed one colony under a single chief, split into five parts with their own seats. The entry gives the joint count of souls and the shape of its joint councils, part named by the crown and part picked.
britannica-1911-loco-weeds: Loco-weeds, or crazy-weeds, are pod-bearing plants of the Astragalus and Lupinus kinds. Cattle that eat them fall ill with loco-disease. The name most likely comes from the Spanish loco, mad. The sickness strikes the nerves of the beast. Waste and drain of strength go with it. The entry is a brief note: plant, sickness, and name in a few lines, with no more ground to draw on.
britannica-1911-magellanic-clouds: Magellanic Clouds are two cloud like masses of stars in the southern sky, named for Ferdinand Magellan, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes. They lie in the southern constellation of Mensa, far south in declination. They stand apart from the Milky Way, with clear space between. Yet their stars match the stars of the Milky Way in spectra and in physical make up, the text stresses. That likeness, joined with their lone place in the sky, is what makes the pair stand out for study.
britannica-1911-marshall-islands:
Marshall Islands is an island group in the western Pacific Ocean, in Micronesia, belonging to Germany at the time of this 1911 Britannica article. The group is made of a number of atolls ranged in two near parallel lines running from north-west to south-east. The north-east line, with fifteen islands, is called Ratak, and the other, with eighteen, is called Ralik.

These atolls are of coral build and of uneven shape, and they rise but little above the high water mark. The highest ground, on the island of Likieb, is only thirty-three feet. The lagoon is scarcely more than 150 feet deep and can be entered through many breaks in the reef. On the outer side the shore sinks fast to a great depth. The surface of the atolls is covered with sand, save where decayed plants have turned it into soil.
britannica-1911-mascarene-islands: Mascarene Islands is the joint title of a group in the Indian Ocean east of Madagascar. Its brief entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica names the group as Mauritius, Reunion, and Rodriguez. The title derives from the Portuguese navigator Mascarenhas, who discovered Reunion. That island was at first called Mascarenhas after him, before the group name spread to cover all three islands as one named set in reference works.
britannica-1911-orkney-islands:
The Orkney Islands are a group of islands off the north coast of Scotland, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica counts and places them. The Pentland Firth parts them from the mainland of Scotland. The group is commonly put at sixty seven islands in number. Of those, thirty are inhabited by settlers. In four cases the people are only the keepers of lighthouses.

If rocky islets are counted in, the number may rise to ninety. Those islets likely once formed part of the larger islands. The group spans fifty miles from north east to south west. It spans twenty nine miles from east to west across the sea. In all the islands cover some 240,476 acres of land. The entry opens a full county survey of the northern isles.
britannica-1911-pelew-islands:
The Pelew Islands are the subject of a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The group, also called Palau, counts twenty six islands in the western Pacific Ocean. They belong to Germany. The islands lie inside a coral barrier reef. In the south they are of coral, and in the north of volcanic rock. They are well wooded, the air is healthy, and the water supply is good. A few rats and bats are the only native mammals, but the sea is rich in fish and shell life.

The whole area is one hundred seventy five square miles. The largest islands are Babeltop, Uruktapi, Korror, Nyaur, Peleliu and Eilmalk. The people number about three thousand one hundred. They are Micronesians, darker and shorter than their kin the Caroline Islanders.
britannica-1911-phthalic-acids:
Phthalic acids are a set of compounds treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. They are benzene acids with two acid groups, and they come in three forms. The forms are the ortho, or phthalic acid in the strict sense, the meta, and the para. The article gives the make of each and how each is got.

The first form was won by Laurent in 1836 by work on a compound of naphthalene. He took it for a child of naphthalene and named it for that stock. Marignac fixed its true make-up and showed the guess wrong, and Laurent then gave it its present name. It is made in bulk by work on naphthalene with strong acid. It forms white crystals and breaks down with heat to water and its anhydride. The acid and its kin are used in bulk in the colour trade.
britannica-1911-reading-beds: Reading Beds, in geology, are a series of marine and estuarine beds made of variegated plastic clays and bright-coloured sands. This brief 1911 Britannica article places them, with the Woolwich beds, as a subdivision of the Lower Eocene. The entry is a short definition only, and it points the reader to the fuller article on the Woolwich and Reading beds for detail.
britannica-1911-slate-islands:
Off the coast of Lorne in Argyllshire, Scotland, lies a small group called the Slate Islands. A short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica names them as Seil, Easdale, Torsay, Luing, and Shuna. They sit in the parish of Kilbrandon and Kilchattan.

Most of the group is made of slate rock, and the quarries give work to most of the folk who live there. Seil is joined to the main land by Clachan bridge. Easdale quarries have been worked since sixteen thirty. They yield some eight million slates each year, the entry says. Steam boats from Oban call at Luing and Easdale.
britannica-1911-solomon-islands:
Solomon Islands is a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes a long chain of islands in the west Pacific Ocean. The chain runs in a line from north west to south east. Its total land mass is given as a large figure in square miles.

The entry names the chief islands and their peaks and bays. High forest hills fall in a steep drop to the sea on most coasts. Some peaks are live fire mountains that still smoke. A pact split the chain between Britain and Germany. The entry notes good harbours, rich soil, and land that seems to rise year by year.
britannica-1911-south-shields:
South Shields is a seaport and borough in Durham, England, at the mouth of the Tyne. Its town entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the right bank, facing North Shields across the river. Steam ferries link it with North Shields and with Tynemouth near by.

The entry lists the church of Saint Hilda, the town hall, and a public library. Glass, chemicals, and ship work form the chief trades of the town. Large docks take the biggest vessels for building and repair work. Coal from near pits is sent out in large amounts. A long south pier guards the river mouth from the sea.
britannica-1911-speeton-beds:
Speeton Beds, in English geology, are a series of clays well shown at Speeton near Filey on the Yorkshire coast, says a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. Special interest attaches to them. They are the chief British marks of the sea phase of the Lower Cretaceous system.

The clays pass down without a break into the older beds below them. They are capped by the Red Chalk, held to match a southern English chalk bed. So the beds form a passage set between sea Jurassic layers and clear Cretaceous layers. In that way they match a southern rock set that links shore Jurassic and Cretaceous layers. Zones of the clay are named for the shell remains found in each.
britannica-1911-stolen-goods:
Stolen Goods is a headword in English law, and a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry takes up the rights over goods taken by larceny. The goods in view have not been given back to their owner. The owner has an action against the thief for the goods or their value. How far that civil right can be used in place of a criminal case is less clear.

The entry quotes the words of a judge in a case from 1881. He held that the civil right is not merged in the criminal charge. Nor must a prosecution of the felon come first, as a strict condition of the civil claim. The true principle of the common law, he said, lies between those two views. Readers meet a point of law where civil and criminal paths cross.
britannica-1911-trade-winds:
Trade Winds, the steady winds of the tropical oceans, are the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. They blow from the tropical belts of high pressure toward the belt of low pressure at the equator. In the northern hemisphere they come from the north east, and in the southern from the south east. They are exceedingly regular, above all over the oceans.

Over the open sea no great land masses disturb their flow, so their course holds steady. Their name comes from that feature, trade being used in an old sense of direction or course. Their zone of greatest force runs roughly from three to thirty five degrees north, and south to twenty eight degrees. The westerly winds beyond those belts are sometimes called anti trades, since their direction is opposite.
britannica-1911-turks-and-caicos-islands:
Turks and Caicos Islands are a group in the British West Indies, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. By land form they belong to the Bahamas, though ruled apart. Coral and sand make up the isles, which span a small sea area. The Turks group takes its name from a cactus shaped like a turbaned head.

Grand Turk and Salt Cay are the chief isles of that group. The Caicos chain of seven isles lies to the north-west. Salt raking is the core trade of the isles, with sisal hemp and sponges next. Rain is scarce, and fresh water is short, though sea winds keep the heat mild. Folk from Bermuda first came about 1678 to rake salt from the ponds. Settlers stayed, and the isles passed through Spanish attack and rule from the Bahamas.
britannica-1911-visiting-cards:
Visiting cards are the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Their use as cards of identity for social calls is most often traced to the court of Louis the Fourteenth of France. That court was the centre of the manners of the seventeenth century. The entry, though, holds that the custom is far older.

In a rougher form, it says, the Chinese and perhaps other peoples of the east used such tokens long ago when calling at the homes of absent friends. When and where the cards first came into use in Europe is less sure. The best guess places them in Germany, as early as the sixteenth century. The article cites a German card lately found in Venice. German students at Padua, it explains, left their names on paper slips when they paid farewell calls and found their teachers out.
britannica-1911-windward-islands:
Windward Islands are a group and colony in the West Indies under British rule. Their group entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The group holds Saint Lucia, Saint Vincent, and Grenada as chief islands. A chain of small isles, the Grenadines, links Saint Vincent and Grenada.

The three islands form a loose union, not a single colony in law. A shared governor in chief lives at Saint George in Grenada. Each island keeps its own rules, laws, funds, and trade taxes apart. They share a court of appeal and an audit system for all. Their name comes from trade winds that strike them first in the chain.
bunny-brown-and-his-sister-sue-in-the-bi:
Deep woods and a tent camp frame this Laura Lee Hope tale of Bunny Brown and his sister Sue. Grosset and Dunlap put out the book at New York. Florence England Nosworthy drew the plates. Mother calls from the tent door for Sue and Bunny. Sue steps from bush cover with a finger to her lips.

What daddy brought heads the chapter list. A pail of milk and an old man in the woods come next. A noise at night and a roll down hill for Bunny mark the turns. A lost cow, a missing train, and a search party fill the late run. The front plate shows Bunny outrun by a rolling thing he chases. Woods camp life — milk, cows, dark sounds — forms the stock. Small fears met with home help near keep the Hope frame firm.
camp-and-trail-a-story-of-the-maine-wood:
Isabel Hornibrook wrote a boys' tale of the Maine woods, with plates of moose and camp. Twenty-seven chapters line the frame. Jacking for deer by night light opens the run. A spill-out and life in a bark hut come next. Whither bound and a coon hunt fill the early turns.

Black ducks, a guide post of the woods, and a fresh camp mark the heart. A Sunday among the pines gives a rest beat. Beaver works and a bear chase — go it, old Bruin — raise the fun. Skin rights, a lucky hunter, and a fallen king fill the mid-run. Moose calls, Herb's yarns, and a climb of Katahdin crown the trip. A moose trees one of the band late in the tale. Christmas on the far side closes the list.
cap-n-warren-s-wards:
Joseph C Lincoln's novel Cap'n Warren's Wards appeared in 1911, published in New York by D Appleton and Company. New York lawyer Atwood Graves rides a storm-delayed train to Cape Cod on unwelcome business. His errand concerns Captain Elisha Warren, a retired sea captain living quietly in South Denboro. Warren's dead brother has named him guardian of two children.

Caroline Warren is nearly twenty, and her brother Stephen is a year younger. Neither has ever met their uncle, and both resent the arrangement. Graves explains the will, its trust money, and Warren's right to refuse. The captain must decide where the young people will live and how strictly to rule them. Lincoln builds a warm village comedy about family duty, young pride, and an old sailor learning parenthood late.
catalogue-of-british-columbia-birds:
Catalogue of British Columbia Birds, by Francis Kermode, curator of the Provincial Museum at Victoria, lists every bird proven to occur in the province. Kermode dates his preface August 1904. He aims at completeness and admits failure in advance. The list is incomplete, he says, especially for the northern interior. That country, he is sure, is a valuable field for work. The late John Fannin's 1898 list held three hundred thirty nine species and subspecies. Kermode adds twenty four.

Observers across the province supplied local lists, notes, and specimens. Brooks in the Okanagan, Keen in the Queen Charlotte Islands, and Green at Fairview are thanked by name. The catalogue then proceeds by order and family, from the diving birds and grebes onward. Each entry fixes a species to British Columbia on evidence. Museum science here is a network of country observers, mailing skins and sightings to Victoria.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-african-synod:
African Synods were not general councils of the entire church, since none was ever held in North Africa. They were many national or plenary bishop assemblies for the North African church, commonly called African or Carthaginian Synods. They must not be confused with district or provincial assemblies, also very numerous in the separate provinces. Those Roman provinces lay between Sahara and Mediterranean, from Cyrenaica east to the Atlantic west, roughly modern Tripoli, Algeria, and Morocco.

There the church entered history late in the second century and vanished early in the eighth. About the mid-third century, bishops of the three civil provinces formed a single ecclesiastical province. As dioceses multiplied, they grouped into divisions matching political divisions. Diocletian redistricted North Africa into six civil provinces; by the late fourth century the church had adjusted to those lines, yielding six ecclesiastical provinces lasting until the Arab invasion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-breads:
Altar breads are one of the two elements required for the Eucharist. Whether Christ used ordinary table bread cannot be told from the sacred text. In the Western Church the breads were probably round, as catacomb pictures show, and Pope St. Zephyrinus called the altar bread a round crown-like offering. Eastern churches use round or square breads.

For valid consecration the host must use wheaten flour and pure natural water, oven-baked or pressed between heated irons, and uncorrupted. Western bread is unleavened, Eastern bread leavened, except among Maronites and Armenians. The large host usually bears Christ crucified, and the breads took many names as sacrament or sacrifice, including gift and host.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-cards:
Altar cards print the prayers a celebrant should know by heart, standing at the altar's middle and each end. They date only from the sixteenth century, and bishops do not use them, reading all prayers from the Pontifical Canon. At Pius V's Missal revision only the middle card existed, called the Tabella Secretarum. Later the Gospel of St. John joined it on the Gospel side, and the Deus qui humanae substantiae prayer with the Lavabo psalm on the Epistle side for symmetry.

Only during Mass do the cards rest on the altar, the middle one against crucifix or tabernacle, the side ones against candlesticks or altar steps. At other times they are removed or laid face down under the altar cover, and when the Blessed Sacrament is exposed outside Mass they must be removed. Framed cards should match the altar's architecture as far as possible.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-beguines-begh:
Beguines and Beghards take names most likely from old Flemish beghen, to pray, not to beg, since neither community was mendicant. Other guesses invoke St Bega of Nivelles or Lambert le Bègue, founder of a Liège cloister for crusaders' widows. From the early twelfth century, women in the Netherlands lived alone, vowless, devoted to prayer and good works. Their numbers swelled in the Crusades' age of desolate women, and about 1200 some grouped their cabins into the first Beguinage.

A Beguine was hardly a nun: she took no vows, could wed and return to the world, and kept her property. If poor, she lived by manual labor or teaching burghers' children, not by alms. They waned with the cloth trade, battered by the Reformation's storm and broken by the French Revolution. Belgian foundations fell from ninety-four to twenty by 1856, with membership about 1,600 that year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brothers-of-o: The Brothers of Our Lady of the Fields, a Canadian congregation founded in 1902 at Saint-Damien de Buckland in the Quebec diocese by Father M. J.-O. Brousseau, train orphans in farm and trade work and in settlement arts. The Sisters of Notre Dame of Perpetual Help, founded likewise by Brousseau in 1892, care for the orphans until age twelve, when the brothers take them over. The mother-house stands at Saint-Damien, Bellechasse County, Lac Vert, and the community now counts six brothers and four novices.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-camisards:
The Camisards, likely named for their black work blouse, the camise, worn as a uniform, were French fanatics who terrorized Dauphiné, Vivarais, and above all the Cévennes early in the eighteenth century. Their roots lay in the lingering Albigensian spirit, the apocalyptic preaching of French Calvinists, and Louis XIV's harsh methods of conversion after the Edict of Nantes was revoked in 1685. The murder of the Abbé de Chaila in 1702 opened open war.

Armed bands under Séguier, Laporte, Castanet, Ravenel, and Cavalier fought a guerrilla war until about 1705, when they surrendered or were destroyed, and Cavalier's 1709 attempt to revive the revolt failed. A peace treaty with England in 1711 cut off their support, and on 8 March 1715 Louis XIV proclaimed the sect wholly extinct. Much debate surrounds their prophets, some writers holding that Du Serre trained young recruits in a school of prophecy, while Calvinist writers deny any such school existed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caroline-isla:
East of the Philippines in the Pacific lie the Caroline Islands, some 500 small coral islands. Yap, one of the larger islands, lies 1,200 miles from Manila. Spaniards discovered the group in the sixteenth century and named it for Charles V. Jesuit missionaries John Anthony Cantova and Victor Walter tried the mission in 1731, but Cantova was soon murdered and Walter forced to flee, with two more Jesuits killed later.

After the Jesuits' suppression in 1767, no missionary trace appears for 120 years, until Leo XIII settled a German-Spanish dispute for Spain and Spanish Capuchins arrived in March 1886. The Propaganda set up the mission that May in West and East sections, formerly under the Vicariate of Micronesia. The islanders, of Polynesian race, lived by hunting and fishing without farming. A Jesuit weather station on Yap, begun in 1905, cabled typhoon warnings to Manila twice daily.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-communion-und:
Patrick Toner's long entry treats Communion under both kinds, set against Communion under one kind alone. One kind means bread alone or wine alone. Both kinds mean distinct reception under bread and wine together, sub utraque specie. Toner works under three heads: Catholic doctrine and modern discipline, history of disciplinary change, and theological speculation. The priest's Communion under both kinds belongs at least to the sacrifice's integrity, and for some theologians to its essence.

History runs from the first century to the twelfth, when public Communion in East and West ordinarily ran under both kinds. Variations fill the record: sick Communion under bread alone at Alexandria, children's Communion before reason, the Presanctified Mass, and intinction, forbidden at Braga. The Utraquist controversy tested the doctrine, and John chapter six supplied texts for both sides. Speculation closes by weighing whether the chalice adds grace by prolonging the species and fervor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-faroe-islands:
The Faroe Islands are a Danish group some four hundred miles west of Norway. Fourteen inhabited islands span about 500 square miles of dark, rocky ground. Sheep graze the flowery pastures, and over 100,000 live outdoors all year-round. Fishing, cattle, and bird-catching feed the 16,000 islanders.

Irish monks found the islands first, and Norsemen settled them soon after. Norway ruled them until 1814, and twenty-three Catholic bishops served there. The Reformation ended Catholic life by the close of the sixteenth century. An unfinished Gothic cathedral at Kirkebö still recalls the Catholic age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gilbert-islan:
The Gilbert Islands form a vicariate apostolic of sixteen low atolls near the Equator, the easternmost link of Micronesia, together with the Ellice and Panapa islands. Its chief atolls include Tapiteuca, Arorai, Apemama, Maiana, Marakei, and Nonouti. A Catholic Encyclopedia article describes a people under nominal British protection but practically self-governing, living chiefly by copra.

The vicariate was erected on 17 July 1897, when the Vicariate of Micronesia was divided, under Mgr. Joseph Leray of the Congregation of the Sacred Heart. Of a population reckoned at thirty to forty thousand, fourteen thousand were Catholics. Twelve churches and fifty-six chapels served them, with nineteen priests and ninety-six parish schools. Twelve orphanages sheltered four hundred children, beside houses of religious men and women.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-grand-rapids:
Grand Rapids is a diocese created on 12 May 1882 from Detroit, covering the lower peninsula of Michigan north of Ottawa, Montcalm, Gratiot, and Saginaw, an area of 22,561 square miles. At its creation it held about fifty thousand Catholics served by thirty-four priests. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a diocese that prospered steadily under its first bishop.

Henry Joseph Richter, born at Neuenkirchen in Oldenburg in 1838, was ordained at Rome in 1865. He was consecrated at Grand Rapids in April 1883. Belgian and Dutch colonies, with Irish admixture and later Poles, settled its rural regions. By the article's statistics the diocese counted 133 priests, 91 churches with resident priests, 66 parish schools with 13,545 pupils, and a Catholic population of 126,057.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guilds:
Medieval guilds were voluntary associations for worship, fellowship, and trade, reaching their height among the Teutonic peoples, above all the English. The entry sorts them into four kinds, religious guilds, peace or frith guilds, merchant guilds, and craft guilds, and traces the word itself to an Anglo-Saxon verb meaning to pay.

English evidence runs from Ina's seventh-century laws and the Abbotsbury charter under Canute, with its almsgiving, sick care, burials. Masses, to merchant guilds that guarded town trade monopolies, fined outsiders, watched the quality of goods, and doubled as the town's governing body. Craft guilds, later chapters, and the guilds' slow decline carry a vast survey that opens with Brentano's theory of family origins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-imposition-of:
Laying hands on someone is a symbolic rite meant to pass on a gift, a quality, or an excellence, most often spiritual, or to appoint a person to an office. People have used it for worldly ends as well as sacred ones. It reaches back to patriarchal days.

Jacob gave Ephraim and Manasses blessing and inheritance by laying hands on them, and Moses handed Hebrew leadership to Josue the same way. In the New Testament, the Lord used the rite to bring Jairus's daughter back to life and to heal the sick. Its sacred use shows first when Aaron and his sons were set apart as priests, and when priests placed hands on animals offered in sacrifice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ionian-island:
Seven islands west of Greece, with their islets, make up the Heptanesus of this geography entry. Corfu, Paxos, Leucadia or Santa Maura, Ithaca, Cephalonia, Zante, and Cerigo stretch between 36 and 40 degrees north. Together they cover about 1,095 square miles. Their population is put at 261,930. Most islanders belonged to the Greek Orthodox Church, with 6,615 Latin-rite Catholics, a few thousand Jews, and a small Muslim minority.

Mild and healthy air and mountain land still yielded cotton, wine, oil, and raisins in fair amount. The entry's real weight lies in the islands' tangled past and in Catholic life among an Orthodox majority, from bishops and churches to the Latin minority's standing. Readers get both a map and a short history of a borderland between East and West.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-shields:
Soldier and senator James Shields, born at Dungannon, County Tyrone, Ireland, on 12 December 1810, died at Ottumwa, Iowa, on 1 June 1879. After emigrating to America in 1826 he took up law at once, opening practice at Kaskaskia, Illinois, in 1832. Illinois voters sent him to the state legislature in 1836, and he went on to serve as state auditor in 1839 and judge of the state supreme court in 1843. War with Mexico found him commissioner of the general land office.

Commissioned brigadier general by President Polk on 1 July 1846, Shields served with distinction under Taylor, Wool, and Scott. He won a major-general's brevet at Cerro Gordo, where a shot passed through his lung. Severely wounded again at Chapultepec, he mustered out in 1848, then governed Oregon Territory briefly before resigning to sit in the United States Senate for Illinois as a Democrat. His life runs from battlefield to Senate chamber.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-julian-edmund:
Julian Edmund Tenison Woods was an English-born Australian priest, scientist, and founder. Born at Southwark in London in 1832, he worked for the Times, tried the Passionists, and taught at Toulon, where he caught a love of geology. In 1854 he sailed with Bishop Willson to Tasmania as a schools assistant and was ordained at Adelaide in 1857.

Given a parish of twenty-two thousand square miles around Penola, Woods founded the Sisters of St. Joseph of the Sacred Heart in 1866 with Mary MacKillop, and the Brothers of the Sacred Heart in 1869. He also preached missions across three colonies for eleven years. He died at Sydney in 1889, honored as priest and naturalist alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lauds:
Lauds, meaning praises, is the Roman office of psalms and canticles usually said after Matins, whose whole purpose is praising God. Its name comes from the office's last three psalms, 148, 149, and 150, where laudate rings out again and again.

At first Lauds named only those three psalms with their conclusion, as Greek Ainoi and St. Benedict's Rule still show, while the whole dawn office passed as Matutinum in the fifth and sixth centuries. Gradually Lauds swallowed the whole office and Matins became the Night Office instead. The word also meant the Mass alleluia after the Epistle, in Toledo's phrase, and the public acclamations shouted at a prince's accession, long kept in church on set occasions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leeds:
Leeds is a diocese covering Yorkshire's West Riding and York south of the Ouse. It is one of fourteen in the Westminster province, though it was not erected at Pius IX's 1850 restoration of the English hierarchy. That year Rome created Beverley for all Yorkshire, anticipating its later division, from the Yorkshire District formed in 1840 out of the Northern District of 1688.

John Briggs, St. Cuthbert's College president and last vicar apostolic of a vast northern territory, became Beverley's first bishop, counting about 180,000 Catholics in 1839, only 13,000 in Yorkshire. His episcopate was a heroic struggle for schools and churches for a destitute, Irish-immigrant population, with thousands of Yorkshire children receiving no Catholic schooling at all. Robert Cornthwaite succeeded him in 1861 and won the 1878 brief dividing Beverley, though it stayed unpublished until February 1879.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-literary-or-p:
Literary or profane legends are the great hero tales that grew up where early history shades into story, told and retold until they took fixed literary shape. This long survey treats them as a group, asking how spoken tales gain detail, lose facts, borrow motifs, and harden into books.

Germanic hero saga opens the run, followed by Charlemagne and Roland, Genevieve of Brabant, and Arthur. Then come Tristan and Isolde, Lohengrin, Tannhauser, Robert the Devil, the Wandering Jew, the Flying Dutchman, William Tell, and Faust. Each section retells the tale, weighs its sources, and sorts what may be history from what is pure fancy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liturgical-us:
Creeds in worship began with baptism, where converts learned and recited the faith before receiving the sacrament. That use appears as early as Hippolytus and Cyril of Jerusalem, and may be older still, so wide was its spread.

At the Eucharist the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed entered at Antioch in 471 and Constantinople in 511, though Rome held back until the eleventh century. The entry then maps creed use rite by rite: Roman, Ambrosian, Gallican, Mozarabic, Celtic, and Anglican, plus the Eastern churches. Each rite has its own place for the Apostles' Creed, the Nicene Creed, or a local form.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lollards:
Lollards were the followers of John Wyclif, a dissenting body thick in England from the late fourteenth century into the first half of the fifteenth. The nickname reached them in 1382, when Henry Crumpe used it at Oxford, and bishops' papers took it up by 1387.

England had long been free of heresy, yet anger at clerical wealth, pride, and power ran deep. War in France, plague, and social strain fed the mood, and Wyclif's teaching gave it a voice. The entry traces the causes of the spread, the doctrines condemned by church courts, and the sect's fate under persecution, from pulpit preaching to revolt and suppression.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mariana-islan:
Mariana Islands, also called the Ladrones, form a chain of fifteen islands in the northern Pacific, between 13 and 21 degrees north and 144 and 146 degrees east. Magellan found them in 1521 and named them Thieves' Islands for native thieving. Spain planted a regular colony in 1667 and renamed them Marianas for Queen Maria Anna of Austria.

Their people then numbered 40,000 to 60,000, but fierce resistance nearly wiped them out before Spanish rule held. Spain kept them under the Philippines until 1898, when Guam passed to the United States after the Spanish-American War. In 1899 the rest, with the Carolines, were sold to Germany for about four million dollars. Guam, 32 miles long and about 200 square miles, held 11,490 people, with Agana capital at 7,000, serving as a United States naval station. A prefecture apostolic of 1902, entrusted to Westphalian Capuchins in 1907, served a wholly Catholic people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marquesas-isl:
Marquesas Islands, in Polynesia, numbered eleven islands between 7 and 10 degrees south and 138 and 141 degrees west, covering 480 square miles. Their people, called cannibals in the entry, lived mainly by fishing in huts of wattles and branches. Breadfruit, coconut, banana, orange, and sugar cane were chief crops, with horses, pigs, sheep, cotton, and tobacco brought by missionaries.

Mendana found them in 1595 and named them for the Marquess de Mendoza, then Viceroy of Peru, and the first Mass was said there on 28 July 1595. Picpus missionaries landed at Vaithu on 4 August 1836 and found natives given to tattooing and cruel, defective morals. Whalers had left phthisis in 1774, and population fell from 17,700 in 1804 to 8,000 in 1830 and about half that later. Baptisms rose from 216 adults in 1838 to 1848 to 986 in 1848 to 1856. Schools at Taiohae taught 300 children in 1900, and by 1900 opium and alcohol were banned and schooling compulsory, though France's Associations Law closed the schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marshall-isla:
Marshall Islands were a German Pacific possession since 1885, east of the Carolines, between 4 and 13 degrees north and 161 and 171 degrees east. Spanish sailors found them in 1529, and Marshall and Gilbert explored them in 1788. Fifty low atolls, highest point just thirty-three feet, with Nauru included, covered about 150 square miles.

Population in 1908 reached 15,000, only 162 Europeans, most natives still pagan. Sacred Heart missionaries began in 1891, were forced out by civil authorities, and resumed in 1898. The islands first joined the New Pomerania vicariate, then became a separate vicariate in September 1905, without episcopal character yet. Superior Augustus Erdland lived on Jaluit. By 1907 the mission counted seven priests, eight brothers, thirteen sisters, 323 Catholics, 520 catechumens, six churches and stations, and eight schools with 225 pupils.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-national-syno:
National synods, by recent canon law, are deliberating assemblies where all bishops of a nation meet, convoked by patriarch or primate. To cover ancient synods too, it is better to call them a legitimate assemblage of a nation's episcopate, whose decisions bind an entire national Church. The classic definition fits ancient councils poorly, just as it fits ecumenical councils imperfectly.

Councils divide into general or ecumenical and particular, with particular ones split into national and provincial by their scope. Diocesan clergy assemblies are diocesan synods rather than councils. Writers warn the classification cannot be exact. Arles in 314, where Constantine with the pope gathered the empire's episcopate, and African bishops' assemblies, test the boundaries. The entry sorts the kinds, their authority, and their place in church law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philippine-is:
The Philippine Islands were an archipelago of 3,141 islands between the China Sea and the Pacific, south of Japan and north of Borneo. Luzon covers 40,969 square miles and Mindanao 36,292, with a total land area of 115,026. Mount Apo in Mindanao tops 10,000 feet, Mayon rises as the world's most symmetrical volcanic cone, and the Cagayan, Rio Grande, and Agusan run over 200 miles. This vast Catholic Encyclopedia survey treats land, peoples, history, and church.

Magellan reached the islands, and Legaspi sailed from Mexico in 1564 with the Augustinian Urdaneta, founding Spanish rule that friars then civilized for centuries. Later sections count peoples and faiths, trace the American occupation, and reckon a Catholic population above five million served by secular clergy and fewer than 500 religious in 1906. Missions among Moros, schools, and dioceses complete the picture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-seleucids:
The Seleucids were the Macedonian dynasty founded by Seleucus, a general of Alexander the Great, which ruled Syria from 312 BC. This entry opens with Seleucus receiving Babylonia in 321, losing it to Antigonus, and winning it back after Gaza in 312. That year starts the era counted from his name. Taking the royal title in 306, he subdued upper Asia to the Indus and gained Syria at Ipsus. He founded the great residential cities of Seleucia on the Tigris and Antioch on the Orontes.

His son Antiochus I Soter moved the court to Antioch for fear of the Parthians. Under Antiochus II Theos the long wars with Egypt over Phoenicia and Palestine began. A marriage alliance with Berenice, daughter of Ptolemy II, paused the fighting. After Ptolemy's death the disowned first wife Laodice returned and took revenge. The entry carries the dynasty's tangled succession forward from there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-southern-solo:
The Southern Solomon Islands prefecture took its name from a Spanish explorer's hopeful guess, and this entry traces the islands from first European contact to mission days. Alvaro Mendana de Neyra found Ysabel, Guadalcanar, and San Christoval in 1567, named the group for King Solomon after admiring its natural riches. And saw Mass said by his Franciscan chaplain before sailing back to Peru.

A second voyage in 1595, carrying 368 emigrants, landed at Santa Cruz and ended with Mendana's death two months later, his widow and pilot bringing the survivors home to Spain. The entry then turns to the modern prefecture, its parishes and missionaries, giving readers both the romance of discovery and the slow work of building a church in the Pacific.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-bahama-is:
A chain of coral islands north of Cuba and east of southern Florida is surveyed here, the most northerly group of the West Indies. Twenty-five islands hold permanent settlements, with countless cays and rocks besides, stretched between about 21 and 27 degrees north. Nassau, on New Providence, the only island with a safe harbour, serves as capital.

Origins of the names Bahama and Lucayos, the latter from Spanish Los Cayos, open the account. Population, largely of African descent through slavery, follows, with emancipation on 1 August 1834, when 10,086 slaves were freed and owners paid compensation. Church history, schools, and missions round out a portrait of island life at the start of the twentieth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-canary-is:
Seven chief islands and scattered islets off Africa's western coast form the archipelago described here, lying between about 27 and 29 degrees north. Lanzarote and Fuerteventura stand nearest the mainland, then Tenerife and Gran Canaria, with Palma, Gomera, and Hierro farther west. Their total area runs about 3,256 square miles, and the 1900 census counted 358,564 people.

Mountainous and volcanic throughout, the islands crown themselves in Tenerife's Pico de Teyde at 12,200 feet. Caverns, springs, and torrents mark the landscape, while dromedaries and canary-birds enliven a fauna otherwise European. Conquest, church foundations, and missions complete a compact island history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-five-sacr:
Hands, feet, and side of Christ, pierced in the Passion, anchor the devotion described here. Religious revival under Bernard and Francis in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, joined to crusaders returning from the Holy Land, gave fresh force to honouring the Five Wounds. A Mass and an Office grew around them.

Polish bishops told Clement XIII why these parts deserved special cult: they bore special pains for salvation and shine as marks of love. Beads, images, confraternities, and feasts spread the practice, which the entry follows through prayer books and popular piety. Readers see how a meditation on suffering became a lasting form of prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-netherlan:
Low Countries under Charles V and his heirs form the historical sweep here, from Burgundian lands to Spanish and then Austrian Netherlands. Charles's organisation joined what is now Holland and Belgium, and later histories of Burgundy and Charles himself carry the earlier tale. Holland's secession as the United Provinces in 1579 sheared the north away.

Philip II, succeeding his father, found the seventeen provinces at their zenith of wealth and good government, as Guicciardini wrote in 1567. Antwerp had replaced Bruges as the trading queen. Religious revolt, war with Spain, and the slow forging of two nations follow, with church life, art, and commerce woven through a long and tangled history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-washing-of-fe:
Washing of feet and hands treats a courtesy owed to guests in sandal-wearing Eastern lands from earliest times, given deep religious meaning by Christ's action after the Last Supper in John 13. Down to St Bernard, church writers sometimes called the ceremony a sacrament in the wider sense, meaning it held the virtue of what we now call a sacramental.

Christ's command to wash one another's feet was understood literally from the start, Paul implying that a widow honoured by the Church should be one who had washed the saints' feet. Tradition, the entry argues, never broke, though early evidence is scattered. Elvira's council in AD 300 directed that baptismal candidates' feet be washed not by priests but by clerics or layfolk.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-reyno:
William Reynolds, also Rainolds, was an English Catholic scholar who helped translate the Reims Testament. Born near Exeter about 1544, second son of Richard Rainolds and elder brother of John Rainolds, an Authorized Version scholar, he died at Antwerp in 1594. Schooled at Winchester, he became a fellow of New College, Oxford, from 1560 to 1572. The Jewel-Harding controversy and Allen's personal sway converted him, and in 1575 he publicly recanted at Rome.

Reynolds studied for the priesthood at Douai from 1577, moved with the college to Reims in 1578, and took orders at Châlons in April 1580. He stayed to lecture on Scripture and Hebrew and to aid Gregory Martin's Reims Testament translation. Later he served as chaplain to the Beguines at Antwerp. His books include a refutation of Whitaker's attack on Reims, a 1590 treatise on Christian commonwealths against impious kings under the name Rossaeus, a sacrament treatise, and Calvino-Turcismus.
child-s-book-of-water-birds:
Leavitt and Allen of New York published an anonymous picture book for children in 1855, one short page per bird, each with its illustration. The swan comes first, white and graceful on water, an awkward waddler ashore. A black swan from Australia is noted as a rarity. The coot follows, nesting in flags and reeds at the water's edge.

The dabchick dives at any alarm and plays hide and seek on ponds. The teal, smallest of ducks, feeds by night and flies swiftly. Geese are bred in Lincolnshire flocks of thousands, plucked for quills. The oyster catcher pries shellfish from rocks with a long, stout bill. Plain facts, told simply, make a first natural history.
christmas-stories-and-legends:
Phebe A. Curtiss compiled twenty Christmas pieces at Indianapolis in 1916, opening with her own legend of the White Gifts. A beloved king, strong, just, and gentle with the poorest child, inspires it. His people search for a gift that would show their love. Plan after plan is rejected before the happy solution arrives.

Hans Andersen appears twice, with The Fir Tree and The Little Match Girl. Nora A. Smith tells Little Piccola and the story of Christmas itself. Lucy Wheelock explains the Christmas tree, and Carolyn Bailey retells Babouscka. The Magi in the West follow their star to a peasant cottage in one later tale. A shepherd who didn't go, a worker in sandalwood, and a boy with a box round out a Sunday-school shelf.
city-ballads:
City Ballads, by Will Carleton, was published by Harper & Brothers in 1885 and dedicated to Adora, named on the page as friend, comrade, lover, wife. The poems are grouped under blunt heads: Wealth, Want, Fire, Water, Vice, Virtue, Travel, and Home. An illustrated list of plates faces the contents.

Recurring figures give the book its voice, above all Farmer Stebbins, who discourses on rollers, the Bowery, and Ocean Grove in dialect verse. Set pieces include A Sewing-Girl's Diary under Want, and Flash: The Fireman's Story under Fire. The Boy-Convict's Story sounds the Vice section's note. Carleton mixes city scenes with farm humor throughout.
come-lasses-and-lads:
Come Lasses and Lads is a picture book built on an old May Day song, with drawings by Randolph Caldecott marking nearly every verse. Lasses and lads go to the maypole, every he with a she and a minstrel standing by. Willy has gotten his Jill, and Johnny his Jone, to jig it up and down.

The talk runs in rhymed exchanges. Strike up, says Watt; agreed, says Kate; and I prithee, Fiddler, play. The dancers argue over Packington's pound and Sellenger's round, then blame the fiddler for playing false. After an hour they retire to a bower for ale, cakes, and kisses held as stakes. The quarrel over taking the kisses back ends the game.
cross-roads:
Margaret E. Sangster gathered her magazine poems in Cross Roads, a book named for the choice-points where her preface sonnet leaves the reader standing. Sangster writes of woods and city windows, tenement mothers and Fifth Avenue, gloves, porcelain puppies, and old schoolhouses, all in plain rhymes meant to be understood at first hearing. Many pieces first ran in the Christian Herald and Good Housekeeping.

The last part turns to war: poems on Château-Thierry, ruined churches, transports, and a prayer for boys killed in action, closing with Independence Day 1919. Sangster, an editor as well as a poet, aimed at consolation rather than experiment. The collection maps what ordinary American magazine readers asked poetry to do between the wars of her lifetime.
daily-strength-for-daily-needs:
A daily devotional book, picked by Mary Wilder Tileston, fills this volume. Its motto is the promise that as thy days, so shall thy strength be. Tileston also edited Joy and Strength for the Pilgrim's Day and Quiet Hours.

Each day opens with one or two short scripture texts. A poem or prose passage follows, drawn from many hands. January the first pairs a psalm with Oliver Wendell Holmes's verses on building statelier mansions of the soul. Later pages praise those who leave the camp of ease for fresh service. The book is meant to be read one page a day, all year. It shaped the quiet hour in many homes of its time.
departmental-ditties-and-ballads-and-bar:
Two sets of Kipling verse fill this volume: the Departmental Ditties and the Ballads and Barrack-Room Ballads. A contents list sorts them as volume one and volume two. India, its offices, and its army stand behind nearly every piece.

The ditties mock the work of government in India: army headquarters, the foreign office, public waste, and a code of morals. The ballads turn to soldiers' speech and song. Danny Deever, Tommy, Gunga Din, and Mandalay stand among the best known. The Ballad of East and West opens the second set. Kipling speaks in many voices, clerk, trooper, and officer among them. The book holds the verse that made his name on two sides of the world.
dick-hamilton-s-airship-or-a-young-milli:
Howard R Garis wrote Dick Hamilton's Airship, or A Young Millionaire in the Clouds, for his boys' series about the richest lad in America. The contents open with a falling biplane and a colonel's offer: a twenty-thousand-dollar prize for a transcontinental flight. Dick resolves to build an airship with a stabilizer of his own design and enter.

Army aviators, suspicions of spies, and Dick's first flight lead to Hamilton Corners, where his miserly Uncle Ezra visits, acts queerly, and even flies, with an accident to follow. The government will assign an officer to the flight and may buy the winning patent. Garis, creator of Uncle Wiggily, keeps the machinery simple and the pace brisk.
doe-osti-17152719-reviewing-and-releasin:
Sabine Fuierer of Los Alamos wrote a procedures guide for reviewing and releasing records in Granta, issued 5 October 2026. Granta is a materials information database, and its records must pass review before users can rely on them. The guide covers sets of records moving through that gate.

One part covers review: the roles involved, what each role owes, and step by step procedures for checking records. General guidelines come first, so judgment calls follow shared rules. A second part covers release: putting new records live, editing records already released, and related tasks. The aim is steady quality and a clear audit trail for every record the lab publishes into the system.
doe-osti-2583338-basic-research-needs-fo:
A brochure for the June 10 to 12, 2025 ASCR workshop on inverse methods sums up a research agenda for the Department of Energy. Inverse problems run measurements backward to infer what cannot be seen directly: the inside of a fusion plasma, the structure of a nucleus, the state of the ground before a tsunami. Uncertainty in the data and in the models makes many answers plausible, which is the field's core difficulty.

Experts from laboratories and universities identified four priority research directions. The first targets structure: using the mathematical and physical patterns inside models and data to beat ill-posedness and compute faster. The others take up model limits, mixed data streams, and goal-driven solving, and are detailed in the full workshop report. The brochure frames the opportunity plainly: machine learning, AI, and exascale computing have converged just as these problems grow harder, and foundations must catch up.
doe-osti-2583339-basic-research-needs-fo:
Workshop report with DOI 10.2172/2583339, prepared for the Advanced Scientific Computing Research program, records the June 2025 meeting on inverse methods for complex systems under uncertainty. Co-chairs Jeffrey Donatelli of Berkeley Lab, John Jakeman of Sandia, and Michael Shields of Johns Hopkins led the work, with a thirteen-member organizing committee. Inverse problems, inferring hidden properties from data, sit underneath many department missions.

Four priority research directions structure the agenda. The first exploits mathematical and physical structure to tame ill-posedness. The second confronts model limitations, building solvers that correct misspecification during inversion. The third integrates data of mixed type, scale, and fidelity, including fast-moving streams that must be assimilated in time to act. The fourth solves inverse problems backward from the downstream task, adapting data collection and computing on the fly. Science drivers range from fusion and wildfire prediction to geophysical imaging and digital twins.
doe-osti-2584141-expedition-ut-gom2-2-me:
Methods volume for the UT-GOM2-2 expedition documents how the hydrate coring campaign was executed. Peter B. Flemings, Carla Thomas, and Stephen C. Phillips lead a forty-name author list. Fourteen institutions collaborated, from the University of Texas at Austin and the U.S. Geological Survey to Geotek Ltd. Such a volume earns its keep years later, when a scientist with a core sample needs to know what was done to it.

Chapters standardize the work end to end. They cover drilling and coring from the Helix Q4000, and pressure coring that keeps samples at seabed conditions. Downhole logging follows, then the shipboard and shore-based splitting, sampling, and analysis flow. Photographs show the Salt Lake City laboratory where split cores were processed. Every later result in the proceedings rests on these routines, so the volume fixes terms, file conventions, and handling chains in one place, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.13971228.
doe-osti-2584730-s-amp-tr-june-2025-r-am:
The June 2025 issue of Science and Technology Review, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory's magazine, is filed as report LLNL-TR-2005991. Holly Auten, C Meissner, Lilly Ackerman, Elliot Jaffe, and N Pflueger-Peters produced the issue, which leads with the laboratory's R&D 100 Awards. Those awards honor the year's top hundred innovations across United States research and industry.

Inside, short articles cover recent Livermore work in plain language for a general reader. Stories describe a 3D-printed electrode that improves energy storage, iron atoms forming unusual quasicrystal-like structures at alloy interfaces, and tools that shape laser pulses for National Ignition Facility experiments. A commentary by Rebecca Dylla-Spears opens the issue, and a news section reports Livermore leading a new lithography research effort.
doe-osti-3013239-assessment-of-heavy-dut:
National Renewable Energy Laboratory report NREL/TP-5400-91062, by Jamie Kee, Taichi Kuroki, Krishna Reddi of Argonne, and five co-authors, dated November 2025, assesses heavy-duty hydrogen fueling methods and components through modeling. Fast, safe fills for Class 8 trucks are a bottleneck for hydrogen freight. The team combined NREL and Argonne simulation tools to study the full fill, from station storage through the dispenser into the truck's tanks.

The models cover high-pressure buffer storage, precooling chillers, and multi-tank truck configurations, including a nine-tank semitruck simulator. Fueling protocols are compared in the analysis tables, with fill times ranging roughly from ten to nineteen minutes across the cases shown. The work supports station design and the standards that govern how trucks take on hydrogen.
doe-osti-3013240-storage-stability-of-50:
National Renewable Energy Laboratory report NREL/TP-2A00-96381, by Gina Fioroni, Jennifer Cavaleri, Nimal Naser, Richard Nelson, and Robert McCormick, dated November 2025, tests how biodiesel keeps in storage. The fuels sampled span the North American market: two petroleum diesels, seven neat B100 biodiesels, three B20 blends, and fourteen B50 blends, half biodiesel and half diesel.

Aging followed the ASTM D4625 protocol, twelve weeks at 43 degrees Celsius, standing in for about twelve months of clean, dry storage. Samples were drawn every two weeks for oxidation measures. The diesel controls showed no oxidation at all. B100 samples aged slowly; the least stable fell below a two-hour induction period, while fuels starting above six hours stayed sound. The results guide storage practice for high-blend fuels.
doe-osti-3013259-regional-energy-deploym:
National Renewable Energy Laboratory report NREL/TP-6A40-93617, dated December 2025, is the 2025 documentation for ReEDS, the Regional Energy Deployment System model. Thirty-four NREL authors are listed. ReEDS is the lab's flagship capacity expansion model: given costs, policies, and demand, it computes how the United States power system should build and run generation and transmission over coming decades.

The documentation spells out the model's structure, spatial and temporal resolution, and resource adequacy methods. Two approaches get detailed treatment: stress periods, which test the system in its hardest hours, and capacity credit, which scores each resource's dependable share. Caveats are summarized up front. Analysts across government and industry rely on this volume to run ReEDS studies and defend their assumptions.
doe-osti-3020690-assessment-of-heavy-dut:
National Laboratory of the Rockies CRADA final report NLR/TP-5700-99088, CRD-21-17844, with Shaun Onorato as technical contact, assesses how heavy-duty hydrogen trucks should be fueled. Chevron, the laboratory, Argonne, and NextEnergy partnered to evaluate fueling protocols and hardware for fuel cell trucks, building on international work. Refueling a Class 8 truck quickly and safely needs rules that stations and vehicles share.

The team tested components against the European PRHYDE protocols and the SAE J2601/5 protocol, and validated strategies at the laboratory's heavy-duty hydrogen fueling station. Techno-economic analysis with the H2FillS, HDRSAM, and T3CO tools weighed fueling time, station cost, and total cost of ownership for long-haul sleeper trucks and short-haul tractors. Findings identify where protocols and hardware need improvement before industry standardization.
doe-osti-3343523-development-of-powder-p:
Laura K. Sudderth, Joshua Nicholas Zelina, and Michael J. Moorehead of Idaho National Laboratory develop fuel powder methods in report INL/RPT-25-84412, dated April 2025. New low-enriched uranium fuel ideas rely on powder metallurgy, pressing metal powder into fuel forms. Early powder runs worked but missed the quality bar. The team built and tuned a rotating electrode system, which melts a spinning rod tip so droplets fly off and freeze as round powder grains.

Benchtop tuning chased the best yield in the 38 to 150 micrometer band. The spindle spun at 40,000 revolutions per minute, with current from 60 to 110 amps and feed speeds from 0.077 to 0.186 inches per second. The rig then moved into an argon glovebox, sharing a water-cooled power feed with a small arc furnace.
doe-osti-3364733-report-on-lightning-sim:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2026-21189R, by Logan Robinett, surveys how lightning is simulated in laboratories and what standards govern the testing. Real lightning cannot be scheduled, so aircraft and explosives are certified against reproduced strikes instead. Sandia's own Lightning Simulator recreates a severe flash waveform, but its age brings operating difficulties and inconsistent output worth comparing against other facilities.

The report reviews lightning models, including an end-to-end modeling approach that connects strike physics across scales, then walks through testing standards and the methods peer facilities use. Comparisons aim to show where Sandia's simulator can improve and where its design quietly excels. The document was prepared as a course-linked study, ECE 551, and reads as a structured literature and facilities review.
doe-osti-3365761-inter-year-variability-:
A 2026 study by Mark Boris, Leslie O'Brien, Rumy Petrova, and co-authors checks whether energy dispersive spectroscopy standards drift from year to year. Laboratories calibrate their X-ray microanalysis against reference materials of known composition; if the standards themselves vary, every measurement inherits the error. Ten standards were compared across years, from lutetium fluoride and rhodium to table salt and pure copper.

Each standard gets its own results section, with relative standard deviations tabulated per material and per spectral peak in appendices. Recommended actions include acquiring fresh standards, reacquiring the mercury telluride standard, and reviewing older data. Selection guidance closes the report. For a microscopy facility, the study answers a quiet but basic question: can last year's calibration still be trusted this year?
doe-osti-3409217-electricity-rate-design:
Berkeley Lab technical brief, dated August 2026, updates how utilities charge very large power users such as data centers. Natalie Mims Frick and Peter Cappers of Berkeley Lab wrote with Goksin Kavlak, Long Lam, Ryan Hledik, and others from The Brattle Group. Demand from large loads is set to grow fast.

Rate tools covered include demand response, interruptible rates, and forced cuts in grid emergencies. Some tariffs pay large users for flexible load. Others give utilities access to on-site generation. States and utilities can compare these tools as they race to connect big loads without harming reliability or shifting costs unfairly.
farm-ballads:
Carleton's Farm Ballads gathers Will Carleton's dialect poems of farm life. The record dates this copy to 1882. Betsey and I Are Out opens the ballads, followed by how the couple made up. Gone with a Handsomer Man and Johnny Rich come next.

Over the Hill to the Poor-House is the best known piece here. Its answer, Over the Hill from the Poor-House, follows at once. Uncle Sammy and Tom was Goin' for a Poet add humor. Other poems include The New Church Organ and Our Army of the Dead. Illustrations quote famous lines, such as the lawyer drawing up papers. Carleton writes rural quarrels, partings, and returns in plain speech. The ballads made his name across America.
five-little-friends:
Adams writes for the smallest readers in Five Little Friends. Sherred Willcox Adams follows Bob and Betty, Paul and Peggy, and little Dot, at school and in vacation. Maud and Miska Petersham drew the pictures. The five go to the same school, where Miss West is their teacher, and the book says more than once that these five are the ones the story is about.

The sampled pages move to the farm. The girls set pans round a maple tree and play at dairy work. Mary and Betty make the cream rise, and Dot and Peggy skim it into bottles and old cans to sell. Molly the cook lends them her skimmers, since the dirt is clean dirt. Red Chief, the proudest rooster in the yard, stalks up to ask if it is feeding time. The book's world is safe, sunny, and sized for a child.
five-little-peppers-and-their-friends:
Five Little Peppers and Their Friends, by Margaret Sidney, answers the demand her preface describes. So many friends of the Peppers, she writes, were only faint outlines in the earlier books. Readers demanded a volume for the outer circle. The happenings came to her from the Pepper children themselves. Even Phronsie whispered some of it to her, begging for Rachel's story to be told.

Sidney dedicates the book to her daughter Margaret, who embodied Polly Pepper to her friends. Eugenie Wireman illustrated it. The little brown house's circle widens ever, in the preface's phrase. Stories left untold while the five grew up are filled in here. Sidney's series ran for decades on this loyalty. The friends' book is its annuity volume, written because the audience refused to let the family go. Hand in hand, the circle widens ever.
frank-roscoe-s-secret-or-the-darewell-ch:
Chapman's Darewell Chums plan a dinner in the opening chapter, and a conspiracy is revealed at once. Ned is captured and hears strange talk, while Frank gets a letter and is warned. The chums' vacation takes them into the woods and toward a sanitarium.

Hiding behind a tree, Frank watches a sad little procession of patients pass, guarded by attendants in dark blue. One face at the line's end makes him cry out and step into view before he knows what he is doing. Allen Chapman published Frank Roscoe's Secret in 1908. The secret itself is held back until the rescue is planned.
gold-of-the-gods: Arthur B. Reeve's Craig Kennedy mystery opens with the theft of an ancient Peruvian dagger from a museum's South American section. Professor Allan Norton, a South American explorer, calls on Kennedy, whose laboratory science traces paper fibres, shoe-prints, poison and X-ray clues. Curses, Wall Street promoters and treasure hunters thicken a case that turns on a relic called the gold of the gods.
golden-lads:
Arthur Gleason and Helen Hayes Gleason wrote Golden Lads in 1916, with an introduction by Theodore Roosevelt. Its title quotes the old song: golden lads and girls all must, as chimney sweepers, come to dust. A front picture shows the French Fusiliers Marins, sailor boys of Brittany called the demoiselles with the red pompon for their youth and their cap tassels. The Gleasons had reported from the war zone.

The book honors the very young soldiers and sailors of France and Britain on the Western Front. It tells of boys who left school and farm for the trenches, and of the grace with which they bore mud, wounds, and death. The tone is tender and patriotic, of its wartime moment. It stands as a record of how the first years of the Great War were mourned and praised in print.
govdocs-archive_org-OperationNorthwoods:
An encyclopedia article on Operation Northwoods, captured from Wikipedia, sums up the 1962 plan by senior Defense Department leaders. The Joint Chiefs, under Chairman Lyman Lemnitzer, proposed staged attacks that could be blamed on Cuba. President Kennedy rejected the plan, and Lemnitzer was soon moved from his post.

The article lays out the proposed incidents, the paper trail of memos, and the plan's release to the public decades later through declassification. As a reference capture it gives the accepted outline in one place, with the sources a summary can offer. It serves readers who want the shape of the episode before turning to the declassified documents themselves, which the archive also holds.
govdocs-archive_org-northwoods:
Operation Northwoods was a set of proposals drawn up at the Pentagon in 1962, at the height of the Cold War with Cuba. Senior American officers proposed staging incidents that could be blamed on Fidel Castro's government, to justify a war against it.

The declassified papers lay out the suggested deceptions in official language, a record that stayed secret for decades before its release. The plans were never carried out, and the civilian leadership rejected the approach. The file endures as one of the most cited declassified documents in American history, proof on paper of what was once proposed.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia_Court_Reject: A federal court rejected the National Security Archive's lawsuit over Donald Trump's handling of the records law. A briefing book page carries that defeat under a telling headline. The headline names both the ruling and the claim: that the president abused the Presidential Records Act. The Archive had argued that destroyed and removed records broke the law governing a president's papers. Only the page capture is preserved in this entry's evidence, marking one courtroom round in the fight over who controls a president's record, the president or the public.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia_National_Pub: Donald Rumsfeld ran the Pentagon with short typed memos his staff called snowflakes, thousands of them, and after his death those memos became a key to his management and his wars. National Public Radio featured the Archive's Nate Jones discussing that legacy, and an Archive news post notes the broadcast. Jones has worked the Rumsfeld record for years through the Archive's requests and postings. The item here is the announcement, not the interview, marking a radio audience hearing an archivist explain a defense secretary through his paper blizzard.
grammar-and-vocabulary-of-the-lau-langua:
Grammar and Vocabulary of the Lau Language, by Walter G Ivens, describes the speech of the artificial islets off the northeast coast of Big Malaita in the Solomon Islands. Ivens published the work through the Carnegie Institution of Washington as its Publication 300. His preface maps the language carefully: Lau runs along the coast from Uru to Langalanga lagoon, with the purest form spoken at Sulufou, one of the built up islets near Atta Cove.

Inside, a grammar sets out the language's sounds, words, and sentence patterns, and a vocabulary gives Lau words with English meanings. Ivens notes where the neighboring Fiu language mixes in, and where earlier word lists, such as Codrington's, probably recorded Fiu by mistake. Two villages on Little Malaita also speak Lau, carried there, tradition says, by migrants from near Atta Cove. The book preserves a lagoon people's language in scholarly form.
guns-of-the-gods:
Talbot Mundy published Guns of the Gods in 1921, subtitled A Story of Yasmini's Youth. Yasmini, a dancing girl of mystery in his tales of India, here stands at the center while she is still young. Her voice opens the contents: set down my thoughts, not yours, if the tale is to be worth the pesa. The chapters turn on the Maharajah Gungadhura, whose throne and treasure draw plots from every side.

British officers, loyal sepoys, and palace intriguers move around the girl whom all sides want to use. Gold is where you find it, says one chapter head; duty is what I am paid to do, says another. Mundy mixes treasure hunt, mutiny talk, and Eastern romance at a gallop. The book is a prime sample of his Indian adventure tales, in which Yasmini outwits every man in the story.
history-of-the-philippine-islands:
Antonio de Morga's History of the Philippine Islands covers the islands from their discovery by Magellan in 1521 to the beginning of the seventeenth century. Morga, alcalde of criminal causes in the Royal Audiencia of New Spain, wrote his Sucesos de las Islas Filipinas in Mexico in 1609.
